R133 fixed three bands — `net ≥ +2`, `−2 < net < +2`, `net ≤ −2` — and gave the reason in the registration:

> The bands are ±2 because the discordant count is ~8: a difference of two cases is the smallest one this sample
> can distinguish, and stating the band in advance is what keeps the readback from becoming a story.

That justification is a **claim about the control's discordant count**, made before the control ran, from R132's
raw reading of 8 discordant pairs (5 repaired, 3 broken) against the learn draw. The control produced **16** —
twice the estimate, because a fresh draw disagrees with the treatment on both sides rather than only on the
failures. The measured net is therefore

> +2 of 74 = +2.70pp, SE = √(16 − 4/74)/74 = **5.40pp**, 95% **[−7.88, +13.28]**

and the smallest difference this sample distinguishes is **±4 tasks**, not ±2. `+2` landed exactly on the
`net ≥ +2` boundary — the row fired, on a band the measurement says does not exist.

**Both halves of that are recorded, and neither is edited.** The row fired: the readback says so, and R134 is a
conditioning arm on that ground. The justification is refuted: the readback says that too, in the same table.
What the lane may not do is quietly re-cut the bands to ±4 after seeing the number, which would make the
registration a post-hoc summary of the data rather than a constraint on it.

**The rule.** A band's justification is itself a measurement to be checked on readback. When a registration says
"the bands are ±2 because the count is ~8", the readback must report the count it got and whether the band it
used is the band its own arithmetic supports; when they disagree, the row fires *and* the disagreement is filed.
A decision rule stated in advance buys the freedom to decide without a story; it does not buy immunity from
having its premises measured.

**What this does not license.** Reading `+2` as evidence *for* conditioning. The row's premise — "the store is
right on its own cases and misapplied elsewhere" — is what the interval refutes: +2.70pp with a lower bound of
−7.88pp is not "right on its own cases". R134 is therefore registered as conditioning executed on the **pack's
composition** rather than on the threshold, and its registration carries the argument: at a 55.00% repair rate
among the failures and a 13.0% damage rate among the passes, a gate tuned until it stops breaking the seven also
stops repairing most of the eleven.

## 34.168 One word, two denominators

R133's first readback printed this sentence:

> `11 repaired / 9 inert of the 20 that failed without memory (55.00%); 7 broken and 47 kept of the rest; harm
> share 38.89%; against a no-memory replay: 9 repaired / 7 broken = +2 net of 74 task(s) (2.70%), harm share
> 43.75%`

Two `repaired` counts, eleven and nine, in one sentence, both correct. They are the same cell measured against
two different without-sides: the learn half's own run — the draw that *selected* the store's cases — and a fresh
no-memory draw of the same 74 tasks. The sentence named neither. A reader who checks the arithmetic finds
11 + 9 = 20 and 9 + 7 = 16, two partitions of the same 74 tasks that do not agree, and no way to recover which
clause was which after the fact.

This is AUDIT 34.164's family one layer down. There the denominator was also the selector; here the *word* is
the selector — the same noun counting two populations — and the ambiguity is in the prose rather than in the
statistic. The four cells are right; the sentence that reports them was not.

**The fix, and why it is a code change rather than a wording change.** `rehearsalLine` now says which population
each clause divides by: "the 20 **the learn half itself failed**" and "of the 54 **it passed**" for the raw
reading, "against **a fresh no-memory draw of the same task(s)**" for the control. The control clause's three
absences say the same thing, so an arm that bought no control cannot be read as one that bought a control and
found nothing. The test pins the property rather than the sentence: a fixture whose two draws disagree 2-to-1
asserts that each count follows its own named reference, and that the two references appear in the order the
counts do.

**The rule.** A reading with more than one without-side names every one of them, in the sentence, at the point
of use. "Repaired" is not a quantity; "repaired against the draw that selected the store" is, and the two
differ by two tasks out of seventy-four in this arm — which is the size of the effect the whole round was
trying to measure.

## 34.169 The instrument measured the answer and threw it away

`_census_of` has returned `system_chars` and `conversation_chars` for every call since the cache census
was written. `_record_usage` sums them into `_cache`. `cache_census()` reads `seen_chars`, `last_chars`,
`prompt_tokens` and `cached_tokens` — and never reads the two that separate a pack from a conversation.
The module's own comment says the point is to know "whether those tokens were the pack, the conversation
in front of it, or the observation appended behind it", and the field that would answer it was discarded
on every arm for the whole life of the census.

The cost of that is a wrong published mechanism. R133's AUDIT 34.166 said:

> The mechanism is not the items' length — it is that a four-item pack **replaces the prompt prefix on
> every call**, so 2.5M tokens arrive uncached instead of 0.59M.

R134 tested it the only way a mechanism can be tested — by moving the thing the mechanism names. The pack
went from 4 items and 2,239 characters to 1 item and 747 characters; nothing else changed. The multiple
went from **2.43× to 2.25×**. A mechanism whose cause is removed by two thirds and whose effect moves by
seven per cent is not the mechanism. And the number that would have refused the claim on day one is a
number the instrument already had: `system_chars`.

**The rule.** An instrument that computes a quantity and does not report it is an instrument that has
published a story instead of a measurement. This is the fourth time in four rounds that the defect is not
a missing measurement but an unused one — R127's one-sided ladder, R131's unjoined arrays, R132's
selector-as-denominator, and now this. The check to add is mechanical: every key `_census_of` returns must
be read by `cache_census()` or be deleted from `_census_of`, and the Python self-check now asserts the
split's arithmetic rather than the counter's existence.

**What is still not known, and is now measurable.** Where the +1,218.7 uncached tokens a call actually go.
Three candidates, three fields: `system_tokens_per_call` (the pack and the preamble),
`conversation_tokens_per_call` (the agent's own turns), `residual_tokens_per_call` (the tools block and the
chat template, which no message carries). R135 buys all three on an arm whose treatment does not move.

## 34.170 A share above 100% is not a cache that held extra

Both of R134's arms printed this sentence:

> `cache first (reference): prefix-honoured — the provider credited 226.4% of the 1880-token prefix it had
> seen, and the newest message was 163 tokens: the 420 uncached tokens a call are the turn's own material,
> not the memory's`

and the same shape at **147.5%** for the memory arm. `prefix_coverage` is `cached / seen`, `seen` stops two
messages short of the end by construction, and the provider routinely credits the newest of those excluded
messages as well. So the ratio is a quotient by a **lower bound**, and it lands above 1 on arms whose
prefix is held perfectly well.

The classifier read `coverage >= 0.85` as `prefix-honoured`, which is true of 2.26 in the same sense that
"at least one" is true of "one thousand" — and then drew a causal conclusion from it. 226.4% of what a
provider was shown is not a provider being generous; it is the lane dividing by a number it knows is too
small, and then attributing the remainder.

**Both halves of the fix are arithmetic.** The state is `prefix-undercounted` above 1.02, `repair` is
`unmeasured`, and the sentence says the denominator is the defect — because nothing downstream *can* be
attributed from a share above 1, and a verdict that names a repair anyway is a verdict that will be acted
on. The attribution clause ("and the two newest messages account for all of them") is now printed only
when `residual_tokens_per_call` says they do, which is a measurement rather than an inference.

**What this does not retroactively fix.** Every arm whose log carries a `cache first` / `cache second`
sentence was produced by this classifier, and a scan of the two artefacts that carry a per-call census
finds exactly two records above 1.02 — both R134's (2.2639 and 1.4752), so the sentences that need this
entry beside them are R133's replay and R134's pair. They stand as recorded: the numbers in them (2.5M
uncached against 0.59M; 1,639 against 420 a call) are measurements and survive; the sentence attached to
them does not. R123a is outside the class — its premium came from `premiumSplitOf`, which divides the
served characters rather than a cache coverage, and is unaffected. A reading's numbers and a reading's
story fail separately, and only one of them is repairable after the fact.

## 34.171 A caveat that outlives its arm is a caveat that misleads

`itemLedgerLine` closed with:

> Deleting the negative ones recovers at most +N case(s) if each item's cases are its own, and a pack that
> serves four guarantees they are not: this is an upper bound on a deletion arm, not a prediction of one

The bound is real: when a request is served four ids, one break is counted against all four, so `Σ|net|`
over the negative items cannot be recovered by deleting them. But the sentence asserts the pack's shape
rather than reading it, and R134's arm serves **one** item a request — 40 item-requests, 40 packs, no
sharing at all. On that arm every case an item carries *is* its own, `Σ|net|` is the exact number a
deletion recovers, and the tool was printing "this is an upper bound, not a prediction" over an exact
measurement.

A reader who trusts the caveat discounts a figure that needs no discount, and — worse — the discount is in
the direction that makes a deletion arm look unpromising, which is the arm the literature's largest
published effect belongs to.

**The rule.** A qualifier is a claim about the data and gets the same treatment as any other claim: it is
derived from the run, or it is not printed. `itemLedgerLine` now takes the number of served requests that
carried more than one id, and says either "no served request carried a second item, so the sum is exact,
not a bound" or "N served request(s) carried more than one item, so their cases are shared: this is an
upper bound on a deletion arm, not a prediction of one". Both halves are produced by a committed test.

**Why this one mattered enough to file.** It is the third defect in three rounds of the same shape —
R133's two `repaired` counts under one word (34.168), the verdict's 226.4% (34.170), and now a caveat that
describes an arm nobody ran. In each case the arithmetic was right and the sentence around it was not, and
in each case the sentence is what a reader takes away.

## 34.172 A residual of a residual is not an attribution

`residual_tokens_per_call` shipped in R135 defined as `uncached − last − tail2`, documented as "material no
message carries — the tools block and the chat template's framing". On R135's own two arms it reported
**1409.7** for the memory arm against **179.5** for the reference — 99.7% of a premium of 1,234 tokens a
call.

The premium is not that. Measured against the prompt column, the same arms give: prompt **+675.7**
(system **+559.3**, conversation **+26.7**, tools **+5.5**, framing **+0.5**) and cached **−558.3**. The
"residual" was not isolating a quantity at all: `uncached` is `prompt − cached`, so subtracting two message
sizes from it leaves *both* the prompt growth *and* the cache loss in one number, and one number cannot say
which. Whenever two arms cache differently — which is the case the field existed for — the residual
inherits the entire premium by construction.

**Why it survived the design.** The field was written in the same hour as the guard above it (34.170), and
its name carried the argument: a "residual" sounds like what is left when reasoning is finished. It was
what is left when *arithmetic* is finished, which is a different thing. The verdict then printed a
conclusion from it on the arms that read below 1.02, and the composition — four columns that add to the
prompt — was available the whole time.

**The fix, and the rule it restates.** The residual is measured against the **prompt** (messages and tool
schemas subtracted), so it is the chat template's framing and nothing else: 84.2 tokens a call on the
memory arm against 83.7 on the reference, a difference of half a token. `prompt_tokens_per_call` gives the
four columns a denominator. The verdict now prints the composition and draws no conclusion from it, because
the arithmetic of a premium is a subtraction and a sentence that performs it in prose has to get the same
answer as the numbers — R135's sentence did not.

**The self-check assertion that would have caught it.** A fixture whose prompt is exactly its messages has
a framing residual of **0.0**; under the old definition the same fixture reported 116.7 of "material no
message carries". The test asserts the zero.

## 34.173 Forty episodes, forty-one boundaries, and the row that no task names

R135's memory arm opened **41** episodes and served **41** packs; the scorer holds **40** task rows, and
`per_task` has 40. The arm's own `queries.distinct` is **41** with 41 distinct texts, and
`memory.recallRepeats` is **0** — so this is not a turn that failed to grow, it is a **task simulated
twice**: τ²'s retry path constructs a fresh agent, the agent recalls on its first turn, and unless the
first attempt's episode is removed the pack ledger keeps a row the scorer never names.

Nothing silently mis-joined: `l4-pair` printed `serve split: not measured (boundary-disagrees) — 41
boundar(ies) against 40 trial row(s)`, and `itemLedgerOf` refuses a ledger whose row count disagrees with
the task list. That refusal is the record working as designed — it is the reason R135 has no per-item net
instead of a wrong one. What is missing is the *diagnosis*: the guard says the two arrays disagree, and no
reading says which task was run twice, so the run cannot be repaired without reading the log.

**Why this is a defect and not a nuisance.** Every positional join downstream — `pack.ledger[i]` against
`per_task[i]`, `perRequest[i]` against both, `turnCensus.rows[i].task` against `per_task[i].id` — assumes
one row per episode. A retry breaks all three at once and breaks them *after* the retried episode, so the
counts still look right (41 vs 40 is one row) while every row past the retry names a different case. R132's
readback was one such join, and it was right only because that arm had no retry.

**The fix.** The boundary records the task it opened for, from the query text the agent already holds, so
the ledger can be joined by identity and a retried task's second boundary is visible as a second boundary
of a known task. Until then, the guard is the reading: a mismatched pair is refused rather than paired, and
a refused pair is a dispatch that bought an instrument rather than a measurement — which is what R135 was,
and it said so before its numbers were read.

## 34.174 A dispatch into the peak window, and a guard that cost nothing to obey

**What happened.** R136 was dispatched at **08:02 UTC** into the 06:00–10:00 band, where the same tokens
bill at exactly twice the off-peak rate. Both arms exited in under two seconds with
`tau2-peak-window: dispatched at Tue 08:02 UTC, where the same tokens cost exactly twice the off-peak rate;
the window closes at Tue 10:00 UTC`, and the pairing and every readback step after them failed on missing
artefacts.

**Why it is a defect and not an accident.** The guard is `--require-off-peak` in `run_split.py`, and the
workflow carries a `not_before` input that makes a dispatch wait for the band instead of being re-sent —
written precisely because "dispatch inside the window" is a rule an operator has to remember at the hour
they are least likely to (R78 paid 1.90× what R79 paid for 96% of the same calls, nine minutes of clock
apart). The dispatch that failed here used neither: the input was left empty, so the job started at once
and the driver refused.

**What it cost.** Nothing, and that is the point of the guard existing at the driver rather than at the
dispatch: a refusal before the first model call is a red job and a printed sentence, not a half-priced run
that then has to be discounted. The bill for `44043271824` is **$0.00**; the re-dispatch names
`not_before: 10:00` and waits 114 minutes instead.

**The rule this adds to the record.** A dispatch is read off its own log before its numbers are trusted —
the same discipline as a gate: a job that failed in two seconds did not measure anything, and treating its
absence as "the arm did not move" would be the tenth occasion this lane read a missing measurement as a
result.

## 34.175 The wrapper, the fixture and the forty-five rounds

**What was wrong.** `MicrogliaAgent.generate_next_message` copied `LLMAgentState` and appended the recalled
block to `state.system_messages`. The copy was written to protect the caller's state and the comment above it
claims the copy is what prevents accumulation. It is the opposite: τ² threads the **returned** state into the
next turn, so the copy is exactly the object the next turn appends to, and an episode of ten turns carried ten
copies of the same block.

**How long it was wrong.** From the commit that introduced the injection, which is R92's arm, to R136 — every
memory arm this record has run. The block's cost was billed on every turn, the model was told up to ten times
per episode which data to act on, and the block sat at the front of the prompt, so each new copy ended the
provider's cached prefix and the whole conversation behind it was re-billed.

**Why no test caught it.** `episode_step`, the fixture every agent case shares, called the agent with one
state object and **discarded the returned state**, then appended the turn's messages to the object it had
kept. So the agent's copy was never handed back, the accumulated list was never re-read, and
`the_pack_does_not_accumulate` — a case that exists for exactly this defect and names it in its own comment —
asserted `[1,1,1,1,1]` against a fixture that could not produce anything else. The test was not weak; it was
testing a caller that does not exist.

**How it was found.** Not by a test and not by a score. R136's census reported `system_chars_per_packed_call`
of 11,105.9 against an injected message of 705.1, and the arithmetic of one known population closed it: the
control arm's `system_chars_per_call` solves the policy prompt at ~6,600 characters, so 11,105.9 − 6,614 −
705.1 = 3,787 characters are 5.4 copies of the block, which is the mean of 1..10 on an episode of ~10 calls.
**An instrument built to name a remainder named a defect instead.**

**The correction to the record.** R102.0 measured the block at *"1,497 prompt tokens a call and 31 uncached
ones"* and concluded that a cached block cannot be the cache a memory destroys. 1,497 tokens is ~7,300
characters at the corpus's own ratio: ten copies of a 725-character pack, cached because they are all at the
front of the prompt. The conclusion is true of a different object than the one it named. R135's "559-token
system growth" is the same quantity seen through a mean that mixed the agent's calls with the simulator's.

**What is amended, and what is not.** No published score is retracted: every arm's rate is what that arm
scored. What is amended is the **attribution** — no memory effect measured between R92 and R136 is separable
from the duplication, and every memory-side cost figure in that window is an upper bound. The mask-and-
relative docket of 34.168, R99's "supply is an anti-constraint" and R134/R135's bracket around zero all stand
as readings of the arms that produced them; they no longer stand as readings of *the memory alone*.

**Three rules this adds.**

1. **A fixture that models a foreign contract must model the inconvenient half.** A test double that
   normalises away the part of the caller's behaviour the implementation depends on certifies the
   implementation against itself.
2. **A remainder is not an attribution until its contents are counted.** 17.142's carriage was a correct
   subtraction and an empty noun; the copy count is what filled it, and the field should have come first.
3. **An instrument that reports a number the registration did not anticipate is worth more than the arm that
   was dispatched for it.** R136 was registered as an instrument arm with a negative control, and its one
   useful output was neither the rate nor the carriage it predicted.

## 34.176 A prediction table read back, including the one that was wrong

R137 registered its criteria before the dispatch. Reading them back is the whole point of having registered
them, and one prediction missed in a way that matters.

| prediction | reading | verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `pack_copies_per_packed_call == 1.00` | 1.00 | hit |
| `packed_calls_with_copies == 0` | 0 of 428 | hit |
| `system_chars_per_packed_call ≈ 7,320` | 7,793.9 | **missed high by 6.5%** |
| `uncached_tokens_per_call` toward 500 | 431.5 | hit, and below the mark |
| `cached_tokens_per_call` above 4,232.7 | 4,435.5 | hit |
| cost below 1.5× the control | 1.08× ($0.0996 against ≈$0.0923) | hit |
| the score's direction | +7.50pp [−5.00, +20.00] | direction hit, not resolvable |

**The miss is the useful line.** 7,320 was built from an estimate of the policy prompt at ~6,600 characters,
solved from the control arm's `system_chars_per_call` on R136's corpus under an assumption: that the control's
450 agent calls and 213 simulator calls were the same split as the memory arm's. 17.143 printed that estimate
as a *range* (6,614 – 7,062) and then used its lower end in the forecast, which is the arithmetic version of
rounding towards the answer one expects. The measured carriage, 7,056 characters, sits at the top of the range
the same entry printed. **A range used as a point is a point.**

**What may not be read from this round.** The score improved by 12.5pp against R136's pair, and none of it is
attributable to the fix: the two runs drew different stores (69 servable items against 66) and different
numbers of abandoned attempts (two against one). What the fix owns is the carriage, the copy count, the cache
and the bill — each moved 30–72% in the direction its mechanism predicts. The score moved inside a sample
whose minimum detectable difference is 18.53pp, and is reported as a reading of *this* arm rather than as an
effect of that change.

**The lesson, which is the third time this section has written it.** An instrument bought to size a remainder
found a defect (34.175); the repair's readback found that the remainder was the policy prompt and the defect
was the whole premium. Neither result was the one the arm was dispatched for, and both were only visible
because the registration fixed the *instrument's* criteria before the *treatment's* number.

## 34.177 R129 refused on evidence, and the entry that had to be corrected twice

**First the correction.** PROGRESS 223 said the refused serve split "costs every per-item reading"; the same
entry was amended within the hour to say it costs only the gate comparison, because `pairAttribution` returned
its trial-level 5-and-2 while the split refused. That amendment was also wrong: `item-ledger` refuses
separately, on `42 request(s)` against `40 episode(s)`, so the per-item census *was* suppressed. The entry now
names all three — trial transfer computes, gate comparison lost, item census lost — and the sequence is
recorded rather than tidied, because two wrong statements about one refusal is what "read it before publishing"
is for.

**Then the refusal.** R129 registered "an item whose outcomes are net-negative is quarantined rather than
served". The mechanism can now be priced without a dispatch, because R137's artefact carries the ledger and the
trial table:

- 19 distinct items across 40 requests, one item a request.
- **2 negative, −1 each**; **4 positive, +5 together**; 45 never served.
- Deleting the negatives recovers **at most +2 cases**, and the sum is exact.
- The two negatives are the two broken trials: one served **once**, one served **ten times with eight passes**.

A deletion rule therefore either deletes an item on a single failed case or trades eight passes for two
failures. A support threshold protects against the second and can never judge the first, which is the one that
broke a trial. **The counter is not the missing piece; recurrence is.**

**Why this is a refusal and not a deferral.** A deferral says "later, with more data". This says the
configuration cannot produce the data: with 19 items over 40 requests and 45 never served, no item accumulates
a sample, and the same cardinality was measured from the store's own labels two rounds ago (41 labels over 57
items, `sup2` 2 of 66). Writing the field first and coarsening later would have bought a schema that records
one case per item and a quarantine that deletes on it.

**The rule this adds.** *Price a deletion rule against the artefact that would feed it, before writing the
field it reads.* `item-ledger` exists for that reason and had never been pointed at an arm whose treatment was
sound; pointing it at one took ten minutes and refused a four-round-old registration without a model call.

### 34.178 The key that was read as a finding: fifteen rounds of `sup2` measurements were measurements of a filter

**The finding.** From R124 to R138 every statement this record made about corroboration — `sup2` 2 of 66,
"nothing is corroborated by two tasks", "the store writes a distinct statement per correction" — was read off
a pass whose linkage key removed **34 of the 35 duplicate pairs** before the similarity test ran. The numbers
were true and the sentences were wrong: the store knew 43 distinct claims over 64 statements, one claim
repeated nine times, and the pass merged one.

**Why no instrument caught it.** Three instruments existed and each answered a different question:

| instrument | what it counts | why it stayed silent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `skippedScope` | pairs removed by the key | it counts *all* of them, including pairs with no overlap, so a large number read as "the store is 64 unrelated claims" |
| `redundancy` (R120) | distinct claims over the whole store, **keyless** | it was in the same artefact as `merged`, and nobody subtracted the two |
| `merge.support` (R120) | routines taught by ≥2 corrections | it describes the *corrections*, not the items, so its `atLeastTwo 12` looked like a different subject rather than a contradiction |

The missing field was the intersection: pairs the key removed **after** every other test admitted them. R139
adds it as `skippedKey` and prints it on the operating line ahead of the population verdict, because the
sentence a reader needs is not "how many pairs did the key remove" but "did the key remove any pair that would
otherwise have merged".

**The correction this makes to R138.** R138's decision rule said the next dollar goes at the *category* — cut
the item so 57 corrections become ≤12 kinds. The premise was that the store cannot corroborate because its
unit is too fine. R139 shows the unit was never given a chance: the same store already contains 43 claims, and
a pass that compared every pair would have merged a third of it. The category may still be worth cutting, but
it is no longer the precondition for R129's counter, and R138's rule is superseded rather than extended.

**Two errors of this round, both mine, both caught by existing tests.**

1. **The split `continue`d before the merge.** The first version of the redundancy key split counted a pair
   and then skipped the union-find step for any pair with a key on one side only. Four pre-existing cases in
   `store-redundancy.test.ts` went red — the census reported three distinct claims over three statements while
   its own `joined` said one — which is precisely the class of defect the census exists to prevent, committed
   inside the census. The fix moves the split into the loop body; the case is now a test.
2. **A registration that quoted the wrong denominator.** R139's first draft said "1,953 live pairs, 35 above
   the floor" — `C(63,2)` over the sample's active items — while the pass considered **70** items and tested
   **2,415**. The registration now cites the pass's denominator and the census's sample separately, and the
   prediction is stated against the population the arm will actually run on.

**The rule this adds.** *A filter and a measurement are different instruments, and a field named after the
filter is not a measurement of it.* `skippedScope` counted what the key did; nothing counted what the key
cost. When a mechanism is introduced to make something affordable, the round that introduces it owes the
rounds after it a counter for what it removed — and the counter has to be positioned **after** the other
tests, or it reports the mechanism's activity instead of its price.

### 34.179 A conservative join that refuses is not free: it cost two readings in three rounds

**The pattern.** R136's ledger join refused a 42-versus-40 pair and suppressed the per-item census on the one
arm whose carriage was clean (R138). R138's serve split refused the same pair and suppressed the gate
comparison. Both refusals were *correct* about the defect and wrong about the cost: the arms' treatments were
sound, the instruments were not, and each round lost a reading it had already paid for.

**Why the refusals were written that way, and why that reasoning expired.** A join that guesses is worse than a
join that refuses — R135 spent a whole course on positional joins that paired one episode's requests with
another's outcome. But "refuse rather than guess" is only right while there is no *third* option. Here there
was: the boundary already carries the identity of the attempt it opened, and the only ambiguity left is
*absent* versus *wrong*, which are distinguishable at the point of reading (§TECH-DESIGN 17.147).

**The audit finding.** An instrument that refuses must state what it refuses **and** what the refusal costs,
and every refusal has to be re-read in the round after it fires. Three of this record's refusals (R135's join,
R138's ledger, R138's split) were each written when the alternative was a guess; one of them (R140) had a
correct refusal replaced by a correct drop, and the other two are now the same question: *is the ambiguity the
refusal names actually irreducible?*

**What is still refused, and why.** A boundary naming a task the arm never scored. That case has no third
option: the name is evidence of a mislabelled artefact, and excluding its requests would hide the break behind
a smaller denominator. The rule that separates the two is not "be lenient" — it is whether the missing
information can be recovered from the artefact. Null is recoverable (an attempt that died is an attempt);
a wrong name is not.

### 34.180 A floor that removes the harm and the gain in equal measure is not a result yet

**The reading.** R139's arm served 21 distinct items over 40 requests. Nineteen of them had **one task** behind
them; the two that were corroborated carried `+1` and `0` between them:

| support at serve time | items served | broken | kept | net |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 19 | **5** | **5** | **0** |
| 2 | 2 | 0 | 1 | **+1** |

Every net-negative item was a singleton — and so were three of the four net-positive ones. A floor at 2 removes
five broken trials and five kept ones from this arm: it is a *composition* change, not an improvement, and a round that reported only the
harm it removed would be reporting half of its own table.

**Why that is still worth a dispatch.** Because the alternative is a counter with no population. R129's
outcome-based quarantine was refused in R138 for want of recurrence: an item served once cannot be quarantined
on one observation. A floor at 2 changes the denominator by construction — eleven items over forty requests is
3.6 serves each — so the *next* round's quarantine has something to count. The claim this round can support is
therefore about identifiability, and the registration says so before the number exists.

**What would falsify it.** `broke` not falling while `retained` is in band. Then corroboration is not what
separates the harmful items from the helpful ones, the three −1s were three singletons by coincidence, and the
axis for the following round is what the served claim *says* rather than how many tasks agreed with it. That is
the same shape of correction R137 forced on the carriage hypothesis, and it is cheaper to make on a $0.20 arm
than on a 114-task one.

**The instrument this round adds, and the pattern behind it.** `supportFloor {total, retired, retained, floor}`
travels in the learning block and in the diagnostics of a refusal. The pattern is now three rounds old in this
record: a mechanism whose population is not in the artefact gets read as a mechanism that did not work
(R121's merge, R137's carriage, and — the earlier one — R42's empty store). The floor's own retired count is
what makes "44 of 55 retired, 11 servable" a reading rather than a guess about why the pack got shorter.

### 34.181 The floor removed the harm and kept the gain, and the unit of one prediction was wrong

**The reading, and the one table it changes.** R141's arm retired 50 of 83 items for want of a second task and
served 41 renders from the 14 that survived. Against its own control it scored **0.925 against 0.825** —
`+10.00pp [0.00, +22.50]`, p = 0.2187, **5 repaired and 1 broken** — where R139's floorless arm, on a store
with the same pass, had repaired 6 and broken 5. The harm share fell from **15.63% to 3.03%** of the control's
passes. The registration had predicted the opposite sign on the mean ("flat and may be worse") and the
prediction that fails is the informative one: the floor was supposed to trade harm for gain one-for-one
(`−3` removed against `+4` removed) and instead removed the harm and left the gain.

**What the prediction that failed by unit cost.** `serveSplit.served` "falls from 33 of 40 to at most 13" is a
sentence comparing a *request* rate to an *item* count. The split counts requests — 37 of 40 were served — and
the population that fell to 13 was the served *records*, 14. Both numbers are in the artefact; the prediction
put one in the other's column. The previous round's readback made the same slip in the opposite direction
(reading 43-of-64 unserved as a rate over items when the census counts statements), so this is now the second
occurrence of one defect: **a prediction written in a unit the artefact does not print is unfalsifiable in
practice and looks falsified in the readback.** R142 states its own quantities by the field that will carry them.

**The two counts that were out of band are one fact.** `retired` 50 against a 40–46 band and `retained` 14
against 9–13 are the same observation: the pass merged 19 items where R139 merged 15, so the population the
floor acted on was larger and less corroborated than the band forecast from R139's ratios. A band built from one
arm's ratios carries that arm's merge rate, and the merge rate is content. The registration's own margin was
four items wide on an axis whose round-to-round movement is five.

**No refutation condition fired, and that is the weaker of the two statements available.** The rules were
`retired < 30`, `retained ≥ 20`, a served singleton, and `broke` flat while `retained` is in band. None fired.
The hypothesis survives at n = 40, which is a statement about a sample that can resolve 17pp; the harm-share
difference the round actually produced is Fisher's p = 0.10 on 33 and 32 trials. A surviving hypothesis is not
a supported claim, and this entry does not write it as one.

**The instrument that did not fire, and the audit's own timing.** `serve support` — the join the round's
criterion is written in — is absent from the log because it was committed twenty minutes after the head the
workflow checked out. So the round's criterion ("no served item carries support below the floor") was answered
from a *different* line: the pack's `support ≥2 41, ≥3 9, max 3`, which says every render carried an item two or
more tasks taught. That is the same fact read from the pack rather than from the join, and it is worth recording
that a round can pass its criterion without its instrument firing — the criterion is about the pack, and the
instrument is about the reconciliation between the pack and the store sample. The reconciliation is what R142
buys.

**What the round hands forward, as arithmetic rather than as a hope.** The next arm is the same treatment on the
lane's 0.5 cut of all 114 tasks — 57 learn, 57 held out — because the two ways this reading is wrong are that
the 40 tasks the benchmark chose are a lucky sample and that one broken trial in thirty-three is an accident of
the schedule. At n = 57 the pair resolves ~14.4pp, so the delta will most likely be unresolved again and the
claim the round grades is the **harm share**, which can separate: 1 in 47 is 2.13% against R139's 5 in 32,
Fisher's p ≈ 0.04. A round that states it cannot resolve its own mean before it runs is a cheaper round than one
that discovers it afterwards.

### 34.182 A guard evaluated per phase is a guard that fires after the money is spent

**The loss.** `44210655651`, dispatched 2026-11-18 at 00:47 UTC. The learn half ran 00:48–01:19 and cost
**`$0.1617`**; the eval phase started at 01:19, thirteen minutes into a peak window, and `--require-off-peak`
refused it. The reference arm was refused next, the pairing step found nothing to pair, and the arm the round
was registered for produced no score. Two of the round's four predictions were nonetheless readable from the
half that ran — `retired` 41 against a 30–42 band and `retained` 10 against 8–14 — and that is a statement about
the store, not about the treatment.

**Why no existing check caught it.** Three checks exist and none of them asks this question. `planBandWait`
answers "how long until the window" and is used only when a dispatch names `not_before`. `isPeak` answers "is it
peak now", per call. `--require-off-peak` answers the same question at each phase boundary, which is the layer
where being wrong is expensive. The missing question — *will the run still be off-peak when it finishes* — is a
comparison of two numbers that were both known before the first episode was paid for.

**The class this belongs to, and its third instance.** The record has twice been bitten by a check placed where
it can only report rather than prevent: R42's empty store, read as "the mechanism did not work" instead of "the
store was never written"; R137's carriage, where the copies were counted in a process that could no longer act
on them. This is the same shape at the billing layer: a guard whose refusal arrives after the spend. The repair
is the same in all three — move the decision to the earliest point where it is still free, and make the number
it decides on a field rather than a habit.

**What the guard must not become.** A waiting mechanism. `not_before` already exists, it is priced, and it is
capped at 240 minutes; a guard that sleeps to avoid a refusal would convert "this dispatch was mistimed" into
"this job held a runner for two hours", which is a different cost with the same cause. The guard's whole output
is a sentence and an exit code, and the sentence ends with the hour to name.

**One number of mine, corrected in the same round.** The comment written first said the lost half cost `$0.10`.
The learn phase's own `cost.usd` is **`0.1617`**, which the log states and the sentence in `window-fit.ts` now
quotes. An estimate of a cost in a file about not estimating costs is the smallest possible version of this
record's recurring defect.

### 34.183 An instrument graded the arm it was built for, and the grade was the instrument's

**The finding.** `serveSupportCensus` — the join R141's criterion is written in — reads the store sample to learn
how many tasks stand behind a served record. The sample is capped at 64 rows and records the 19 it left out. The
census read every id outside those rows as one task. On R141, **six of the fourteen served records were in the
omitted nineteen**, and all six were members of consolidation groups with two or three tasks behind them.

| reading | shipped join | corrected |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `belowFloor` (floor 2) | **6** | **0** |
| printed verdict | `6 of the 14 served item(s) carry support below it` | `no served item carries support below it` |
| `support ≥2` bucket | 8 items, 1 broke, 2 kept | **14 items, 1 broke, 5 kept** |
| singleton bucket | 6 items, 0 broke, **3 kept** | — |
| `unresolved` | 0 (claimed) | 0 (resolved through the groups) |

**What the wrong number would have said.** Not merely "the floor failed". It would have said **the singletons
repaired three cases and broke none**, which is the sentence that argues the floor *cost* three repairs — and it
would have been printed beside a round whose actual result is that the floor's survivors did all five. A
criterion failing on a run that satisfied it is bad; a mechanism being argued against by its own instrument is
worse, and this one is both.

**Why nothing caught it.** Three guards exist around this join and none of them can see a *prefix*. `supportMapOf`
returns `undefined` only when the artefact carries no sample at all. The census's own doc argues explicitly
against a bucket named `unknown`, on the ground that the store writes one task per correction — an argument that
is correct for a complete sample and silent about a capped one. And `storeItemSample` records `omitted`, so the
fact was in the artefact the whole time; the reader simply did not ask.

**The class.** Fourth instance of an absence read as a fact (§34.117's empty store, §34.135's unrecorded scope
dimension, §34.181's unprinted denominator), and the first where the absence is the *sample's own size*. The
repair is the same as the previous three: make the absent case a stated field (`truncated`) rather than a
default, and make the thing that cannot be resolved a count (`unresolved`) rather than a bucket.

**The discipline this buys, stated as a rule.** A default is a claim about a population. `?? 1` is "the store
writes one task per correction" — true of the store, false of the sample. Every default in an instrument reads
as a measurement once it reaches an artefact, so it has to be justified for the population it will be applied
to, and re-justified whenever that population changes from "the store" to "a prefix of the store".

**What it cost and what it bought.** $0.00 and one afternoon; in exchange, R142's readback will grade the
round's criterion on the correct population, and the cross-fit — whose denominators rest on the same join — was
built with the guard in place rather than after it failed.

### 34.184 A conservative join that refuses is not neutral: it deleted the arm it was written for

**What was found.** `pairedEpisodes` returned `undefined` for the entire attribution when any boundary resolved
to no trial. R141 opened 41 boundaries for 40 scored trials — one abandoned attempt — and the arm published no
attribution at all. `l4-pair` printed nothing for it, and R232's census was written, wired, tested at 100%
coverage and yet never exercised on the artefact it was built for.

**Why the guard looked right.** It came from R137, where a boundary the reader could not honour was a wiring
finding: the arm had said which task it opened and the join could not match it, so the honest response was to
refuse rather than to fall back to position. That reasoning holds when the unresolved boundary means the join is
broken. It does not hold when the run abandoned one attempt, which is a fact about the *run* — and the arm that
needs the diagnosis most is exactly the arm with an abandoned attempt in it.

**The class, and it is the fourth of its shape.** §34.179 counted the refusals this lane has paid for; §34.181
found a denominator that had never been printed; §34.183 found an instrument grading the arm it was built for.
This is the same defect as §34.179 seen from the other side: **a refusal is not a neutral act.** It has the
shape of rigour and the effect of deleting a measurement, and because it deletes it silently — `undefined` in a
field that may simply be absent — nothing downstream can report that it happened.

| the guard | what it protects against | what it actually did |
| --- | --- | --- |
| any unresolved boundary → `undefined` | a join silently mis-attributing requests | deleted a 40-of-41 table, and left `serve support` and `serve yield` unexercised on the only arm that mattered |
| `unmatchedRequests = ordered.length === 0 ? … : 0` | counting an artefact arm wrong | reported **0** on the one arm that had dropped requests, because it tested the input rather than the output |

**The rule this adds.** A partial join is a reading with a **counted** hole; only a total failure is a refusal.
The test is whether anything remains to publish, not whether anything was dropped — and the dropped quantity is
a field of the result, because a hole that is only in the code is a hole nobody reads.

**The secondary lesson, about test suites.** The census had 10 cases at 100% coverage and could not have caught
this: its unit is a list of renders, and the defect was in the caller that never produced one. Coverage measures
which lines ran; it cannot measure whether the pipeline reaches them. The only check that would have caught it is
the end-to-end read — running the instrument on a real pair artefact — which is now what the round does before it
writes the report, and what R232 did only after the fact.

**Cost.** $0.00, one afternoon, and three cases added to the suite (partial publishes, all-unresolved refuses,
coverage counts the dropped range). Bought: R141's two instrument lines, the `informative` count that every
conditional rate depends on, and the two artefact identities the cross-fit will refuse without.

### 34.185 A guard that reads its own request a second time, and the arm that obeyed it alone

**The reading.** R142's second dispatch (`44219333602`) waited 126 minutes for `not_before: 04:00`, woke at
04:00:22, and was refused five seconds later:

```
##[error]not_before 04:00 is 1440 minutes away; this lane waits at most 240, because the job limit is 340
```

`planBandWait` reads an hour that has already passed as the **next day's** — correct for a dispatch sent at
05:00 naming 04:00, wrong for a guard that runs after the wait it is grading. The wait step had already
consumed the one parse this dispatch needed, and the guard asked the question again with a different clock.

**Two defects, and the second is the expensive one.**

| # | defect | what it did |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | the guard re-parses `not_before` instead of consuming the instant the wait produced | refused every dispatch that named a window and had to wait for it — after the wait, so the sleep was spent |
| 2 | the memory arm's condition names no status function (implicit `success()`, so it was skipped) and the reference arm's names `!cancelled()` (no implicit `success()`, so it ran) | a refused dispatch bought one arm of a run the guard had just rejected |

The guard was added in §34.182 for R142's first failure — $0.1617 of learn half with no eval. It has now cost
R142 three attempts: the first by paying for half a run, the second by paying for a two-hour wait and refusing
it, and neither by the mechanism it was written to protect.

**Why nothing caught it, again.** `window-fit.ts` had 12 cases, all of which passed a `now` and asserted the
arithmetic. The defect was in what the caller passed as `now`: the bin re-derived it, and no test ran the bin
with a `not_before` it had already waited out — because a test cannot wait. The case that would have caught it
is the one added here: a published start plus a `not_before` that has passed, asserting **no refusal**.

**The class.** Fifth instance of "a value derived twice" (§34.117's empty store, §34.135's scope dimension,
§34.181's denominator, §34.183's sample, and this), and the second where the two derivations live in different
processes — which is the version that cannot be caught by reading either one.

| the shape | the field that now carries the single derivation |
| --- | --- |
| a duration and a moment, both derived from `not_before` | `wait_min` (for the deadline arithmetic) and `start_at` (for the window arithmetic), both published by the step that slept |
| a step's exit code used as gating for steps whose `if:` may or may not inherit `success()` | `fits`, an output both arms read explicitly |

**The rule this adds.** A guard is not a step that fails; it is a **value** its dependants read. An exit code
gates only the steps that happen to inherit `success()`, and GitHub's rule for that inheritance is invisible
at the call site: `if: a != b` inherits it, `if: !cancelled() && a != b` does not. Two arms of one dispatch
therefore disagreed about whether the run had been refused, and the one that disagreed in the expensive
direction was the control arm.

**Cost.** One two-hour wait, one cancelled run, **$0.00 of model calls** (the log ends at the label count; no
arm reached an episode). Bought: the guard now works for the case it exists for, both arms obey it, and R143's
two folds — which must each fit a window — are dispatched behind a gate that has been run.

### 34.186 A field withheld for two rounds on a sound argument, and a comment where a test belonged

**What was withheld.** `ServeRender` carried no task id. The reason is written into §17.152 and it is correct:
`itemTransfer` de-duplicates at the episode, where the identity is known, and a second id invites a second
de-duplication at a different grain — two grains of one count are two answers, and the wrong answer is the one
that reads plausibly.

**What it cost.** Three rounds of readings could say *which record* broke a trial and *how many* renders it
took, and could not say *which task* the break landed on. On R141 that left one break with no address, in a
lane whose remaining question is exactly whether the harm is reach (a store used on task families it has
nothing to say about) or interference (a store used on the episode it was taught). Those are fixed by different
mechanisms — a retrieval gate versus a floor — and the instrument could not tell them apart.

**The mistake, stated precisely.** The risk the argument named was real; the remedy was a comment. A withheld
field is a *silent* restriction: nothing in the suite could fail when its absence cost a reading, because
absence is not a defect any assertion was written against. This is §34.184's shape from the other side — a
refusal that looks like rigour and deletes a measurement — and the fourth time this lane has paid for a
decision recorded only in prose.

| the reasoning | the remedy then | the remedy now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a second identity invites a second count | withhold the identity | the identity is **attribution only**, and a case asserts `serveYieldCensus` is identical with and without it |
| the counting grain is the episode | state it in a doc comment | `serveTaskCensus` is the only reader, it groups and never divides, and its rows are the join grain a content axis needs |
| an artefact may predate the field | not applicable (the field did not exist) | the census counts what it could not attribute (`unattributed`) and says so in its own line |

**The class, and the test that would have caught it.** No test can fail for a field that does not exist. The
only instrument that would have caught this is the *question* the lane could not ask — and the discipline that
produces it is to write the question down as a census before deciding the field is unnecessary. The round that
withheld the id had already printed `1 broke`; the next question was "where", and it was never asked because
there was no line that would have answered it.

**What the new instrument refuses.** It does not report a rate per task: a task reached once and broken once is
`net -1`, and the census prints that rather than `-100%` or `0%`, because one render is not evidence at any
level. It also does not fold the armed-but-neutral tasks into the total: `neutral` is 35 of 40 on R141's shape,
which is the same reading as the yield census's 85% inert from a different angle — the store was served and
changed nothing.

**Cost.** $0.00, one instrument round. Bought: the population axis on every future run, the join grain for the
content axis, and a guard (`the task id is attribution only`) that makes the original objection load-bearing
instead of decorative.

### 34.187 An axis the product has, the lane cannot name, and the pool cannot see

**What was found.** Two things, and they compound. `RecallQuery.anchoring` is a published contract with two
values and the τ² lane has only ever run one of them, because no registration could name the other. And the arm's
artefact recorded `tau2.pack.{budget, requests, filled, empty, ledger}` — everything about a pack except **what
filter produced it**. So the lane could not vary the filter, and could not have told that it had varied it.

**How it was found, which is the interesting part.** Not by a failing test — by reading the literature and asking
which of its mechanisms is reachable from here. WikiTrace (arXiv 2611.14320) decomposes degradation events into
52% "followed a retrieved entry", and of those 20% outright wrong and 80% *valid but applied outside its scope*.
The 80% class is what a lexical anchor excludes, and the answer to "do we have that?" was: the kernel has it, the
HTTP route parses it, the Python agent forwards arbitrary knobs — and nothing in the registration vocabulary can
set it. `recall-query.ts` had already written this defect down one layer up ("a capability that exists below the
wire and not on it … is the layer nobody's tests were looking at"); this is the same defect at the *registration*
layer, four rounds after that comment was written.

**The compounding defect.** Even with the knob reachable, the pool would not have known. `treatment` is the
cross-fit's identity — unit, form, scope, model, trace ceiling — and a fold served through `anchoring=lexical`
would have pooled with one served through the default as one corpus. Two filters are two treatments, and a pooled
rate over them is a number about a serving that never happened. This is §34.183's class (an instrument that cannot
see the thing it was built for) with a shorter fuse: it would have surfaced as a pool that "worked" and reported a
mean of two different experiments.

| the field | why it had to be added before the arm, not after |
| --- | --- |
| `tau2.pack.knobs` | it is the only trace of the filter; an artefact written without it can never be re-read for the question |
| `treatment.knobs` | the pool's identity is fixed at the fold, and a fold is expensive: discovering the missing axis after two $0.30 folds costs the folds |
| `serveAnchor` in the header vocabulary | a treatment that cannot be registered is a treatment that will be run by hand and documented by memory |

**The refusal this round added, and why it is not defensive coding.** `packMode: prefix` with
`serveAnchor: lexical` is refused where the three plans are joined. A prefix arm renders every admitted entry, so
a lexical anchor has nothing to filter; on the wire the two knobs would collide (`anchoring=scope` from the mode,
`anchoring=lexical` from the anchor) and the *last key would win in silence*. Every silent conflict in this record
has ended the same way — an arm published under a treatment it did not run — and the fix is one sentence in the
one place both plans are visible.

**What this does not claim.** No model was called, so nothing is known yet about whether a lexical anchor helps on
τ² retail. The round buys the ability to ask, and the pool's ability to refuse a mixed answer. The arm itself is
ROADMAP step 3's next dollar, gated on R142's readback.

**Cost.** $0.00, one round. Bought: a published product axis made nameable, the filter recorded in every future
artefact, a sixth identity field the pool refuses by, and one fewer silent contradiction on the wire.

### 34.188 An artefact that said what the store was made of, in a lane that never asked

**What was found.** R142's memory arm carries `tau2.provenance` — a census written by R62 that joins every
item's evidence back to the trajectory it came from and splits the store into `edited`, `passed`, `itemsMixed`
and `itemsUnattributed`. R142's reads:

```
{"edited": 9, "passed": 48, "itemsEditedOnly": 11, "itemsPassedOnly": 50, "itemsMixed": 0}
```

**Eighty-two per cent of the store was distilled from a trajectory that already passed.** Eleven rounds of
readbacks quoted `created`, `retired`, `servable`, `support`, `meanIds`, `top1`, `render(s)` and `net`, and not
one of them quoted the field that says what the sixty-one items were *made of*. The field has been in the
artefact since R62 and in the log since the same round; the readback regex list is the artefact of this audit —
sixteen patterns, none of them `provenance`.

**Why it mattered, in the numbers the same artefact carries.** `distillScope: all` has been in every
registration since R131, and the reason is one line away: the consolidation pass needs two tasks behind one
routine, and a failures-only store has one witness per routine. Widening the population to passes buys the
witnesses — and then `support ≥ 2` certifies two tasks whose *successful episodes read alike*, which is a shared
**description** and not a shared **repair**. R142's `cross-task 11` reads as eleven routines with independent
evidence and is in fact eleven routines two passing tasks describe similarly. The floor was in force, no
singleton was served, and six of the nine served records broke a trial.

**The class.** This is not a missing instrument; it is a missing *reader*. §34.183 and §34.187 are instruments
that could not see the thing they were built for, and both cost a paid round. This one cost nothing to fix and
had already cost eleven rounds of direction: the store's population was chosen for supply in R131, the content
axis became the registered next step in R142, and the number that says why was in every artefact in between.

| what carried the fact | since | who read it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tau2.provenance.itemsPassedOnly` | R62 | nobody, until this round |
| `tau2.learning.edited` (beside `distilled`) | R62 | nobody: the readback quoted `created` from the log line instead |
| `distill.scope` | R62 | the cross-fit's identity, which compares it and never reports it |

**What was done.** The number is quoted in the readback patterns and in §PROGRESS 175, and the axis it names is
what `prereg/R151-the-failures-only-store.md` measures. No code was needed to obtain it, which is the audit's
point: the fix is a reader, and the rule it leaves behind is that a census an artefact carries and no readback
prints is a census the record has paid for twice.

### 34.189 A ladder that priced a rung nothing could choose

**What was found.** `pack.margins.ladder` counts, for each rung of the margin grid, how many requests that rung
would withhold. R142's reads `0.01 4 / 0.02 6 / 0.05 11 / 0.10 23 / 0.15 30 / 0.20 38 / 0.30 50` — and the only
question a rung is chosen by is **which** requests it withholds, and whether those are the ones that did damage.
The ladder answers the first half and cannot answer the second, and the artefact carried the answer anyway:
`margins.perRequest`, `pack.ledger` and `per_trial` are three arrays of one row per request, in arrival order,
and the episode join that pairs them was written in R128 for the attribution table.

**So the defect is a census that counts without joining.** R135 wrote `perRequest` for exactly this question and
said so in its own comment ("the ladder above is a *count* of requests under each rung, which prices a rung in
advance but cannot answer the question a rung is chosen by"). Four rounds later the lane was still one dispatch
away from every candidate rung, and R142's registration listed "the margin rung" as the fallback axis with no
way to choose a value for it.

**What was done.** `serve-sweep.ts` joins the three arrays and prices every rung against the measured outcomes;
`l4-pair` prints the line and publishes `serveSweep`. On R142 it reproduces the hand reading exactly — rung 0.30
keeps 2 repairs, withholds all 6 breaks, serves 7 of 57 trials — and it says what the maximum would hide: the
margin separates a repair from a break at **AUC 0.625** on four against six with an exact permutation
**p 0.305**, which is not a lever, and the
cleanest rung is clean because it withholds 88% of the traffic.

**The rule this leaves.** A census of a knob must carry the join that decides the knob's value, or it is a
pricing table without a buyer. The cheap version of that rule was available four rounds ago at the cost of one
function; the expensive version is one dispatch per candidate value, and the lane was on the expensive one.

**Cost.** $0.00. Bought: every future pair prices every rung at readback time, and the next arm's margin is
chosen from a number rather than from a guess.

### 34.190 A minimum detectable effect computed on one half of the pair it describes

**What was found.** Every MDE this record has published — 23.23pp, 17.16pp, 15.55pp, 17.72pp — is computed
from the **discordant pairs inside one dispatch**, which treats the control arm's outcome as a fixed quantity.
It is not fixed: it is one sample from a stochastic agent on a stochastic model. Nobody had measured that.

**The measurement, which cost nothing.** R142 and R151 dispatched the *same* reference configuration, on the
same 57 tasks, with the same model, forty minutes apart. Two transfer ledgers, joined by task id:

| cell | count |
| --- | --- |
| both passed | 44 |
| both failed | 3 |
| passed at R142, failed at R151 | **3** |
| failed at R142, passed at R151 | **7** |
| agreement | **82.5%** |
| McNemar exact, two-sided | p = 0.344 |

The arm did not change. **It moved 7.02pp and flipped 17.5% of its tasks.**

**What that does to the arithmetic.** A per-arm flip share of `f` on `n` trials is a sampling SD of
`√(f(1−f)/n)`; on 17.5% of 57 that is 5.0pp. A delta between two independently sampled arms carries `√2 × 5.0
= 7.1pp`, against the **5.55pp** paired standard error `l4-pair` reports — and 80%-power MDE is `2.802 × 7.1 =
19.9pp`, against the published 15.55pp. Every row is light by the same factor, and none of the three deltas the
lane has produced (−3.51, −8.77, +10.00) clears even the published bound.

**The class.** This is the same defect as §34.188, one level up: an instrument that reports a number about a
population it did not sample. `l4-pair`'s interval is exact *given* two draws; the question a reader asks is
whether the treatment moved the outcome, and answering it needs the variance of both draws. The pair refuses to
average two treatments (§AM.5's fold identity) and then silently assumes one of them does not vary.

**Why it was invisible.** A test–retest needs two dispatches of one treatment, and this lane has always spent
its dispatches on two *different* treatments — the control is a means to a delta, not an object of study. The
two reference arms existed as a by-product of two mechanism rounds; nobody joined them. The join is ten lines
against artefacts already on disk.

**What it changes.** No effect this record has measured is claimable, and the next dollars buy resolution rather
than mechanism. A third mechanism reading at a 20pp MDE would produce a sentence nobody can act on. The
registered instrument for resolution is the R143 cross-fit — 114 independent task pairs rather than 228
correlated trial pairs — and it is now the head of the queue for a reason that did not exist when it was written.

**Cost.** $0.00. The two reference arms were already paid for. What the round bought is the knowledge that the
lane's own noise floor is ~7pp per arm, which is larger than every effect it has reported.

### 34.191 Two guards that refused every artefact this lane writes, and the fixtures that agreed with them

**What was found.** R143's two folds cannot be pooled, and the reason has been committed in the pair artefact
for three rounds, in two fields nobody read:

| field | value the artefact carried |
| --- | --- |
| `foldSplitAbsent` | `the arms scored different splits: 'memory' learned 57 and answered 57, against 0 and 57` |
| `treatmentAbsent` | `the arms do not both state unit: reference record none, so nothing can compare it` |

Both sentences describe the **design**, not a defect. The reference arm serves no pack and distils nothing, so
`controlRaw` records `train: []` on purpose — "this arm learned nothing" — and it has no unit, form, scope or
knobs to report. `foldSplitOf` required both arms to state the same two halves and `treatmentOf` required both
to state every field, so the pair could never state what a cross-fit pools on. The pool then refused the
artefact with *"fold(s) that do not say what they learned from"*, which blames the file for the guard's
assumption.

**The third instance, in the same feature.** `bin/cross-fit.ts` typed the artefact's `treatment` without the
R150 `knobs` field and its loader dropped it, so two folds served through two different anchors would have
reached `identityOf` as `'none'` and `'none'` and been pooled. The pool's comparison was tested; the wiring
that feeds it was not. Measured: before the fix, the command exited 0 on two folds whose filters differed.

**Why it was invisible.** Every test of both guards used a **symmetric fixture** — two arms, each stating the
same halves, each stating a unit — because the fixtures were written from the function's contract rather than
from an artefact. Forty-six cases in `cross-fit.test.ts` and not one of them is a control arm. The shape that
fails was in the committed `poc-l4-pair.json` the whole time; so was the sentence explaining it.

**The class.** §34.188 (a `provenance` field written for eleven rounds and read by nobody) and §34.189 (a
ladder computed and never connected) are the same failure one layer over: an instrument whose output is never
confronted with the input it claims to describe. Here the instrument is a guard, and its output is a refusal —
which is why it looked like diligence.

**What was fixed.** `foldSplitOf` now requires an **evaluation** half from every arm and takes the learning
half as the union of the non-empty ones, refusing two different non-empty halves, refusing a pair where no arm
learned anything, and refusing an overlap between the two halves. `treatmentOf` compares the arms that **state**
a field and still refuses a disagreement. The loader carries `knobs`. Five guard expectations were rewritten to
the shape the driver writes, three command cases were added (two filters pool, two filters refuse, one filter
pools), and two end-to-end cases publish a pair from a reference arm carrying `train: []` and assert the
artefact now states `foldSplit` and `treatment`.

**What it costs and what it saved.** $0.00 — no dispatch. It was found while R143's official fold was in
flight, whose pair artefact is written by the **old** guards; the two arm files are uploaded as evidence, so the
fold is regenerated locally from them with the fixed code rather than re-bought.

### 34.192 The 28% wider MDE was an unpaired model applied to a paired estimator

**What was claimed.** §34.190 concluded, from two reference arms that moved 7.02pp, that the lane's minimum
detectable effect is **19.9pp** rather than the 15.55pp the pair artefact prints, and that "no effect this lane
has measured survives that correction". The second sentence of that conclusion is withdrawn here.

**What the two reference arms actually say.** The same four cells, read as proportions rather than as a flip
count:

| quantity | value | from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| control arm, R142 | `p₁ = 0.8246` | 47/57 |
| control arm, R151 | `p₂ = 0.8947` | 51/57 |
| disagreement two **independent** draws would produce | `p₁(1−p₂) + (1−p₁)p₂` = **0.2438** | the same two rates |
| disagreement actually observed | **0.1754** | 10 of 57 tasks flipped |
| SD of a difference between two independent arm means | `√((p₁(1−p₁) + p₂(1−p₂))/57)` = **6.47pp** | the same two rates |
| observed difference | **7.02pp** | 1.08 of that SD |

The observed disagreement sits **below** the independence expectation, which is the direction of a positive
task-level correlation across dispatches — tasks that were hard in one round were hard in the next. The
observed 7.02pp is 1.08 standard deviations of the independent-draw model: ordinary sampling noise, not a
dispatch effect.

**Where the 19.9pp came from.** `√(0.175 × 0.825 / 57) = 5.0pp` treats the **flip share** as if it were the
outcome proportion; multiplied by `√2` it produced a 7.1pp "delta SD", and `2.802 × 7.1 = 19.9pp`. Two errors
compounded: the wrong `p`, and `√2` applied to a quantity that was already a difference.

**Why the estimator is not unpaired.** `comparePaired` forms its interval from the discordant pairs of **one**
dispatch; that is the variance of the paired difference and it already contains the control arm's noise. What
the test–retest measures is the variance of an **unpaired** comparison. Put side by side:

| reading | SE | what it estimates |
| --- | --- | --- |
| McNemar, as published | **5.36pp** | the paired difference, both arms in one dispatch |
| independent draws of one arm | **6.47pp** | the unpaired difference of two rates |

The ratio gives the within-task correlation `1 − (5.36/6.47)² = 0.31` — and the flip share independently
implies `1 − 0.1754/0.2438 = 0.28`. Two estimators, different data, one number: pairing buys about 0.3 of
correlation, and the interval the artefact prints is on the right scale.

**What survives and what does not.** The task-level outcome of one arm is **not reproducible**: 17.5% of 57
tasks flipped between two dispatches. That is the binomial noise the protocol already models, and it is why one
trial per task resolves ~15pp. What does not survive is the claim that the lane's intervals are 28% too narrow,
and the sentence that no measured effect survives. Both are retracted; the numbers they were about are R142's
−3.51pp [−14.04, +7.02] and R151's −8.77pp [−21.05, +3.51], which are unresolved against a 15.55pp bound for
the ordinary reason — the sample is small — not because the estimator is wrong.

**What it changes for R143.** Nothing in the plan; everything in the reading. The two-fold cross-fit is held to
**10.98pp**, and 19.9pp is withdrawn from every document that quotes it.

**Cost.** $0.00. Two committed pair artefacts and one afternoon of arithmetic that should have been done before
the claim was published.

### 34.193 The first test–retest of a *delta*: one pipeline, two dispatches, 7.5pp apart

**What was found.** The record has had a test–retest of one **arm** (§34.190) and none of a **delta**. R141 and
R143 `official` are the same registration parameters — `distillScope: all`, `distillUnit: correction`,
`distillForm: lesson`, `consolidate: routine/all`, `serveSupport: 2`, `speakMargin: 0`, `packBudget: 2400`,
`packLimit: 1`, `taskSplit: official`, 74 learn / 40 held out, one trial — dispatched two days apart. Joining
their two ledgers by task id:

| reading | R141 | R143 `official` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| memory arm | 37/40 | 37/40 |
| reference arm | 33/40 | 36/40 |
| delta | **+10.00pp** [0.00, 22.50] | **+2.50pp** [−10.00, 15.00] |
| McNemar p | 0.2187 | 1.0000 |
| lost / gained | 1 / 5 | 3 / 4 |
| resolution | 17.16pp | 18.53pp |
| store created / servable | 83 / 14 | 77 / 11 |

**Per task, both arms moved.** The control arm flipped **9 of 40 tasks (22.5%)** and the memory arm **6 of 40
(15.0%)** between the two dispatches, and 10 tasks changed their *within-run* difference. The store is not the
same object in the two runs either: distillation and consolidation are model calls, so 83 records against 77 with
14 servable against 11 is the same pipeline producing two stores.

**What it licenses.** The difference between the two deltas is **7.5pp**, and its standard error computed from the
paired per-task differences is **10.97pp** — 0.68 of an SE. Two dispatches of one pipeline on one population
therefore agree as closely as the design's own noise allows, which is the empirical counterpart of §34.192's
retraction: the paired interval is not 28% too narrow, and a delta at this size is reproducible to about its own
resolution and no better. Both flip shares also sit at the independence expectation (23.7% expected against
22.5% for the control, 13.9% against 15.0% for the memory arm), so there is still no measured extra-binomial
discharge that a widened bound would be pricing.

**What it saves.** §34.190's arithmetic created a case for buying a third `official` dispatch to measure the
delta's reproducibility. This comparison answers that question for **$0.00** and with the same population, so the
dispatch is not made. The two artefacts it reads were both already paid for, and the join is ten lines against
ledgers that were already committed once the artefact could be fetched.

**The class this belongs to.** §34.188 through §34.192 are all one defect: a reading the record makes and does
not confront. Two of them were found by joining artefacts across rounds, which is the cheapest instrument this
lane has and the one it forgets most often.

### 34.194 The treatment identity had five fields, and the serving policy would have arrived as a sixth that nobody compared

**The defect, found before it could be paid for.** R152's arm bounds how many times one item may be served. The
pair artefact states a treatment as `unit`, `form`, `scope`, `model`, `traceClaims`, `knobs` — five of the six
fields the record has added one at a time, each *after* the round in which the omission mattered. The rotation
was about to be a seventh addition, and it was about to be omitted in exactly the same way: the arm's own
artefact would carry the reading, the pair would not state the policy, the pool would normalise the silence to
`none`, and R152's bounded fold would have pooled with R143's two unbounded ones as one treatment at 114 pairs.
The number that would have come out is an average of two servings, which is the error §34.191 records at the
guard below this one.

**What surfaced it was writing the guide.** §32.2's table says what each header value records in the artefact, and
the row for `serveRotation: off` claimed `serveRotation.cap: 0`. The code did not do that: a declared identity
built no ledger at all, so the artefact carried no block, which made a declared control indistinguishable from a
switch nobody had mentioned. The row was wrong, and the reason it was wrong — the artefact had no field for the
*policy* as distinct from its *reading* — is the same reason the pool would have had nothing to compare.

**The repair, in the order the record is read.**

| layer | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the arm artefact | `serveRotation: { cap, maxRenders, … }` | `serveRotation: { mode, cap, maxRenders, … }`, and a declared `off` ships `{ mode: 'off' }` with no reading |
| the pair artefact | `treatment` had six fields | `treatmentOf` compares `rotation` as a seventh, stated by the arm that declared one and silent on a control that serves no pack |
| the fold record | `TREATMENT_FIELDS` had six names | seven, with `rotation` in a `STRICT_FIELDS` set |
| the pool | `identityOf` compared five names | six; `rotation` absent and `rotation: 'off'` are different values (`none` / `off`) |
| the guide | the row above | `serveRotation.mode: 'off'`, and a paragraph saying why the mode travels separately from the reading |

**The one place the new field breaks a rule the other six follow.** `fold-records.ts` *carries* a field that one
fold states and the other does not, with a derivation line, because an older artefact's silence usually means "the
field did not exist yet" and refusing it would let one artefact's age decide that two folds ran different
treatments. For a serving policy that reasoning inverts: silence means the arm **did not bound anything**, so
carrying it would convert an unbounded fold into a bounded one. `rotation` is therefore refused rather than
carried, and the refusal names the asymmetry:

```
the folds are two experiments, not one corpus: rotation is 'fair-share' on official and unstated on swapped
  — a field whose absence is the control may not be carried
```

**The class, and the count.** This is the fourth field this record has added to a treatment identity after the
round in which its absence produced a number (R109's unit, R120's split, R150's knobs, and now the policy). Three
of the four were found by a *readback* joining artefacts that disagreed. This one was found by writing the
sentence that describes the field, which is the cheapest instrument in this record and the one it uses least.
What makes the sentence harder to get wrong next time is the type rather than the prose: `ServeRotationReport`
has a mandatory `mode`, so a block cannot ship without the policy it belongs to, and the guide's table is
checked against that type by hand once rather than re-derived on every readback.

### 34.195 A spread is a field the type cannot see, and a snapshot is a reading taken at the wrong moment

**Two defects, one dispatch, one red gate.** R152 bounded how many times one item may be served and reported
`+2.50pp` at a harm share of 5.88%, and its job failed on one blocking row:

```
[gate fail] [l4-pair] FAIL l4-projection-complete: memory: serveRotation
```

`V16-transfer-resolvable` and `l4-effect-resolved` also failed and are non-blocking in both readings (§34.190: a
count too small to resolve and an effect the sample cannot separate are facts about the arm). The projection row
is a defect, and it is the third time this class has cost a round.

**Defect 1 — the field was emitted through a spread, so the compile guard was never asked.**

```ts
...(primary.rotation === undefined ? {} : { serveRotation: primary.rotation })   // driver
```

`PROJECTION` is typed `{ [K in keyof Tau2Raw]-?: 'carried' | 'reduced' }`, and its comment claims *"a field added
to the driver's record fails to compile until it is given a decision"*. That is true of a field the type declares.
A spread member is exempt from excess-property checking, `Tau2Raw` never grew the key, and the table stayed
exhaustive over a type that no longer described the record. §34.161 found this hole with `memory` and
`turnCensus`; the repair it installed was the runtime one — `armRecordFromDriver` names every key without a
decision and the pair refuses the arm. **That repair worked, one dispatch late.** The arm file carries
`unprojected: ["serveRotation"]` and no block.

The declaration is now in `Tau2Raw`, which restores the compile-time guard in the direction that matters: a
declared field with no table entry does not build, so the only way to emit one is to declare it, and the only way
to declare it is to decide about it.
