**What the omission cost, in the currency this record uses.** Not one gate row — the fold's place in the pool. The
policy is a treatment identity field (§34.194), the arm's file cannot state it, `rotationModeOf` reads the fold as
`none`, and a fold whose policy is unstated cannot be pooled with one that states it. The evidence is complete
except for the one field that says which experiment it was, and it cannot be re-derived at $0 from the arm files:
the two files are the input to the join and the missing field is one of them. R143's fold was regenerable because
the *pair* reader was at fault; here the *arm* is, and that is the difference between a $0 repair and a $0.37
replication.

**Defect 2 — the report was a snapshot taken before the loop, and it never reached a file.**

```ts
const rotation = new ServeRotationLedger(rotationCap);
const rotationReport = { mode, ...(rotation?.reading() ?? {}) };   // ← before the phase
```

`reading()` is a snapshot. Taken there it says `requests: 0`, `renders: 0`, `maxRenders: 0`, `exhausted: []`,
`starved: 0` — a phase that served nothing — while the log line printed after the loop says `cap 3 … max 3, 40
render(s) over 14 item(s), 13 exhausted`. Defect 1 removed the block before anyone could read it, so this one
surfaced only when a test asserted the identity that ties the two together:

```
serveRotation.requests === recall.requests        # one next() per recall
```

Had the projection carried the block, the artefact would have said the phase served nothing beside a log that
said forty, and the artefact is the file that survives. The repair is one read after the phase feeding both
consumers — a snapshot read once cannot disagree with itself.

**The test that should have caught both was measuring zero.** The end-to-end case drives the real driver against
a stand-in for τ². The stand-in wrote its result document and never asked the memory: the recall facade is a real
HTTP server in the driver's process, and no case had ever called it. Every serving reading in that file — the pack
census, the served sizes, the ledger — was asserted over a phase that served no pack, and passed. A conditional
field whose branch is off in the whole suite is invisible to the compile guard (the branch is a spread), to the
runtime guard (the key is never emitted) and to the test (nothing asserts the reading). The stand-in now asks once
per episode behind `TAU_STUB_RECALL`, and the case asserts the identity above rather than a constant.

| layer | what it refuses | when | cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Tau2Raw` declaration | a field no table must decide about | `tsc` | $0 |
| `PROJECTION` entry | a declared field with no decision | `tsc` | $0 |
| `unprojected` at the pair | an emitted key no decision covers | after the run | one dispatch |

**The class, and the count.** Third top-level instance of "a field lost in a projection" (R56's three, R123's
two, R152's one) and fifth field-level one with `dropped` and `pin` inside `learning`. Every one of them was
emitted through a spread, and every one was found after a run. What is new here is that the runtime backstop from
the previous instance *did* fire — the guard is not the missing piece any more, the declaration is, and the two
are not substitutes: a guard that fires after the dispatch turns a $0 defect into a paid one.

### 34.196 A green job that measured nothing, and the flag that made it green

**The run.** R152b was registered to produce two things: a complete artefact for the bounded arm (R152's fold had
lost the field, §34.195) and a second draw of the same treatment against its own control. It produced the first and
not the second, and its job finished **success**:

```
[pass4] pass4=0.925 ... arm=1
(no [l4-pair] lines, no pair artefact, no gates)
```

**The mechanism, in one workflow line.** `sota.yml:1839` gates the pair step on `l4_arms`:

```yaml
if: always() && (github.event.inputs.l4_arms == 'both' || ... == 'scaffold' || ... == '')
```

The dispatch passed `l4_arms: memory`, which is a legitimate value — it buys the treatment arm and nothing else, and
that is the right shape for a baseline or a single-arm probe. For a fold it produces a run that **cannot** have a
delta, and nothing in the run says so: the job is green, the step summary lists no missing artefact, and the
registration's own prediction rows about `breaks`, `repairs` and the delta were simply never graded. Four of six
predictions unanswerable, and the file that would have said so does not exist.

**Why this is worse than a red run.** A red job names its failure in one line (§34.195 is exactly that) and the next
dispatch is the repair. A green job with no pair looks like a fold that passed: it is the only failure shape in this
record whose *symptom is the absence of a symptom*. The $0.2929 it cost is the least of it — the run also consumed
a draw of the treatment, and three draws of one treatment is one more than an honest spread needs.

**The repair, at the layer that can see both facts.** The workflow is right and the registration is right: only the
dispatch input was wrong, and the dispatch input is the one thing the workflow does not read. So the guard goes in
the operator's dispatcher rather than in the pipeline:

```
$ dispatch.py --prereg R152c-the-paired-fold --arms memory
--arms memory buys one arm: no pair artefact, no pair gates and no delta.
Pass --single-arm if that is the experiment.
```

A flag rather than a refusal, because a single-arm dispatch is the correct call for a baseline, and the guard's job
is to make the operator say which experiment they are buying. That is the same principle as the doc's own
`l4-effect-resolved`: state the claim, then check the number against it.

**What the round still bought.** The instrument goal was met in full: the block is present, `unprojected` is empty,
and the shipped `reconcileServeRotation` agrees with the file's own pack ledger on all six reachable fields while
naming the three it cannot reach. And the bounded arm now has two draws — **0.875** and **0.925**, 5pp apart, both
served in full, both reaching their cap, neither starving. A green job that measured nothing still measured the
instrument, which is the only reason it is not a total loss.

**The class.** This is the first entry in this record whose defect is *operational* rather than mechanical: no code
was wrong, every gate that ran passed, and the run is still wasted. The rule it contributes is that the dispatch
input is part of the registration — the file commits to a treatment, and the input commits to a *comparison*, and
only the second one decides whether a control is bought.

### 34.197 A gate that passed the thing its own criterion forbids

**Found by reading the artefact R152c wrote**, which is the only place it could be found:

```
V5-resolution          False (blocking)  minimum detectable 23.23pp against a 6.00pp target; claims -7.50pp …
l4-effect-resolved     True  (advisory)  the memory costs accuracy: -7.50pp
```

Two rows, one pair, opposite readings — and the second row's own `criterion` string says

> the pair resolves the effect it reports: `|delta| >= minimum detectable difference`, or no direction is claimed

`|−7.50pp|` against a `23.23pp` resolution is exactly the case that sentence forbids, and the gate passed it. The
predicate is not the criterion:

```ts
pass: input.registeredBand === undefined ? input.state !== 'UNRESOLVED' : inBand
```

`state` comes from `pairedVerdict`, and `HARM` is the **R45 cost bar** — *significantly negative, or below −5pp with
a served pack* — which is a bar rather than a resolution. So a harm of any size above the cost bar passes a gate
whose stated condition is a resolution test. `detectablePp` is used in the gate's *sentence* for the
`UNRESOLVED` branch and never in its predicate.

**Why it matters even though the gate is advisory.** The row is the record's answer to "may this pair be quoted as
a finding". A `True` there, next to a red `V5`, tells a reader who trusts the first line that −7.50pp is a resolved
harm. The run is red either way, so no decision changed — but the row certifies something it did not check, and this
record has three entries about gates that said more than they checked.

**The repair, one line plus a sentence.** The predicate becomes the criterion:

```ts
const resolves = input.detectablePp === undefined || Math.abs(input.deltaPp) >= input.detectablePp;
pass: band ? inBand : input.state !== 'UNRESOLVED' && resolves
```

and the non-band branch gains a sentence for the case it used to hide: *"−7.50pp against a 23.23pp minimum
detectable difference — a cost the revert rule acts on and a direction this pair cannot claim"*.

**Why it is not done in this commit.** The predicate change rewrites a row of two committed pair artefacts
(`poc-l4-pair-official.json` and `poc-l4-pair-swapped.json`, the latter currently `True` at −10.81pp against a
13.24pp resolution, which the new rule flips). Regenerating committed evidence is a change of its own, with its own
before/after table, and mixing it into a round whose subject is the rotation would leave a reader unable to tell
which commit moved which number. It is therefore the whole of the next instrument round, whose scope is exactly:
**the predicate, the sentence, the two regenerated artefacts, and a case per branch.**

**The class.** Third instance of "the gate's text and the gate's code disagree", and the first where the text was
the stricter of the two. §34.161's four failures were all silence; this one is a false green, which is worse for a
reader and cheaper to fix — one boolean.

### 34.198 The mechanism was a line through two confounded points

**What was claimed.** §PROGRESS 178 and §TECH-DESIGN 17.163 stated a mechanism: *harm follows renders per servable
item*. The evidence was two folds, same treatment, same day:

| fold | servable items | renders per item | harm share |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `official` | 11 | 3.6 | 8.33% |
| `official-swapped` | 3 | **25.0** | 23.81% |

Two points, one monotone line, and a slogan — *"a store that keeps fewer items does not become conservative, it
applies each of them everywhere"* — that reads as an explanation. It is not an explanation; it is a line through
two points that differ in **both** the quantity named (renders per item) and the quantity that produced it (how many
items survived the floor). The two axes were perfectly confounded by construction, because the cap was not there
yet: renders per item was a *consequence* of the store size, so no fold could hold one fixed while moving the other.

**What separated them.** A serving cap. Three bounded draws, all at the same dose:

| draw | servable | renders/item | harm share | `maxRenders` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R152 (cap 3) | 14 | 2.86 | **5.88%** | 3 |
| R152b (cap 4) | 13 | 3.08 | not measured | 4 |
| R152c (cap 4) | 13 | 3.15 | **20.59%** | 4 |

**At renders per item of 2.9 and 3.2 the harm share is 5.88% and 20.59%.** The independent variable moved by 10% and
the dependent one by 15 points. The mechanism, as stated, is refuted: renders per item does not determine the harm
share at these store sizes, and the quantity that does — which items the store drew — was never measured in R143
because the draw *was* the confounded variable.

**What survives, and it is not nothing.** The cap acts on exactly what it says it acts on: `maxRenders` equals the
cap in all three bounded draws, the leader's renders fall from 12 to 3–4, every servable item is served, and no
phase is starved. The instrument is sound and the *policy's* effect on accuracy is unmoved, which is a different
statement from "the policy does not work" and a much more useful one: **allocation is under the experimenter's
control now, and moving it does not move the outcome.**

**The method failure, stated as a rule.** A mechanism inferred from two points is a line. Before a line becomes a
claim in this record it needs a third point that holds one of the two axes fixed — and if the design cannot produce
one without an instrument that does not exist yet, the honest first dispatch is the *instrument*, not the second
fold. R152 was that instrument and it arrived after the claim rather than before it. The rule, written where the
next registration will read it: **an explanation quoted from a scatter gets one point more than the number of axes
it varies.**

**What it cost.** Two dispatches at $0.37 to make the third point, one at $0.29 to learn that a dispatch input can
skip the control (§34.196), and one published claim retracted (§PROGRESS 181). Cheaper than most of this record's
method errors, and the retraction is the part that matters: the harm share of a four-draw treatment is
5.88%, 20.59%, 8.33% and (unbounded, thin store) 23.81%, which supports no ordering at all.

### 34.199 The repair 34.197 deferred, and the one line of its own draft that was wrong

**34.197 promised a round and this is it**: the predicate, the sentence, the two regenerated artefacts and a case
per branch. The predicate is now its criterion —

```ts
state !== 'UNRESOLVED' && Math.abs(deltaPp) >= detectablePp   // band replaces the question entirely
```

— and the row that certified `−7.50pp` at a `23.23pp` resolution now reads `false` with the sentence that says why.

**The one place the entry's own draft was wrong.** 34.197 wrote the predicate as
`detectablePp === undefined || Math.abs(deltaPp) >= detectablePp`. The first disjunct reads "no resolution was
estimated" as "any effect would have shown", which is the opposite of what `undefined` means in this lane: it is
what a pair with **no discordant task** reports, and a pair that changed no task has not resolved anything. Under
the draft, a `HARM` on such a pair would have gone green — a smaller false green than the one being fixed, in the
same gate, written by the same hand that was fixing it. It is dropped, and `pair-gates.ts` carries a case whose
only purpose is to keep it dropped. **An audit that prescribes code owes the same scrutiny as code that prescribes
nothing**, and this record has now paid for that lesson twice.

**The criterion changed too, and that is not cosmetic.** The old text ended *"or no direction is claimed"*, which
**neither** version implemented: an `UNRESOLVED` pair has always read `pass: false` here, because a row asking
whether an effect resolved is false when nothing resolved. Two disjuncts in a sentence and one in the code is how
the gate stopped saying one thing (34.161's class, in the opposite direction). The new text says only what is
computed: *may this pair be quoted as a finding?* — it publishes a direction **and** that direction clears its own
resolution.

**Regenerating evidence without re-measuring it.** The two committed artefacts could have been re-bought for ~$0.75
and would then have been two different draws of 40 tasks, with the row under test confounded by the draw. Instead
`pair-regrade.ts` recomputes the `l4-*` rows from the numbers the file already carries, and refuses three things:

| refusal | the failure it prevents |
| --- | --- |
| a file whose serialisation round trip is not byte-identical | a two-row re-grade that reindents 43 kB, hiding the change inside a rewrite |
| an input it cannot read (every accessor throws; there are no defaults) | `detectablePp: undefined` turning every regraded row false, which reads as a finding |
| a row the file predates | dating an artefact to a driver that did not have the gate |

The diff is four lines across two files, and both files are byte-identical to the committed blobs outside them:

| artefact | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `poc-l4-pair-official.json` | `pass: false`, old criterion | `pass: false`, new criterion |
| `poc-l4-pair-swapped.json` | `pass: true` at −10.81pp / 17.76pp | `pass: false`, with the sentence for it |

**The class, counted.** This is the fourth entry about a gate whose text and code disagreed, and the only one where
the text was the stricter of the two. The other three were silences — a gate that measured nothing and said
`true`. A false green is cheaper to fix and more expensive to catch: a silence eventually shows up as a number that
never moves, while a green row is the one a reader stops reading. Which is why the re-grade is now wired into
`pnpm check`: the row cannot drift from the rule again without the build failing first.

**And the instrument half is the useful half.** Nothing in this round changes a measurement. The withdrawal of the
serving policy (34.198) and the correction of its gate are the same lesson from two sides: on this lane, a reading
that cannot be checked against its own evidence is worth less than no reading, and a reading that *can* be checked
is worth keeping even when the policy it was built for is withdrawn.

### 34.200 The bound nobody computed, and four conclusions it invalidates

**What was measured.** Every pair artefact has carried the control's `pass^4` since R42, and the protocol has
carried a minimum detectable difference since the same round. Nobody multiplied them into the one number that
matters: **a memory can only repair a trial the bare agent failed, so `1 − controlPass⁴` is a hard ceiling on any
delta the fold can express.**

| fold | n | control | ceiling | resolution | margin |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `official` (committed) | 40 | 0.9000 | 10.00pp | 18.53pp | −8.53 |
| `swapped` (committed) | 74 | 0.8514 | 14.86pp | 17.76pp | −2.90 |
| R152 | 40 | 0.8500 | 15.00pp | 15.66pp | −0.66 |
| R152c | 40 | 0.8500 | 15.00pp | 23.23pp | −8.23 |
| R143 pooled | 114 | ≈0.86 | 14.0pp | 13.24pp | **+0.76** |

**Every fold but one has a ceiling below its resolution.** On those folds an oracle store — one that repairs every
failure and breaks nothing — would have produced a delta the design is forbidden from reading, and `V5-resolution`
would have blocked the claim with the arithmetic that proves it. So `UNRESOLVED` was not a reading about the store
on any of them; it was the design reporting its own limit.

**The five conclusions it touches, and how far the damage goes.**

| round | conclusion | status after this |
| --- | --- | --- |
| R133 | +2 net, 2.70% | consistent with any store between harmful and perfect; the fold could not separate them |
| R134 | `packLimit: 1` costs −5.00pp | a 15.00pp ceiling against a 17.50pp half-width: the direction is as unsupported as its opposite |
| R139 | +2.50pp, harm 15.63% | same fold shape, same limit |
| R141/R142/R151 | the counter has no headroom to test on | unchanged — this is the *other* headroom, and it was measured correctly |
| R152/R152c | the policy is withdrawn, the mechanism refuted | the withdrawal stands on R45's cost bar, which is a rule rather than a resolution; the *mechanism* claim was refuted by a third point, which is a different argument and survives |

None of these is a reason to un-publish a finding, and none is a licence to re-interpret an artefact. What they
share is a defect in the *reading*: each was written as a statement about memory when the file also contained,
unread, the statement that no memory could have been certified there.

**Why the record kept missing it.** Every round asked "how fine can this fold see" (resolution) and never "how far
can it move" (headroom). The two are computed from different columns of the same comparison — discordance for one,
the control's pass rate for the other — and only the first was ever put beside the delta in a printed line. The
`ceiling` block that has been in artefacts since R42 is a *different* ceiling: the scenario's task supply against
what a 5pp half-width would need. Two objects, one word, and the word was doing the work of hiding the second.

**The rule.** A design owes two bounds before it is dispatched, and both are computable from one earlier fold of the
same split: the finest effect it can distinguish, and the largest it can produce. **A fold whose headroom is below
its resolution cannot certify an effect at any treatment quality, and buying more of those folds is buying silence
with extra steps.** The arithmetic that selects the next fold — 164 pairs, retail's 114 plus airline's 50, for a
≈11.5pp resolution under a 15.0pp ceiling — took one subtraction and would have saved four dispatches.

**And the second-order lesson, which is the expensive one.** This record has spent three rounds learning that a
`p` value is not an effect size (34.167, 34.197) and one round learning that a line through two points is not a
mechanism (34.198). This is the third face of the same error: **a significant reading is not a resolved one**, and
six discordant pairs give `p = 0.0156` on a fold whose ceiling is 15.00pp and whose interval is [3, 27]. Every time
the error has been a quantity that looked like evidence and was a property of the instrument.

### 34.201 The delta was a mixture, and four rounds of "the mechanism moved" were its weights

**What was never divided.** Every delta this record has published is `(repairs − breaks) / n`. The two counts come
from disjoint populations — a repair only from a trial the control failed, a break only from one it passed — so the
delta is a **weighted average** whose weights are the corpus's composition:

```
delta = f·r − (1−f)·b
```

On τ² retail `f ≈ 0.14`. The delta therefore reports 14% of the store's behaviour on the population it exists for,
and 86% of its behaviour on the population where it can only lose. **Four dispatches were read as four facts about a
mechanism; pooling them gives one repair rate and one break rate, both stable, and a delta that is their weighted
difference.**

| draw | trials | failed | repaired | passed | broken | repair rate | break rate | break-even | net |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `official` | 40 | 4 | 4 | 36 | 3 | 100.0% | 8.3% | 11.1% | +2.50pp |
| `swapped` | 74 | 11 | 7 | 63 | 15 | 63.6% | 23.8% | 11.1% | −10.81pp |
| R152 | 40 | 6 | 3 | 34 | 2 | 50.0% | 5.9% | 8.8% | +2.50pp |
| R152c | 40 | 6 | 4 | 34 | 7 | 66.7% | 20.6% | 11.8% | −7.50pp |
| pooled | 194 | 27 | 18 | 167 | 27 | **66.7%** | **16.2%** | **10.8%** | −4.64pp |

**The finding, stated so it can be refuted.** The store repairs two thirds of the trials the bare agent fails
(`18/27`, 95% `[47.8%, 81.4%]`) and breaks one in six of the trials it already passes (`27/167`, `[11.4%, 22.5%]`).
Its break-even on this corpus is 10.78%; it is at 16.17%. A store that cut its break rate to 10% would read positive
on retail without changing its repair rate at all — which is a testable prediction and the first one this lane has
had for the harm side that does not require a bigger sample.

**Why this is an audit entry rather than a progress note.** The record has spent three rounds discovering that its
*instruments* could not certify what they reported: a resolution gate whose predicate was not its criterion (34.197),
a serving policy withdrawn on a delta below its own MDE (34.198), a headroom bound that made four folds silent
(34.200). This is the fourth face of one error and the most elementary: **the quantity itself was a mixture.** Each
earlier entry blamed a bound; this one says the number those bounds were applied to was never a rate.

**The bar's own price, which nobody computed either.** `tasksForDelta` inverts the protocol's formula to
`n = z²·d/effect²`. At this lane's observed discordance (0.232) the `−5pp` revert rule needs **729 paired trials**
to be resolvable; 3pp needs 2,024; the largest fold ever run is 74. So every revert this lane has made on the cost
bar — R134's `packLimit`, R152c's serving policy — was a decision taken on a reading the design could not certify,
and the rule's direction is the expensive one: it reverts on noise. That does not un-make the decisions (a cost rule
may legitimately be conservative), but it does mean the record must stop describing them as findings about harm.

**The two defects the round found in itself.**

| defect | how it surfaced | why it is the same class |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a duplicated `wilsonInterval` | `Multiple exports with the same name` broke 20 test files at import time; `reproduction.ts` has exported one since the BIRD lane | two formulas for one quantity is two answers — the failure mode `detectable.ts`'s header exists to prevent |
| a gate that failed on scheduling | 5,830 tests passed and the run exited 1 with `[vitest-worker]: Timeout calling "onTaskUpdate"` | a green reading that is not a measurement; a gate people re-run until it passes is a gate nobody reads |

**And a comparability fact that makes the rank claim weaker, recorded rather than repaired.** R152c carries
`metrics.k = 1` beside a field named `pass4`, and the pair protocol carries no `k`; the published bars are `pass^4`.
`bar_backbone_matches = 0` already disqualified the level comparison on backbone grounds. This disqualifies it
again on metric grounds, and the pair artefact cannot even show the mismatch because the field is absent — which is
the same shape as 34.199's finding one level down: *a claim the artefact cannot check is a claim a reader has to
take on trust.*

### 34.202 The re-grader repaired a recorded failure into a green

**Found by re-grading evidence this round had just recovered.** R152's pair artefact contains, in its own
`gates` array:

```
l4-projection-complete   false   memory: sidecarCensus, recallQueries
```

That row was written by the run that produced it: two fields the driver emitted did not reach the artefact.
`pnpm eval:l4-regrade` recomputes every `l4-*` row from the pair artefact, and for this row it reported

```
l4-projection-complete   fail -> pass   both arms carried every field the driver emitted
```

**The recomputation cannot fail.** The gate grades whether the driver's emitted fields arrived; the artefact
records the fields that *did* arrive; so a reader of the file can only ever confirm them. The same holds one row
over for `l4-rotation-reconciles`, whose inputs are the arm's `serveRotation` block and its `pack.ledger`, both
of which live in the arm artefact. A re-grader that recomputes a row from evidence it does not have does not
re-grade it, it overwrites it — and it overwrote it in the direction that hides a defect.

**Why this is the worst direction.** Every other error this record has caught made a claim weaker. This one made
a file say a defect had not happened. Had the allow-list not been introduced, the recovered R152 artefact would
have entered the repository asserting a projection completeness that the run itself denied, and no later read
would have had a reason to look.

**The repair, and why it is an allow-list.** Three rows have every input in the pair artefact —
`l4-paired`, `l4-effect-resolved`, `l4-same-split` — and those are re-graded. Everything else is preserved and
printed with the reason. A block-list of the two known-bad rows would have been wrong the other way: any row
added to `pairGates` later would be recomputed by default, which is the same defect with a delay. The fourth rule
is a sentence: a row graded under `TAU_BAND` is preserved too, because the band came through the dispatch
environment and the only trace of it is the row's own `actual` string (34.128).

**A second defect in the same function, found by the same test.** `inputOf` did not read `planted_arm`, so a
distractor arm's `l4-paired` row was recomputed as if the arm were a treatment and its sentence rewritten to
claim a cost the arm never claimed. Fixed by reading the field the artefact already carries — R57's distractors
now re-grade to "this row does not apply", which is what the rule says about them.

### 34.203 The metric was one level off, and no artefact could say so

**The fact.** All four registrations behind the pooled fold declare `trials: 1`. Read from
`prereg/R143-fold-official.md`, `R143-fold-swapped.md`, `R152-the-travel-budget.md` and
`R152c-the-paired-fold.md`; confirmed for R152 against its arm artefacts, recovered from run `44363599721`'s
evidence bundle, which carry `metrics.k = 1`, `episode_trials = 40` and 40 `per_trial` rows on both arms.

So every headline this record has published on τ² retail — **0.925, 0.900, 0.875, 0.850, 0.851, 0.775, 0.743** —
is a per-task pass rate over **one** trial, stored in a field named `pass4`, and compared to two bars that are
`pass^4` (0.575 and 0.6754).

**Why nothing caught it.** The arm wrote `metrics.k`; the pairing step passed the protocol
`trialCount: first.metrics?.k ?? 4`; and `trialCount` is read by no gate in the table. The pair artefact copied
`pass4` and not `k`, so the one file a reader opens had the metric's *name* and not its *value*. §PROGRESS 181
found this for R152c alone and queued it as a comparability note; the queue item is what R156 implements.

**The repair, three layers down.** `bar_k_matches` on the arm (beside `bar_backbone_matches`), `k`/`kAbsent`/
`barK`/`barKMismatch` on the pair, and a blocking `l4-same-k` that is **absent** rather than green when an arm
states nothing. `PUBLISHED_K` moved from a private constant in `bin/l4.ts` into `l4-scenario.ts`, so the three
readers that need it cannot drift.

**What the corrected comparison says.** Under trial independence, `pass^1 = 0.925` restates to `pass^4 = 0.7321`
and `0.85` to `0.522`. Against the baseline bar of 0.575: the memory is +15.7pp and the control is −5.3pp. The
memory also clears the competitor's submitted 0.6754 by 5.7pp — cross-sample and cross-backbone, as the
artefact's own notes say. **The published "+35pp" was a metric difference**, and the honest version is a
smaller claim that separates the treatment from its own control for the first time.

**The assumption is stated, not buried.** `restatedAtBarK.assumption` travels with the number: trials within a
task are treated as independent, which flatters a store whose misses cluster. An estimate with its premise
attached is a reading; the same number alone would be a rank claim this record cannot defend.

**And a reproducibility hole closed in passing.** Two of the four draws had never been committed, so `b* =
10.78%` could not be recomputed from the repository. Both are now in `eval/results/`, recovered through the
GitHub artefacts API — which needs the `Authorization` header stripped on the cross-host redirect to blob
storage, or the download answers 401 — and a census file records each draw's `k` with its evidence. A command
reconciles the census against the artefacts and exits 1 on disagreement.

### 34.204 The pay statistic divided by the corpus a second time, and three arms that helped were filed as losses

**The defect, in one struct.** `ExchangeReading` carried `helpPerHarm`, `hurdle`, `clearance`,
`requiredRepairRatePp` and `pays` is what it lacked. Net accuracy change is `repaired − broken`, so the bar on
`helpPerHarm` is **1**:

```
pays ⇔ repaired ≥ broken ⇔ helpPerHarm ≥ 1 ⇔ repairRate ≥ breakRate · (breakable / repairable).
```

The rightmost term is `hurdle = breakable / repairable`, and `requiredRepairRatePp = breakRatePp × hurdle` is the
same condition in rate units — which the module has computed, correctly, since R34. `clearance = helpPerHarm /
hurdle` therefore applies the corpus's odds twice, and the doc comment's claim, "a clearance below one is a
memory that loses", is false on committed data:

| arm | repaired | broken | net | `helpPerHarm` | `hurdle` | `clearance` | `requiredRepairRatePp` | `repairRatePp` | `pays` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| BIRD dev, lexicon grain | 78 | 67 | **+11** | 1.164 | 1.328 | **0.877** | 10.17% | 11.84% | **true** |
| BIRD dev, rule grain | 67 | 62 | **+5** | 1.081 | 1.349 | **0.801** | 9.49% | 10.26% | **true** |
| BIRD mini-dev, recall order | 19 | 17 | **+2** | 1.118 | 1.059 | 1.056 | — | — | **true** |
| BIRD train | 187 | 237 | −50 | 0.789 | 1.393 | 0.566 | 8.10% | 6.39% | false |

**Two fields of one struct disagree about one row**, and the disagreement is not a matter of interpretation:
`requiredRepairRatePp` is derived from `breakRatePp` and `hurdle`; `clearance` is derived from the counts. On the
lexicon row the first says the arm clears its break-even by 1.67 points of repair rate, the second says it loses.
Only one of them can be the pay test, and it is the one that agrees with `repaired ≥ broken`.

**What the record did with it.** R37's P4 was recorded as "its exchange rate clears the bare model hurdle —
0.8536 against 1.335 — holds: false", and R34's note says "§147 compared 0.79 against 1.0 and read a near miss
where the arithmetic shows a 43% shortfall". The 43% is the distance to **rate parity**, not to paying: 1 −
0.789 = 21% is the distance to paying, and a −0.71pp net on 7,000 questions *is* the near miss §147 called it.
The R34 "correction" replaced a correct bar with a corpus-invariant-looking one that is not invariant at all —
`clearance` moves with `breakable/repairable`, which is why it reads 0.108 on τ² retail and 0.566 on BIRD train
while the decision statistic reads 0.667 and 0.789.

**The second defect, found while fixing the first: no interval anywhere.** Every clearance comparison in this
record was a ratio of four counts with no interval on it. `exchange.ts` now computes the census with a cluster
bootstrap, and clustering is not cosmetic — BIRD dev is 1,534 questions over 11 databases:

| reading | n | clusters | delta [95%] | netOdds [95%] | verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| BIRD train | 7,000 | 58 | −0.71pp [−1.26, −0.18] | 0.789 [0.657, 0.942] | **loses** |
| BIRD dev, rule | 1,534 | 11 | +0.33pp [−0.61, +1.40] | 1.081 [0.857, 1.382] | unresolved |
| BIRD dev, lexicon | 1,534 | 11 | +0.72pp [−0.78, +2.39] | 1.164 [0.841, 1.650] | unresolved |
| BIRD mini-dev | 350 | 11 | +0.57pp [−3.48, +5.02] | 1.118 [0.500, 3.250] | unresolved |
| τ² retail, pooled | 194 | 114 | −4.64pp [−11.45, +1.60] | 0.667 [0.345, 1.167] | unresolved |

**The only resolved reading in the family is the loss.** Three arms pay by point estimate and none of them
resolves; the one reading large enough to decide says −0.71pp with an interval that excludes zero. And the τ²
"−4.64pp" this record has been narrating was never a finding: `l4-effect-resolved` had refused to call it one
since R153, and the prose had not caught up.

**Why this is the same defect class as 34.202 and 34.203.** In all three the record published a number whose
*relation to the decision* was never checked against the arithmetic that produced it: a re-grader that could not
fail, a metric field that was read by nobody, and now a ratio whose documented meaning contradicts its own
sibling field. The common repair is the same: make the decision a named predicate (`pass`, `k`, `pays`), derive
it from the stored counts, and gate on it.

**Where the field stands on the same question.** Memory Tax (arXiv 2610.34073) runs eleven memory systems against
naive retrieval and finds most losing, with 11.4%–22.6% of sampled facts partially or wholly lost during
construction and up to 38.0% never stored; the NeurIPS 2026 coverage-calibrated evaluation reports that
similarity and an LLM judge "rank the harmful cases no better than chance" and that where no comparable structure
exists the transfer sign is *unidentifiable*. This record's −0.71pp [−1.26, −0.18] is the same shape as the first,
and its three unresolved arms are the second's licensing rule rather than a failure of the measurement.

## 34.205 — The reader that inverted a third of what it counted

**Defect class: a classifier whose label is not the label the decision needs.** Three rounds have now found the
same shape in three different places — a re-grader that could not fail (34.202), a metric field nothing read
(34.203), a ratio that applied the corpus odds twice (34.204). This one is the first where the arithmetic was
right and the *reading* was wrong: the denial census counted a sentence as contradicting the gold when the
sentence was warning the executor away from a method the gold does not use either.

**What the first pass did.** `denialsOf` bound a cue to a construct, and `denialReadingOf` counted every such
binding whose construct the gold query uses as a *hit*. On BIRD train that produced 160 hits — and among eight
hand-audited samples, four were sentences of the form *"doing X without joining does not measure Y"*. The pack
was telling the executor that a shortcut fails. The gold joins. Read as a prescription the sentence inverts, and
the census scored the inversion as a contradiction.

**The fix, and why it is a flag rather than a filter.** A sentence carrying a failure predicate (`does not`,
`cannot`, `fails to`, `inflates`, `drops rows`) is a warning about the wrong method; `Denial.warning` records it,
`denialReadingOf` excludes it from `hits` and counts it in `warnings`, and the composition table publishes
`warn` beside `denial` and `hit`. A filter would have hidden the quantity; as a column it is a finding of its own
— **902 of 3,963 denials on train (23%) are warnings**, against 28 of 257 on dev (11%) and none on mini. A store
whose negative advice is a quarter warnings is a store that can be read backwards, and no outcome reading was
needed to establish it.

**What the correction changed in the numbers, and what it did not.** Train's contradicted stratum went from 160
to 127 cases and its delta from +1.25pp to +1.57pp; dev's stayed at 62. The direction did not move: three of four
arms read a *positive* delta in the contradicted stratum, so the axis is rejected either way. That is the useful
part of the audit — the conclusion was robust to the label error, and the error was still worth fixing, because a
record that publishes 160 when the answer is 127 has no way to notice the next sentence its reader inverts.

**The limitation, stated where the number is.** Eight hits were hand-audited: five genuine, three not (one bound
to a longer object, one conflated select-list `DISTINCT` with `COUNT(DISTINCT)`, one conditional). A lexical
reader is about five-in-eight precise. That is enough to reject a large effect — 127 cases at +1.57pp cannot
carry the corpus's −0.71pp — and not enough to establish a small one, which is why the census publishes `denial`
beside `hit` and why the round's conclusion is a rejection rather than a discovery.

**The structural finding that outlived the defect.** The store distilled **210 statements for 7,000 questions**;
39 of them reach two or more databases and entirely compose **60.6% of packs**. The pack is not a library of
case-specific experience with a few bad entries — it is a generic curriculum with a thin layer of local notes.
That is the Memory Tax shape (11.4–22.6% of facts lost during construction, up to 38.0% never stored) with a
different loss mechanism: not facts dropped, but facts abstracted until nothing case-specific remains. It also
explains why every content axis so far has been null — coverage (AM.15), imported identifiers (R31), and now
denial have all been asked of a store that has little content about any particular case to be right or wrong
about.

## 34.206 — The interval that was comparing databases while it described sentences

**Defect class: an estimator whose unit of comparison is finer than its claimed unit of inference.** The last four
audits have found a re-grader that could not fail (34.202), a metric field nothing read (34.203), a ratio that
applied the corpus odds twice (34.204), and a classifier whose label inverted a third of what it counted (34.205).
This one is the first in which **the number was right for the question it answered and wrong for the question it was
printed under**.

**What R158 printed.** The all-boilerplate stratum at **−0.94pp [−1.50, −0.40]**, described as "the only stratum
interval in the table that excludes zero" and read as a content effect: packs made entirely of lessons from other
databases lose about a point.

**What it measured.** Which cases received all-boilerplate packs is not random: the store has local notes for some
databases and none for others, so the stratum and its complement are **different databases** — and databases differ
in difficulty. The estimator was a between-database comparison with a clustered interval that resampled databases,
which is internally consistent and answers "does the all-boilerplate stratum sit lower than the rest of the corpus",
not "does an all-boilerplate pack cost anything".

**The corrected estimate.** Re-estimated inside a database — exposed against rest, weighted by exposed cases,
databases as fixed effects — the same contrast is:

| stratum | cases | comparable databases | delta [95%] |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| none | 948 | 37 | **+1.38pp [−1.47, +4.32]** |
| mixed | 1,811 | 44 | −0.09pp [−1.96, +1.59] |
| all-boilerplate | 2,617 | 43 | **−1.34pp [−3.58, +0.71]** |

The sign survives — it even grows — and the interval triples in width, because 15 of 58 databases have no
case-specific cases at all and the within-database comparison loses a third of the corpus. So R158's headline was
**an estimate whose resolution came from variation between databases, attributed to variation in content**.

**Why this is the second withdrawal and not a scandal.** 34.204 withdrew a ratio that applied the corpus odds twice;
this withdraws an interval whose estimator carried a confound its vocabulary hid. Both were found by the same
method — re-estimating the same quantity with the unit of inference raised to the unit of the claim — and both were
published with the original number beside the correction rather than in place of it. A record that can only add
findings is not measuring; it is accumulating.

**What replaced it, and why the replacement is stronger.** `contrastOf` is the same estimator for *any* stratum, so
the correction cost nothing to write and everything to notice. Applying it to the pack's *prescriptions* — does the
pack name a construct the gold does not use — gives **−1.83pp [−3.13, −0.51]** on 4,894 of 7,000 cases, the first
content axis in this record to resolve away from zero. That reading is not a rescue of the withdrawn one: the
boilerplate stratum and the unsupported stratum overlap but are not the same cases, and the unresolved circulation
contrast is printed beside the resolved prescription contrast in the same table.

**The residual defect this audit does not fix.** Receipt is chosen by retrieval, so within a database the exposed
cases are still the ones the statement looked relevant to. A statement can therefore read as harmful because it is
retrieved for the cases memory cannot help, which is a fact about retrieval and not about the sentence. No
committed artefact separates those two readings, and the module says so where the estimator is defined rather than
in a limitations section. Nothing in this round establishes that rewriting a statement would recover a point; it
establishes that the pack's prescriptions co-occur with the loss and that the two most-delivered of them carry
half of it.

## 34.207 — The extractor that manufactured the number which explained twelve nulls

**Defect class: a measurement whose resolution floor was read as a property of its object.** The previous audit
found an estimator comparing at a finer grain than it claimed (34.206). This one is worse in a specific way: the
wrong number **supported the conclusion that was already being drawn**, and it would have been published as the
explanation for eleven earlier nulls.

**What the first implementation did.** `columnReuseOf` extracted a query's columns with the obvious expression —
everything between backticks — and intersected the two sets. On BIRD dev it reported a median overlap of exactly
**0.000**, with only 2.7% of pairs sharing half their columns. Read at face value that says BIRD's consecutive
questions have nothing in common, which is the strongest possible evidence for the hypothesis the round was
written to test: no reusable answer, therefore no axis that operates on answers can work.

**Why it was false.** The extractor was measuring its own reach. **Only 8% of this corpus's gold queries contain a
backticked identifier**, because BIRD writes `SELECT player_api_id FROM Player_Attributes` without quoting. For the
other 92% the extractor returned an empty set, and an empty set has zero Jaccard with everything — including
itself. The reported 0.000 was therefore not "no overlap"; it was "no columns found", repeated 1,411 times.

**How it was caught.** By a disagreement between two columns of one table rather than by a test: the same script
reported that 46.7% of pairs share **all** their tables. Two answers in one database using the same table and no
common column, for half the corpus, is possible; for the other half to then report zero columns *and* a positive
table overlap is the shape of an extractor that finds tables and not columns. The table list came from `FROM`/
`JOIN` position in the tokenizer; the column list came from a regex. One of them was working.

**The corrected measurement.** `sqlShapeOf().columns` excludes keywords, tables, aliases, output labels, CTEs and
function names, and reads quoted identifiers with spaces as one name — `Free Meal Count (K-12)` is one column, not
five tokens. On the same corpus the median overlap is **0.500** and **50.1%** of pairs share at least half their
columns, against 2.7% before. The finding that survives is much narrower than the one the broken number supported:
reuse is real, it is *not* the binding constraint on average, and the band where it is highest still fails to
replicate (top band **+2.69pp [0.00, +5.66]** on dev against **−1.04pp [−2.20, +0.18]** on train).

**Why this one is recorded rather than quietly fixed.** A wrong number that argues against the project gets
re-checked; a wrong number that argues **for** the project's current hypothesis gets published. The 0.000 was the
second kind, and the only reason it did not reach a document is that a table-overlap column in the same printout
disagreed with it. The rule this audit adds is narrow and mechanical: **a measurement that returns its extreme
value should be asked what it cannot see** — an overlap of exactly zero, an accuracy of exactly 100%, a coverage of
exactly 0 — because the extreme is where a broken instrument and a real result are hardest to tell apart.

**What it does not change.** The round's verdict. Reuse is measurable, the median is 0.500, and the band reading
still flips between corpora. What changes is the sentence that can be written about it: not "BIRD carries no
reuse", but "BIRD carries reuse that does not predict where memory pays". The weaker claim is the true one, and
the gate now compares the tokenizer's reading byte for byte so that a later regex cannot quietly return.


## 34.208 — The pin that was never in force, and the import it was written to prevent

`textworld 1.6.1` imports `ParserConfig` from `tatsu.infos`. A fresh resolve takes 5.15.1, which does not carry the
name, and the failure surfaces at `textworld.logic.parser` rather than at install time — a traceback three frames
deep in a dependency the workflow does not mention.

The workflow answered it with `pip install 'tatsu==5.8.3'`, as its own step. That step ran **after** the textworld
install and **after** the `python -c "import textworld"` check that was there to catch exactly this. The pin
therefore never constrained the resolve it was written for, and the file read as a solved problem while two runs
failed on the same line.

This is the third time in this record that a control existed and did not apply — a floor that retired nothing, an
arm whose cap was never reached, and now a pin that ran second. The shape is the same each time: **the control was
written where it could be read rather than where it executes**, and a reader checking the file would have found it
satisfying.

The fix is that both constraints go in one command, so the resolver sees them together. The check now prints both
versions before any textworld module is imported, because the twelfth run is the one that printed `5.15.1` and
closed the question.

## 34.209 — The gold plan that cannot be replayed, and a failure that looks like a broken driver

Every `.tw-pddl` file carries a `walkthrough` field. It is the obvious thing to assert against before a model is
in the loop, and three runs were spent asserting against it.

It is written in the first-release symbolic coordinates the embodied agent used —
`take toiletpaper_bar__minus_00_dot_12_bar__plus_00_dot_95_bar__plus_01_dot_63 from
toilet_bar__minus_00_dot_54_bar__plus_00_dot_00_bar__plus_01_dot_49`. The text environment refuses every step
with `Nothing happens.`, which is also what it returns when the driver is not stepping at all. The two are
indistinguishable from the log, and the log is all a failing CI run gives you.

Two earlier hypotheses were wrong in ways that kept the defect alive: the first read `games[0]` and blamed the
plan's identity, the second read the same file and said so in the log — which made the second run look like a
better experiment and was the same experiment. The environment publishes `extra.gamefile`, the path it actually
opened, and reading that removed the identity question while leaving the format question, which is the real one.

The gate now asserts what the driver needs rather than what the file offers: reset states a task and publishes
admissible commands, an admissible command changes the observation, an inadmissible one is refused in the
environment's words, and a twelve-step walk keeps the episode alive. **A gate on the score would have been a
statement about a model the job does not call** — and the temptation to write one is exactly why the job prints
its own call count.

## 34.210 — A registration that lied in its own header, and the schema that had no slot for a second lane

The R162 registration was written into `prereg/` with a header describing what the arm actually is: three
arms, 134 games, an identity mode, a cap of twenty, a discordance assumption and the resolution those imply.
`prereg-pack.test.ts` failed it on the push, and it failed it correctly — but not for the reason the file was
written.

`prereg.ts` owns a fixed header schema. `REQUIRED_KEYS` is `id, step, opened, arms, sample, gates`; `split` is
one of `minidev`/`dev`/`train`; `gates` must match `^V\d+$` and every `V`-code is defined in
`tau2-gates.ts` against a τ² artefact field. None of those describe an ALFWorld arm. The `split` is
`valid_unseen`, the gates are contract assertions over a textworld environment, and there is no fold partition
to grade. Honouring the schema would have meant writing `gates: V0,V1,V5,V6,V8` — five codes whose grading code
would never run against this lane — which is a header that lies about what will be measured, in the one artefact
whose entire purpose is to be read by every later round.

**The check that fired was the right check; the slot was missing.** The registration now lives at
`eval/drivers/alfworld/REGISTRATION.md` and says so in its own second paragraph, and the schema gap is this
entry. The gap is narrow and it has a shape: `prereg/` was built for lanes that share a dispatch (`sota.yml`),
a store and a gate family, and the moment a lane with a different environment and a different gate family needs
the same "registered before it ran" discipline, the directory has no way to accept it. The fix, when a second
such lane exists, is a `lane` discriminator that selects a schema rather than a free-form header — building it
for one lane would be a generalization with a sample of one.

**What this round would have shipped without the gate.** A `prereg/` file whose header named five gates the
lane does not run, discovered by whoever next read that file to decide whether the arm had been
pre-registered. The gate caught it in ninety seconds on a push, which is the cheapest place for it to be caught
and the reason the registration is checked on every push rather than only on a dispatch.

## 34.211 — The snapshot that describes an older tree, and the two gates that caught what the round did not

Adding `rule-bank.ts` broke the build twice, and neither break was the one the round was watching for. Both are
worth recording because both are gates doing exactly the job they were built for against an author who had
forgotten they existed.

**The first was the registration schema**, recorded as 34.210. The second was the coupling ledger: `ci.yml` runs
`scripts/check-coupling-ledger.mjs`, whose tenth check is

```js
committed.scanned === fresh.scanned &&
  committed.totals?.modules === fresh.totals?.modules &&
  (committed.gates ?? []).every((gate) => gate.pass)
```

— the committed snapshot must describe the tree it was taken from. A new module moves `totals.modules` from 256
to 257 and `totals.lines` from 73,349 to 73,635, so the snapshot in `eval/results/poc-coupling.json` became a
description of a tree that no longer existed. The check's own comment is explicit that module *counts* are
deliberately not pinned anywhere else, because "adding a module is not a regression, and a check that fails when
the tree grows teaches the project to edit the check". This is the one place a count belongs: not as a target,
but as the snapshot's own identity.

**The diff was verified before it was committed**, and that is the part worth keeping. Eight fields moved:

| field | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `scanned` / `totals.modules` | 256 | 257 |
| `totals.lines` | 73,349 | 73,635 |
| `layers[3].modules` / `.lines` | 191 / 57,312 | 192 / 57,598 |
| `totals.coupledShare` | 0.1597 | 0.1591 |
| `statement` | "... 1,956 of 73,349 production lines across 256 modules ..." | "... 1,956 of 73,635 production lines across 257 modules ..." |

`sql` stayed at 7 modules with every line adapter, `core` stayed at 0 coupled of 47, and the five package edges
stayed downward. A snapshot regenerated without that comparison would have been a rewrite of the ledger by
whoever happened to run the tool — which is precisely how a committed measurement stops being one.

**Why the local run passed and CI did not, which is the subtle half.** The first invocation in this round was
`npx tsx packages/eval/src/bin/coupling.ts` with no `POC_RESULT_DIR`, so it wrote straight to
`eval/results/poc-coupling.json` and the working tree's "committed" copy became the fresh one. Every subsequent
local check then compared the new snapshot to itself and passed, while CI compared the *pushed* snapshot to the
new walk and failed. **A tool whose default output path is also its reference path cannot detect its own
staleness locally**; the CI job, which writes to `$RUNNER_TEMP` and reads the repository copy, is the only place
the comparison is real. That asymmetry is not a defect — the workflow was written that way on purpose — but it
means a green local `pnpm eval:coupling-check` is not evidence about the push.

**The two-gate tally for the round.** Four pushes, three red builds, and every red was a gate rather than a
test: the registration schema, the coupling snapshot, and the first one in this series (the `reset`-on-a-shell
`AttributeError`, which the smoke pass caught at 42 seconds). No test was weakened to get green, and no count was
pinned to make a number stop moving.

## 34.212 — The table that says it is recomputed on every push, and has never been

Found while regenerating the coupling snapshot for 34.211, and not fixed in that round because the fix needs a
decision the round had no basis for making.

`README.md` carries a layer table under the heading "Where the scenario actually is: 1,766 lines, seven modules,
and a gate for the rest", introduced with the sentence *"`pnpm eval:coupling` recomputes it from the source tree on
every push"*. The committed snapshot says something else:

| layer | README | `eval/results/poc-coupling.json` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `core` | 37 modules, 6,821 lines | **47 modules, 10,588 lines** |
| `protocol` | 2 modules, 1,215 lines | **3 modules, 1,922 lines** |
| `sql` | 7 modules, 1,766 lines | 7 modules, **1,956 lines** |
| `eval` | 76 modules, 24,799 lines | **192 modules, 57,598 lines** |
| `browser` | 2 modules, 280 lines | 2 modules, 280 lines |
| `node` | 6 modules, 1,282 lines | 6 modules, **1,291 lines** |

Four of six rows disagree, `sql` agrees on modules and not on lines, and `browser` agrees on both. That pattern is
the diagnosis: the table was written once, by hand, at a point when `sql` was 1,766 lines, and has been edited only
where a module was added to the sentence rather than to the table. **A number described as recomputed, and
maintained by hand, is worse than a number described as hand-written** — the first one stops a reader from
checking.

**Why it is not fixed here.** The README says *production modules*, and the snapshot counts everything the walk
scans, including `bin/` entrypoints and `__tests__`. Replacing the table with the snapshot's numbers would answer a
question nobody asked (how many lines of test code name a database) and would silently change the claim the section
exists to make — *"the scenario is a fifth of the production tree and none of it is in the library"*. The right fix
is a `productionModules` count in `coupling.ts` so the table and the gate read the same walk, and that is a
modification to a gate rather than an edit to a table, which is not a thing to do at the end of a round that has
already spent three red builds on gates.

**What is recorded instead.** The numbers above, so the next round starts from the disagreement rather than from
the table. The section's headline — 1,766 lines and seven modules — is true of `sql` at the snapshot's own count of
1,956 only in the sense that `sql` is still seven modules; the line count moved by 190 and nothing in the repository
noticed.


## 34.213 — A candidate queue that named four mechanisms nobody had read, and the phrase that replaced the reading

The R162 report ended its third answer with four competitor mechanisms offered as R164+ candidates: H²R's high/low
memory separation, an FSM graph memory, AWM's workflow abstraction, and **"Synapse's contrastive retrieval"**. The
user asked the question that should have come first — *are these microglia's, or are they cortex's?* — and answering
it required actually reading them, which had not been done.

**What reading them found, in order of how bad it is.**

*First, "Synapse's contrastive retrieval" describes a system that does not exist.* There are two systems called
Synapse and neither does this. **Synapse (ICLR 2024, Zheng et al.)** is state abstraction + trajectory-as-exemplar
prompting + exemplar memory retrieved by **embedding similarity** — MiniWoB++ 99.2% across 64 tasks using
demonstrations from 48, and a 56% relative step-success improvement on Mind2Web. **Synapse (ACL 2026, Jiang et al.,
UGA)** is a **dual-layer associative** memory with **spreading activation** that refuses when evidence is thin —
LoCoMo **F1 40.5**, +7.2 over the next best agentic system, at **95% fewer tokens** than full-context methods.
"Contrastive retrieval" is neither. It is a phrase that sounds like a mechanism, was never checked against a
source, and would have been written into a queue as though it named one.

*Second, the same word sits on both sides of the boundary.* The ICLR system reports **task success rates**; the ACL
system reports **LoCoMo F1**, on questions asked across months of conversation with no task and no prompt skeleton —
the same family as the LongMemEval number cortex reports. One name, two benchmarks, two projects. Any rule phrased
as "is it about memory" puts them in the same bucket; only a rule phrased against **the score the authors report**
separates them.

*Third, AWM was already registered and priced.* Appendix X.2 carries its three deltas (WebArena 23.5 → 35.5,
Mind2Web 36.2 → 45.1), the three-column comparison against ExpeL and this lane's store at R92, PRAXIS's
counter-argument, and a price: **P2, roughly $0.70 + code**, for values replaced by typed slots at write. Offering it
as a new candidate is not a plan; it is a second copy of a row that already had a price and a failure mode.

**Why none of the three was caught by anything.** `COMPETITIVE.md` has a registration discipline that every
mechanism it documents satisfies: unit, baseline, published delta, whether the competitor ablates it, and where it
is injected. AWM passed through it in R92 and Appendix AA. H²R, the FSM and both Synapses never did — they were
named in a *report*, which is prose that no gate reads. **The registry is a gate, and a candidate that reaches the
queue through the report rather than through the registry bypasses it entirely.** Four names entered the queue and
one of them had no referent.

**The fix is a checked table rather than a resolution to be careful.** `ROADMAP.md` now carries a
`### Candidate registry` whose columns are `candidate`, `the unit it changes`, `side`, `registered`, `its own
delta`, `episodes needed`, `cost at 2 arms`. `scripts/check-docs.mjs` fails the push unless every row names a side
(`microglia` or `cortex`), cites exactly one `AM.n` that resolves to a heading in `COMPETITIVE.md`, and states an
episode count. The check was verified against three deliberate breaks — a renamed definition, a row with
`side: both`, an unclosed fence — before it was committed, because a gate that has never failed has not been tested.

**What the check cannot do, stated so it is not mistaken for more.** It cannot tell whether a row's delta is the
competitor's real number, and it cannot tell whether `microglia` is the right side for a mechanism nobody has read.
It enforces that the columns are filled, which is the difference between a queue and a list of things that sound
important — not the difference between a right answer and a wrong one.

**The finding that outlives the table.** Two of the four names carry published effects *smaller than this split can
resolve at any price*: the FSM's +5.23pp needs **861 episodes** and H²R's +3.5pp needs **1,923**, against a
held-out set of **134**. Repeating 134 games fourteen times narrows the estimate of the same 134 games' difference;
it does not add one independent sample. So those two are not expensive here, they are **unmeasurable here**, and a
queue that listed them with a price tag would have made an unmeasurable hypothesis look purchasable — which is the
same failure mode as AM.22's 16.4-point spread, arrived at from the other end.

**Cost of the correction.** Reading, and nothing else: no dispatch, no model call, `¥0`. The expensive version of
this mistake is the one where the queue is executed first and the reading happens when the result is null.


## 34.214 — "CI is green" was true of one repository, and this one had no gate at all for a month

Found while checking whether the workflow this round added was the first one. It was — and the reason is not that
nobody thought of it.

| when (UTC) | what happened to `.github/workflows/ci.yml` in this repository |
| --- | --- |
| 2026-10-20 02:47 | created, in `287f074c` — *"feat: microglia design, monorepo POC, and live API evidence"* |
| 2026-10-20 03:23 | ran once, conclusion `success` (run 39364021246) |
| 2026-10-20 04:57 | **removed**, in `a63d350a` — *"docs: split the internal documents from the product repository"* |
| 2026-10-20 → 2026-11-20 | **no workflow file exists in this repository at all** |

**Removing it was defensible and the split probably should have removed it.** A repository of five markdown files
cannot usefully run `tsc`, `vitest` or a benchmark build, and carrying a copy of the product's CI into the docs
repository would have produced a workflow that either failed for the wrong reason or was neutered with
`continue-on-error`. That is not the defect.

**The defect is what every round since then reported.** Each round's summary says the CI is green. Each of those
statements was true of `AgentiX-E/microglia` and **silently vacuous about this repository**, which had no gate, no
workflow and therefore nothing that could be red. Thirty-odd rounds of "all workflows green" while one of the two
repositories in scope had no workflows. The phrase was not a lie; it was an unquantified claim, and the quantifier it
was missing is *which repositories*.

**Why nothing corrected it, stated exactly.**

*The local working copy is not a git repository.* `cd microglia-docs && git status` returns `fatal: not a git
repository`, because the directory is a set of files pushed through the GitHub Data API rather than a clone. So
`git log`, `git status` and every habit that notices "a file is gone" are unavailable in this tree — a deletion made
by an earlier round is invisible to every later one.

*Every status check this programme runs queries `AgentiX-E/microglia`.* The run listings, the job step listings and
the failure log fetches all name the product repository. A repository that is never queried cannot report a problem,
and the check that would have caught it — *does each repository in scope have at least one workflow whose latest run
is green* — was never written because the question was never phrased as a set.

**What now exists, and what it cost.** `.github/workflows/docs.yml` runs three checks in `scripts/check-docs.mjs`:
fence parity in every document, every `AM.n` reference resolving to a heading in `COMPETITIVE.md`, and every
candidate-registry row naming a side, a registration and an episode count. The check was broken deliberately three
ways before it was committed, and it then failed on this round's own prose before passing — all three recorded in
PROGRESS 193.1. Its first run, `44656232936`, is `success`, and it is the first green run in this repository whose
green means something ran.

**The sentence that should have been written every round, and now is.** *CI is green in both repositories* — and
where a repository has no workflow, that is a fact to report rather than a colour to assume. A gate that does not
exist cannot fail, which is the cheapest possible way to have a perfect record and the most expensive way to discover
one.

## 34.215 — The prompt prefix that was counted from the wrong strings, four times, and quoted as a price

Found while extracting the few-shot transcripts into the repository so that `agent.py` could render them instead of
describing them. The registration quoted six counts, one per ALFWorld task type, and a mean of **3,574** characters
as the fixed prefix of every prompt. Two of the six were right.

| task type | quoted | measured | what was counted |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `pick_and_place` | 3,199 | **3,199** | correct |
| `look_at_object` | 3,096 | **3,738** | not the `_0`/`_1` pair |
| `pick_clean_then_place` | 3,348 | **4,328** | not the `_0`/`_1` pair |
| `pick_heat_then_place` | 3,732 | **3,837** | close, still wrong |
| `pick_cool_then_place` | 3,782 | **4,403** | not the `_0`/`_1` pair |
| `pick_two_obj_and_place` | 4,286 | **4,286** | correct |
| **mean** | **3,574** | **3,965** | **11% low** |

The file carries three transcripts per task type — `react_<kind>_0`, `_1`, `_2` — and its own template says *"Here
are two examples"*, so the pair is `_0` and `_1`. That much the registration had right; the counts had drifted from
the strings they claimed to describe, and nothing compared them. The means differ by a factor that is inside the
noise of a hand count and outside the noise of a price: **11% of the prefix is 11% of every turn of every episode**,
and both arm quotes in the registration were computed from it.

**Why it could not have been caught where it was written.** The number was produced by reading a file on
`api.github.com` in a session that then ended. Nothing in the repository held the strings, so no test could count
them, no `diff` could show them, and the next round had only the sentence. That is the same failure 34.212 records
about a layer table, and the repair is the same shape: **put the artefact in the tree and assert against it.**

`eval/drivers/alfworld/prompts/alfworld-examples.json` now carries the twelve transcripts with their source blob
(`2b2093ef`), the extraction rule, and the two template strings; `test_agent.py` pins all six counts. The
registration's table is corrected and the two price rows are explicitly marked as computed at the old prefix rather
than silently rescaled — rescaling would multiply a guess about `chars/token` by a correction factor, and the 20-game
calibration is about to replace both rows with the provider's own `usage` anyway.

## 34.216 — The lexical anchor matched on `the`, so the retrieved arm was the always-in arm with extra steps

`agent.py`'s `retrieved` arm selects the bank entries whose words the observation already contains. The first
implementation tokenised both sides and counted the intersection, which is correct and useless: `the`, `is`, `a`,
`you`, `in` appear in every observation and in almost every rule, so **every entry overlapped every observation** and
the arm rendered the whole bank — the `always-in` arm, with a retriever's steps added and a different header.

The test that found it was written to assert the opposite: a bank holding only *"the fridge is cold"* must render
nothing in a room with no fridge in it. It rendered one entry, and the reason was one shared stopword.

The repair is a stopword list (`STOPWORDS`) subtracted from both sides. The larger point is what the defect would
have cost had it shipped: the registration's second prediction is `always-in` beats `retrieved`, and a `retrieved`
arm that is `always-in` under the hood makes that comparison **structurally zero** — the run would have produced a
clean null, reported it, and the null would have been a bug. A retrieval arm that cannot withhold anything is not a
weak treatment; it is no treatment, and it looks exactly like one that failed.

## 34.217 — The layer table said it was recomputed on every push, and 34.212 is now closed

34.212 recorded, without fixing it, that `README.md`'s layer table claimed `pnpm eval:coupling` recomputed it on
every push while the table itself was typed once by hand. It had drifted by an order of magnitude in the layer the
paragraph is about:

| layer | published | measured |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `core` | 37 modules, 6,821 lines | **47 modules, 10,588 lines** |
| `protocol` | 2, 1,215 | **3, 1,922** |
| `sql` | 7, 1,766 | **7, 1,956** |
| `eval` | 76, 24,799 | **192, 57,632** |
| `node` | 6, 1,282 | **6, 1,291** |

Three repairs, and the third is the one that makes the other two hold. `coupling.ts` now exports the scan's own
definition of a production module (`NON_PRODUCTION_DIRS`, `isProductionModulePath`) so that the command and the gate
share one definition instead of two copies of a skip list. `LayerTotal` gained `productionModules` beside `modules`,
because the published column is literally *production modules* and a reader is entitled to know that `__tests__` is
not in the denominator. And `readme-layers.test.ts` walks the tree itself, parses the table and the two sentences
that quote it, and fails on any disagreement — which is what "recomputed on every push" has to mean if it is to be
true.

The test found the drift a second time before it found the corpus: it failed on the `eval` row by 34 lines, because
the round had added 34 lines to `coupling.ts` after the table was corrected. That is the gate doing its job on its
own author.

## 34.218 — The skeleton could not represent a model giving up, so it could not have measured one

The first calibration dispatch (`44671462382`, 04:00:36–04:03:24 UTC) drove **zero games**. On the first one,
`pick_cool_then_place_in_recep-Bread-None-CounterTop-10`, the model reached the end of its patience inside the
50-step cap and began narrating:

> I was unable to complete the task. I found bread 1 on countertop 3, picked it up, and cooled it using the fridge.
> However, when I attempted to put it on the cou…

`parse_reply` read it as a thought, which is correct — it is not a command, and the competitor's own parser would
have wrapped it as `> think: …` too. The loop, however, had been written to **raise** on three thoughts in a row, on
the theory that three means the format was not learned. It raised, the job ended, and the artefact was never written.

**The rule was wrong about what it was protecting.** A model that gives up is not an infrastructure failure; it is
the failure this arm exists to count. An arm whose question is *does the memory help* cannot have a skeleton that
refuses to represent the model failing — the event it most needs to record is the one it crashes on. And the theory
was wrong on its own terms too: three thoughts in a row is exactly what the competitor's *own* transcripts contain
at their most deliberate, so the threshold would have failed on the format it was copied from.

The repair changes what a turn is. **A thought spends one of the `max_steps` turns exactly as an action does.** The
episode ends when its budget does, `steps` counts model turns, `actions` and `thoughts` sit beside it, and a run of
three thoughts is a counted `stall`. A pass in which **no** episode produced an action still fails, because that is
a skeleton nobody read rather than a low score.

Two consequences, both in the conservative direction. The worst case per episode is now `max_steps` calls, where
before it was `max_steps` actions plus an unbounded number of thoughts — the quote loses a tail it could not bound.
And `--trace N` prints the first N replies, because a calibration's first three readings are what the model actually
sent, not what it scored: a rate computed over a format the model ignored is a rate about the format.

## 34.219 — "Never terminated" meant two opposite things, and the diagnostic pass was read as a defect

The second dispatch (`44672529440`, 04:09:57–04:10:47 UTC) failed with `1 episodes never terminated`. It had driven
its single game correctly for twenty turns and stopped, because `--max-steps 20` is smaller than any ALFWorld game.

The field was `truncated = not done`, copied from `floor.py`, where it means the right thing: the floor pass uses
the environment's own 50-step cap, so an episode the environment did not end is an episode the driver cut off — a
defect. On a model pass the cap may be deliberately smaller than a game needs, and then the same field reports the
design working as an error.

Two endings, split: `budget_exhausted` is the pass's own cap doing its job and is **reported**; `truncated` is the
environment undecided with turns to spare and **fails the run**. The distinction is one nobody would get from a
rate, which is why it had to be a field: both endings score zero, and only one of them means the lane is broken.

The trace from that same run is the other half of the answer, and it is the first evidence that the skeleton works:

| turn | reply |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | `> think: To solve the task, I need to find and take a potato, then heat it with microwave…` |
| 2–5 | `> go to fridge 1` · `> open fridge 1` · `> go to countertop 1` · `> go to countertop 2` |
| 6 | `> think: Now I find a potato (1). Next, I need to take it.` |
| 7 | `> take potato 1 from countertop 2` |
| 9–10 | `> go to microwave 1` · `> heat potato 1 with microwave 1` |
| 12 | `> go to garbagecan 1` |

That is the task's own plan, in the competitor's format, at 1.05 s per call. The arm is capable and the win was four
turns away when the diagnostic budget ran out — which is what makes the headroom question worth the twenty games.

## 34.220 — A fifth of the model's actions are refused, and the fix is a new arm rather than a repair

The calibration's counters, which are the reason they are in the artefact: of **728 calls** over twenty games,

| counter | value | share of calls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| actions accepted by the environment | 460 | 63.2% |
| thoughts | 257 | 35.3% |
| actions refused (`invalid_actions`) | **149** | **20.5%** |
| of which not even a command (`off_space_actions`) | 11 | 1.5% |

So 138 of the 149 refusals were **well-formed commands for a world the model was not in**: `> go to desk 1` when
the room has no desk 1, `> take mug 2 from shelf 3` when mug 2 is elsewhere. The model is not failing to follow the
format — it is failing to know where things are, which is precisely the knowledge a memory of previous attempts
would carry.

**It is not repaired, and the temptation to repair it is the point of this entry.** Handing the model
`admissible_commands` — which the environment publishes on every turn and `agent.py` already reads — would raise the
score immediately and by a large margin. It would also make `none` no longer mean *the corpus's own difficulty*:
every arm would be run with an oracle for the action space, the arm's absolute score would stop being comparable to
any published ReAct number, and the memory's contribution would be measured against a control that had already been
given a different kind of help. The list is therefore not passed, and the refusal rate is reported instead.

**What it does change is the queue.** "Where objects live" is a memory whose effect this lane can now size before
spending: at 20.5% refusals, a pack that removed a third of them would be worth roughly six points of turn budget.
That is a different mechanism from the rule bank, it belongs on the microglia side (it changes what the prompt
carries, not the substrate), and it needs its own registration and its own arm rather than an edit to this one.
Registering it is the work; the temptation is to slip it in as an improvement to `none`, which would be a control
that quietly became a treatment.

## 34.221 — The boundary was drawn by a score, and what crossed it left as a prompt rather than a branch

The R163 report ended with four competitor mechanisms offered as candidates. The user asked the question that
ordering should have forced first — *are these microglia's or cortex's?* — and 34.213 answered it for the queue. This
entry records what happened next: three of the mechanisms were found to belong to the substrate rather than to the
delivery layer, and they were handed to a session that owns `AgentiX-E/cortex` instead of being built here.

**The test is the score the authors report, not the name of the mechanism.** That is 34.213's finding and it is the
whole rule:

| what the authors report | whose work it is |
| --- | --- |
| a **task success rate** under a fixed model and a fixed prompt (ALFWorld, τ², BIRD, WebShop, Mind2Web) | **microglia** — the pack's shape and selection |
| a score from **asking the store directly**, with no task and no prompt skeleton (LoCoMo F1, LongMemEval) | **cortex** — the substrate |
| an ablation of *with this block / without this block* | microglia |
| an ablation of *decay schedule on/off*, *one layer / two layers*, *bitemporal or not* | **cortex** |

The reason is not taxonomic tidiness. `microglia`'s product is a block of text rendered into somebody else's prompt,
and every point it reports is bought by some task succeeding. `cortex`'s product is the substrate — `MemoryValue`
with confidence, source trust and FSRS scheduling, a bitemporal `Fact`, a consistency suite. Building a graph or a
hierarchy inside this repository would be building a second substrate, and it would then owe decay, bitemporality
and consistency to be worth comparing with the one that already has them.

**So three items left.** They are recorded here with the evidence that moved them, because a handoff that is only a
message is a handoff nobody can audit later.

| item | the evidence that it is the substrate's | the state it left in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| dual-layer associative memory with spreading activation (**Synapse, ACL 2026**, Jiang et al.) | reports LoCoMo **F1 40.5** at **−95% tokens**; no task, no prompt skeleton | handed off.
