The question it must answer is how much of the 95% is "keep the top-k" and how much is "the activation selects better" — one number for both would be a claim nothing can refute |
| high/low separation with different decay half-lives (**H²R**, 75.9) | reports a direct-to-store score; the ablation is one layer against two | handed off **and** unmeasurable here anyway: its +3.5pp needs 1,923 episodes against a 134-game split (34.213) |
| cortex's own baseline recomputation | **83.55** on LongMemEval is an existing number whose split, commit and budget are not stated in this repository | handed off as a precondition: two of the three mechanisms cannot be externally checked until a decoupled suite exists |

**Why a prompt and not a branch.** The two repositories are in different release states: `cortex` is not on npm, so
this repository keeps a **structural copy** of its types in `packages/node/src/store/cortex.ts`, and
`.github/workflows/cortex.yml` clones and builds it weekly to check the copy field by field. A shared branch would
make one repository's CI the other's gate; a prompt makes the coupling **one-directional and checkable** — the
weekly job is the only thing that crosses, and it crosses as a schema comparison rather than as a dependency.

**What the handoff forbids, and why this repository is the one that forbids it.** The other session is told not to
touch `renderPack`, `shapeFold`, the MMR ordering or the rule bank. Those are not style preferences: the pack's shape
and its **position in the prefix** decide whether the provider's cache holds it, and the τ² lane already paid a 3.7×
bill for getting that wrong (R57 Amendment 4). A pack rendered per turn by the substrate's own code would move
numbers this repository reports, from a repository whose CI does not run this one's tests.

**What this repository keeps.** The projection, its conformance job, and the right to say *no* to a mechanism whose
score is not a task score. Nothing else crosses.

**Cost of the boundary.** `¥0`. No dispatch, no model call: the work was reading three papers' reported metrics
against one rule and writing the four sections above into a prompt.

## 34.222 — The `always-in` arm was rendered in this repository's voice, and the control was never at risk

The arm whose job is to reproduce the competitor's mechanism carried a block headed **`Rules from earlier
attempts:`** — a sentence written here — placed above the instruction and the examples. The competitor's header is
`RULE_TEMPLATE['alfworld']` in `prompts/templates/human.py@LeapLabTHU/ExpeL`:

> The following are some experience you gather on a similar task of completing a household task by interacting in a
> household environment. Use these as references to help you perform this task:

and its placement is `insert_before_task_prompt`: the rule message is appended **after** the few-shot block and
**before** the task line, not at the top of the prompt. So the arm that the registration describes as *"the
competitor's mechanism"* was this repository's prompt with the competitor's name on it, in two places at once.

**Why it is a defect rather than a wording preference.** The registered prediction is `always-in − none` compared
against a published 19pp, and an arm is a treatment only if the treatment is the one whose effect was published. A
paraphrase changes the text the model reads; a different position changes what the text sits next to. Either is
enough to make "we reproduced their mechanism and did not get their effect" an unfalsifiable sentence, which is the
sentence the standard of evidence here exists to prevent.

**Why it was free to repair.** `none` carries no pack. Its prompt is a function of the task, the examples and
`max_steps`, and none of those changed — so the **byte-identical** control the 20-game calibration measured is still
the control, and a test now asserts it directly: the first observation the `none` arm sends equals the environment's
own string, character for character. The two treatment arms have never been run, so moving their block cannot
invalidate a reading that does not exist. **This is the rare case where fidelity cost nothing**, and the reason is
the arm's shape rather than the round's skill: the thing being moved was never in the control's prompt.

**What was not repaired, and why the difference is stated instead.**

| difference | effect on the paired delta | effect on a comparison with a published row |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the two example transcripts are split into alternating turns; the competitor sends one human block | none — identical in all three arms | a different rendering of the same examples |
| the task line sits at the top of the first human turn; the competitor writes `Now it's your turn!` after the rules | none — identical in all three arms | same |
| `max_steps` counts model turns here and environment steps there, at 20 | none — identical in all three arms | 50 turns at the measured 35.3% thought rate is about 32 actions against the competitor's 20 |

Every row is a reason the claim is a **paired** delta and not an absolute number against a published one. Rebuilding
the skeleton to close them would change the control's prompt, which would mean re-measuring the control before
anything could be said — so the limitation is registered beside the prediction rather than argued away in a
paragraph after the result.

**Cost of the correction.** `¥0`, and one test that would fail if the control's prompt ever acquired a prefix.

## 34.223 — Two ports of one arithmetic, and the six expectations the ports corrected

The rule bank needs ExpeL's vote arithmetic in Python, because the ALFWorld lane runs on a runner that has
`textworld` and no `node` guarantee, and it already existed in TypeScript (`packages/eval/src/rule-bank.ts`, ported
in R162 from `agent/expel.py@LeapLabTHU/ExpeL`). Two implementations of one algorithm have exactly one interesting
failure mode — they agree with themselves and diverge from each other — so the pair is checked against **a file
neither of them generates**: `eval/drivers/alfworld/rule-op-vectors.json`, read by `test_distill.py` and by
`rule-bank-vectors.test.ts`. A drift now fails two builds instead of producing a bank the Python lane would build
and the TypeScript package says it would not.

**The contract corrected its author six times out of nineteen cases, and this is the finding.** The first version of
the vectors expected the substring identity to see an extension:

| case as first written | what both ports did | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| bank `Always check the lamp.`, `ADD Always check the lamp before leaving.` → expected rejected | **applied** | the existing text ends in a **period**, so it is not a substring of a sentence that continues after `lamp` |
| bank `Always check the lamp.`, `REMOVE` leaving two votes → expected culled | **survived at one vote** | a removal costs one vote, not two; culling needs a rule already at one |
| `AGREE 9` on a bank that holds no rule 9 → expected the first entry edited | **rejected** | `AGREE`/`REMOVE` resolve by text, never by number; only `EDIT` uses the number |
| tokens identity over two phrases differing in a word | **not the same rule** | normalisation removes order, case and repetition — not content |

The first row is the one worth keeping. **ExpeL's identity test fires almost only on near-verbatim restatement**,
because every rule ends in a full stop and any real extension puts a word between the period and the rest. A bank
maintained by that arithmetic is therefore close to append-only in practice, whatever the prompt says about
`AGREE` and `EDIT` — and the effect is measurable on the first real bank, as the ratio of `applied` operations that
were additions to those that were edits. The vectors now record the behaviour rather than the intent, and the six
corrections are the reason the contract is written by hand from the competitor's source instead of generated from
either port.

**One deliberate divergence stays.** ExpeL checks `rule_num > len(rules)` but not `rule_num < 1`, so `EDIT 0`
reaches `rules[-1]` — Python's negative index — and edits the last rule. The port rejects it and counts the
rejection: reproducing an out-of-bounds access that happens to be legal in one language is not fidelity, and an
operation the model got wrong should appear in the report rather than in a silently different bank.

**What the bank cannot contain, stated where the number will be read.** ExpeL's first criticism compares a
successful trial against *failed trials of the same task*, and both ALFWorld splits give one attempt per task
(AM.24). Only the `all_success_existing_rules` path is available, so the bank this lane distils is the competitor's
extraction **minus its contrast**.

**Cost.** `¥0` to write: the vectors, the Python port and one TypeScript test that reads them.

## 34.224 — The executable bit does not travel through this transport, and the test asserted the checkout

A test asserted that `wait-for-window.sh` was executable. It passed in the sandbox, where `chmod +x` had been run
minutes earlier, and failed on the runner with `0 is not true` — the classic local-pass/CI-fail pair, and the reason
every gate in this record is required to run where the code is actually executed.

**The cause is this repository's transport.** Pushes go through the GitHub Git Data API rather than `git push`,
because the sandbox reaches `api.github.com` and nothing else. The helper that does it wrote **every** blob with mode
`100644`:

```python
entries.append({"path": relative, "mode": "100644", "type": "blob", "sha": blob["sha"]})
```

so a file that was executable locally arrived readable and not executable. Nothing noticed until a test asked.

**The repair is two-sided and small.** The helper now writes `100755` for a path the sandbox can execute. The test no
longer asserts the bit at all — the workflow invokes the script as `bash eval/drivers/alfworld/wait-for-window.sh`,
which needs no bit — and a test records *why* the assertion was deleted rather than leaving a silent hole where one
used to be. Deleting an assertion without saying so is how a suite loses the ability to fail.

**What this says about the suite, stated because it is the reusable part.** A test that reads a file's mode is a test
about the checkout, not about the script. The properties that matter here are the ones the script *does*: start now
when the target has passed, never wait more than a day, refuse a target that is not a time, and never detach itself.
Those are five process-level cases now, and none of them depends on how the file arrived.

## 34.225 — The delta had no denominator, and the literature is what made that a defect

`aggregate.py` could report four things about a pair of arms: the two win counts, the paired difference with a
bootstrap interval, the discordance `b + c`, and the MDE that discordance implies. It could not report **how many
games the treatment changed at all**, and until a 2026 paper made a prediction about where the harm should be, that
absence read as economy rather than as a missing instrument.

**Why the denominator matters, in one line of arithmetic.** A paired delta is a product:

> delta = (share of games the pack changed) × (its effect on the games it changed)

The first factor is delivery — whether the block reached the model at all, whether the model acted on it, whether
the game was decided before the block could matter. The second is the mechanism. A pooled delta of +2pp is
consistent with a mechanism worth +20pp that reached a tenth of the games, and with a mechanism worth +2pp that
reached all of them, and **the two call for opposite next steps**: the first wants a wider door, the second wants a
better rule. Reporting only the product makes the two indistinguishable, and every decision made on it is a guess
dressed as a measurement.

**The instrument is the action digest, and the invariant is what makes it sound.** `agent.py` already records
`digest_of(actions)` per episode, and the environment is a deterministic simulator, so two episodes with the same
digest *must* reach the same verdict. That gives the decomposition a check that fails loudly rather than a
correlation that might be a coincidence: if the same actions produced different outcomes, the join is wrong — two
games under one key, or one slice written twice — and the run stops instead of reporting an effect. The
decomposition is therefore not a new measurement bolted on; it is a property of the simulator that the file had
been throwing away.

**Three readings now sit beside the delta, and each answers a question the delta cannot.**

| reading | the question | why it could not be a footnote |
| --- | --- | --- |
| engagement (diverged / split, delta on those) | did the pack reach the game | a treatment that never reached the model reports a null that is about delivery, not about memory |
| harm share / help share (of the games it changed) | did it help or hurt where it reached | repeats Appendix AS's τ² quantity with the episode as the unit; it is the only column this record can compare across lanes |
| strata (hard = the games `none` lost) | where | `arXiv:2604.27003` predicts negative transfer concentrates on the hard cases; a pooled delta cannot confirm or refute a claim about a subset |
| kinds (six task types) | for which procedures | pooling six kinds is how a mechanism that helps three and hurts three reads as a null |

**And the ordering is the part that is a defect rather than a feature.** The stratification had to be registered
before the delta existed, because after it exists any stratification is a story that fits — six kinds and two
strata are twelve ways to find a positive number in 134 games, and the record would have found one. That is why
`REGISTRATION.md` R165 states both predictions, and the placebo arm's dispatch rule, at ¥0 and before the reading
arrives. **The instrument's cost was ¥0 and its value is that it makes a spent ¥7.77 readable; the registration's
cost was ¥0 and its value is that the reading cannot be reinterpreted after the fact.**

**What the same defect would look like from the other side, so it can be recognised next time.** A pack that
diverges on 2 of 134 games and reports +1.5pp has said nothing about memory and everything about two games; a pack
that diverges on 90 games and reports +0.7pp has said the mechanism engaged and was worth almost nothing per
engagement. Both are now readable in one line of output, and neither can be quoted as "the memory helped".

## 34.226 — The shard arithmetic was a sample, and a completeness check built for something else found it

Run `44685314225` was dispatched at 05:59 UTC, held by `wait-for-window.sh` until 10:00, and at 10:19:49 shard 1
died: **722 successful calls, then one connection closed before its response**, at game 20 of 35. Three shards
finished. The bank job was skipped because a need had failed, and twelve sweep jobs failed forty seconds later on
`Unable to download artifact(s)`. The run's red X pointed at twelve jobs that never ran.

Four defects, in the order they were found rather than the order they matter.

### The three that were visible in the log

`chat()` caught `urllib.error.URLError` and `urllib.error.HTTPError`. It did not catch the exception that actually
happened: `http.client.RemoteDisconnected` derives from `ConnectionResetError`, which derives from `OSError`, and
`URLError` is a *different* `OSError` subclass. So the handler written to turn a network failure into a `LaneError`
was bypassed entirely, the traceback escaped, and a four-hour job ended. **A `try` that names the wrong exception is
worse than no `try`, because it reads as coverage.**

`--out` was written once, at the end of `main`. Twenty games, 1,078 calls, and the artefact that reached GitHub was
330 bytes — the log file, not the record. The money was spent and the evidence did not exist.

The bank job was `needs: distill-train` without `always()`, so a failed slice turned it grey. Twelve jobs then failed
on the absence, each reporting the same missing artefact. The diagnosis — *which* slice died and what it cost — was
four layers away from the red X.

### The one that mattered, and how it was found

The repair for the third defect included `--expect-games`, which reads every episode file and counts distinct games
before distilling. It was written to refuse a *union of two runs* that does not cover the split, because the plan was
to join the three surviving shards to a re-driven fourth. Its first act was to refuse the three surviving shards:

```
FAIL the artefacts cover 82 games but the slice is 140
```

105 episodes, **82 distinct games**, 11 shared between shard 0 and shard 2, 4 between 0 and 3, 10 between 2 and 3.
`AlfredTWEnv.collect_game_files` walks the split with `os.walk(data_path, topdown=False)`, so `game_files` is in the
**filesystem's** order — and `--shard i/n` was taking a contiguous window of an order that two runners did not
agree on. Three quarters of a split, sampled three times from three orderings.

**Why nothing had seen it.** A single-shard pass is unaffected: the `floor` job drives the whole split in one process,
covers it, and its determinism check replays in that same process, so every assertion it makes is true. A sweep would
have refused — `aggregate.py` raises when two arms' games do not coincide — but only *after* 402 games had been paid
for on twelve different orderings, and the refusal would have read as a data-joining bug rather than as a partition
that was never a partition.

**The general shape, since it will recur.** Three of the four defects are the same mistake in three places: *a check
that is satisfied by the thing that is wrong*. A retry that names the wrong exception, an artefact written where the
pass cannot be resumed from, a job that is skipped where it should have spoken, a partition that is a sample. Each
looked like protection. Each was found by asking a question the check did not ask — and the fourth was found by a
check written for a different question, which is the only reason it was found at ¥0 instead of at ¥7.7.

### What is retired, and what is not

| reading | affected | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the 20-game calibration, 55.0% [34.2, 74.2] | **no** | single shard, one process, one ordering |
| `floor.py`'s coverage and determinism assertions | **no** | whole split in one process; the order varies, the *set* does not |
| every sliced training or sweep reading before this commit | **retired** | the slice was a window of an unknown ordering; which games it drove cannot be recovered |
| the 4.4-point "headroom" arithmetic in 34.220 | **no** | it is a difference of two single-process readings |

Retired rather than repaired, because a slice's identity is not recoverable from its artefact: the episodes record the
games they drove, and the games the slice *should* have driven are exactly what the ordering determined.

### The repair, as three properties rather than three edits

1. **A failure is classified, not merely caught.** `transient()` is a table with a test per row, and the retry loop is
   built on it: five attempts at 1+2+4+8 seconds — 15 seconds out of four hours, which is the trade a run this long
   wants, because the alternative was not "no waiting", it was "no result". `400/401/403/404` still fail on the first
   attempt, since retrying them spends four attempts on a fact that will not change.
2. **A paid game is on disk before the next one starts.** Written after every episode through a temporary file and a
   rename, so a killed job leaves a whole file or none, and `--resume` continues it. The header is compared field by
   field; a repeat is refused *before* the write rather than after the bill; a seed pass cannot be resumed because its
   draw stream is a whole-pass stream.
3. **A short union is refused by name.** `--expect-games` refuses rather than distils, and the refusal names both
   numbers. That is the difference between a job that fails and a job that diagnoses.

**Cost of the round so far: ¥1.54** — 105 episodes, 3,915 calls, $0.2156 by the provider's own `usage` object — of
which the 82 distinct games are unusable. **What it bought: a defect that would have invalidated every paired delta
this lane was about to pay ¥5.63 for**, and that would have arrived as twelve arms disagreeing about which games they
drove rather than as a partition that was never one.

## 34.227 — 34.226 named half the cause: the shard was a window of an unstable order *and* it never advanced

The run after the repair (`44731175801`) finished all four training slices, and the bank refused them:

```
FAIL the artefacts cover 35 games but the slice is 140
```

Four artefacts, and **four identical slices**. That identity is the first half of the diagnosis and the proof that
34.226's sort worked: four processes on four runners now agree, to the game, on what the split is. It is also the
proof that the sort was not the whole defect, because a stable order that is never advanced past still yields the
same window every time.

**The mechanism 34.226 missed.** `AlfredTWEnv.init_env` returns a **batch** environment, and a batch environment
starts at the first game of its own list. `--shard i/n` computed `[start, stop)` and drove `stop - start` games — it
never moved the environment to `start`. So every job drove games `0..34` of its own ordering:

| run | jobs | what each drove | distinct games in the union |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `44685314225` | 4 slices, 3 completed | games 0–34 of four **different** orders | **82** of 105 episodes |
| `44731175801` | 4 slices, all completed | games 0–34 of one **sorted** order | **35** of 140 episodes |

The two rows are the same defect measured under two orderings, and they are why the first number looked like a
partial overlap and the second like a total collapse. 34.226 attributed the overlap to the unstable order alone; the
unstable order explained *which* games the windows held, and the missing advance explained why there were windows at
all. Correcting a diagnosis is cheaper than defending one: the first explanation made the sort sound sufficient, and
a single shard of the next run showed it was not.

**The repair, and why it is an advance rather than a selection.** A slice is now reached by calling `env.reset()`
once for each game before the slice starts, and once for each game a checkpoint already holds:

```python
for _ in range(start + resumed):
    env.reset()
```

The alternative was to read `shell.game_files` and ask the environment for named games, which means reaching past
`init_env` into textworld's registration. The advance touches nothing internal and has a bound: at most 139
initialisations for the last slice, and **zero model calls**, because a reset initialises a world and asks it
nothing. That last property is asserted by a test, because an advance implemented with a step would have been 139
games of money spent on games nobody wanted — and it would have looked correct in every artefact.

**What the round cost, and what the guard did.** ¥1.96 on the four identical slices, ¥1.54 on the run before it:
**¥3.50 sunk**. Against that, the completeness check refused the union at ¥0 twice — once at 82 of 140 and once at 35
of 140 — and both refusals arrived *before* a bank existed and before any sweep was paid for. A guard that fires
twice on two different causes in one afternoon is a guard that has earned its line.

**The lesson, stated for the third time in this file because it keeps being true.** Each of the four defects in
34.226 and the fifth here was a check satisfied by the thing that was wrong: an exception handler that named the
wrong class, an artefact written where nothing could resume it, a job skipped where it should have spoken, a
partition that was a sample, and now a *fix* that made the sample deterministic without making it a partition. The
last one is the useful one to remember, because it was introduced by the repair.

**What is not retired this time.** The sort is still correct and still necessary: without it two runs would disagree
about which game index 106 names, and no advance could fix that. The two changes are independent, and the second
one's failure mode was invisible while the first one was missing.

## 34.228 — The repair verified for ¥0.49 instead of believed for ¥1.96

The advance was dispatched against **one** slice — `train_shards: ["3"]`, 35 games, ¥0.49 — on the argument that a
four-shard dispatch would have bought three quarters of an unverified repair. The check was a set comparison against
the previous run's artefacts, which cost nothing because they were already on disk.

| | shard 3, run `44738148591` | shard 0, run `44731175801` (no advance) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| episodes | 35 | 35 |
| distinct games | **35** | 35 |
| games shared with any of the four previous shards | **0** | 35 with each other |
| calls | 1,305 | 1,267 |
| retries | **0** | — |
| wins | 17 (48.6%) | 18 (51.4%) |

The two shards share nothing, which is what a partition of a 140-game split looks like when you check two of its
quarters. The previous run's four shards shared *everything* with each other, which is what a sample looks like.

**Three things this bought beyond the answer.**

1. **`retries: 0` over 1,305 calls is the first reading the retry table has produced in production.** It is a weak
   reading — one slice, thirty minutes, off-peak — but it is the column that was added *because* a pass died without
   it, and it now exists on every artefact.
2. **The off-peak window was not needed.** The dispatch went out at 11:52 UTC, which is outside DeepSeek's peak
   bands, so `wait-for-window.sh` started immediately and the four-hour hold that cost the first run nothing was not
   paid again in wall-clock time.
3. **The bank still refused, correctly, at ¥0.** It read 35 games against a slice of 140 and stopped. A refusal that
   keeps working when the thing it refuses is *expected* is a refusal that will be believed when it is not.

**What the two-phase dispatch costs.** ¥0.49 for the verification, then ¥1.47 for the remaining three slices plus
¥0.10 for the bank plus ¥5.63 for the sweep: **¥7.69**, against ¥7.69 for a single four-shard dispatch. The
verification was free in money and cost thirty minutes of wall clock. That is the trade this record should have made
before the first dispatch of the day, and did not.

**The one number that moved the wrong way.** Wins fell from 51.4% to 48.6% between the runs, which is a different
35 games rather than a different arm: shard 3's games begin with `look_at_obj_in_light` tasks, and the split's six
task kinds do not score alike. It is recorded here so that nobody reads a four-point move between two slices of one
split as a change in the system.

## 34.229 — The guards that stop a payment lived outside the tree, and the first one written crashed instead of refusing

Three contrasts this lane still owes — the placebo (`sham` against `none`), `retrieved@k1` against `k3`, and the
gated retrieval at `--gate-share 0.2` — differ from the registered sweep in one string each. The only way to send one
was to edit `.github/workflows/alfworld.yml` (and remember to edit it back) or to run a dispatcher that lived in
`/workspace/.push/`, outside the repository, outside CI, and with no tests at all.

That is the same defect this record has now found three times in other shapes: **a check that nothing runs is a check
that is not there.** Of that dispatcher's checks, three exist to prevent money being spent — the green-tree gate, the
"treatments without a control" refusal, and the "standalone sweep without a bank" refusal — and every one of them had
been exercised only by dispatching, which is to say by paying.

**The move.** The dispatcher is now `scripts/alf_dispatch.py`, with the decision separated from the network:

| function | what it decides | how it is exercised |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `check(arguments)` | every reason this dispatch must not be bought, cheapest-to-read first | 18 tests, one per refusal, plus 3 for the two numeric boundaries |
| `payload(arguments)` | the workflow's inputs, unnamed keys left out so each default stays in the workflow | 4 tests |
| `green_tree(token, call=call)` | the CI conclusion on the head of master, which is what licenses a purchase | 4 tests, one per state: green, stale, red, still running |
| `call`, `main` | the socket and the polling | 11 tests: a substituted response, a scripted listing, and the four ways `main` ends without a POST |

`scripts/test_alf_dispatch.py` runs in `ci.yml` on the interpreter the lane runs: **40 tests, 99% of the module's
statements, 98% of its branches**, the uncovered line being the `__main__` entry. The file name carries no hyphen so
that the test can import it — a test that has to reach a hyphenated path through a loader is a test somebody deletes.

**Two defects found while moving it, both in code written today.**

1. **The `--gate-share` refusal crashed instead of refusing.** It was written `raise Refused(...) from error` inside
   `except ValueError:` with no `as error`. A dispatch with `--gate-share half` would have died with `NameError` in
   the guard whose whole purpose is to produce one readable sentence. The test existed before the code was run and
   reported it as an error rather than a failure, which is exactly what an untested guard looks like when it is not
   the happy path being exercised.
2. **The first `--arms` rule was too strong.** It refused *any* sweep without a `none` arm, which forbade the
   legitimate case: pair a treatment with the control slices a previous run already paid for. On a 134-game sweep
   that is ≈ ¥2.3 spent twice for no reason. The repair is `--control-run <run-id>`, which names where the left side
   comes from and prints it, so the assumption lives in the log line rather than in the absence of four jobs.

A third, smaller one belongs to the harness rather than the code: a shell loop that ran the guards through `eval`
stripped the JSON quotes, so five of them answered `--arms is not JSON`. The guards were right and the harness was
wrong — but the shape is the one this record keeps meeting, a check that answers from the wrong input.

**What the move does not fix.** `--control-run` trusts that the tree is unchanged between the two runs; nothing at
dispatch time compares the reused control's games with the treatment's. `aggregate.py` refuses a pair whose games do
not coincide, so the assumption is caught downstream — after the money, which is the wrong end. The honest state is
that the reuse is licensed by a human naming a run, and that the readback is the check.

**The rule.** A guard outside the tree is a guard nobody runs, and a guard written to refuse must be tested in the
state where it refuses — not only in the state where it passes and says nothing.

## 34.230 — The scripted caller stood in for the provider and not for the signature

Run `44743739868` drove 140 training games, joined two runs to tile them, and lost the bank to

```
ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)
  at  reply, reported = caller(messages, model, api_key, timeout)
```

`agent.chat` returns three values since the retry table was added. The caller in `distill.py` was not updated with
it, so the one function that spends money on distillation could not run at all: the three slices it had already
paid for, and the twelve sweep jobs behind them, went with it. **¥1.39 and four hours of wall clock.**

**Why thirty-four tests did not see it.** Every test in `test_distill.py` passes a scripted chat function:

```python
def chat(messages, model, api_key, timeout):
    return remaining.pop(0), usage          # two values, because the test wrote both sides
```

The scripted caller is a stand-in for a *provider* — it answers with what a provider would return, and the code
under test treats it exactly as it treats the provider. It cannot stand in for a *signature*: it keeps answering
with the shape of a driver that no longer exists, because the test writes both sides of the seam. A seam with the
same author on both sides is not a seam that is being checked.

| what the suite exercised | what it could not |
| --- | --- |
| the prompt the critique is given | the arity of what comes back |
| the parser, the merge, the cap, the cull | whether the driver this module calls still returns that shape |
| the bill arithmetic, from a usage dict | whether a real reply produces that usage dict |
| the tiling check on the artefacts | whether the job that builds the artefacts could reach this code |

**The repair** is one line, and the test that pins it is the point. `CallerContractTest` passes **the driver
itself** and replaces only the socket — `agent.attempt_once`, which the driver already treats as data:

```python
caller = self.with_socket([self.completion("ADD 1: Open the fridge before taking the lettuce.")])
result = distill.build_bank(self.chunks(1), 20, "deepseek-flash", "k", 1.0, chat_fn=caller)
```

Reverting the one-line fix makes both new cases fail with the production error, verbatim. That is the property a
seam test has to have: it must fail in the same words the run failed in.

**The retry count is now summed into `stats.retries`**, printed beside the bill, and carried in the artefact. A
bank distilled across a provider incident is a bank whose cost has a caveat, and the distillation is the only place
that knows it happened — the same argument that put the column on the arm's summary in `34.226`.

**The rule.** A scripted collaborator is a fixture for the *behaviour* of a dependency. Where the dependency's
*shape* is what changed, the test has to call the dependency.

## 34.231 — `bank_only` was disabled by a directory nothing had created

The mode added for exactly this failure — the slices are bought, the bank dies — was itself disabled on its first
use, at ¥0 and one step before the money:

```
cp: cannot create regular file '/home/runner/work/_temp/slices/': Not a directory
ls: cannot access '/home/runner/work/_temp/slices': No such file or directory
##[error]Process completed with exit code 2.
```

`$RUNNER_TEMP/slices` is created by the step that downloads *this dispatch's* slices, and `bank_only` is the mode
that skips that step. The `find -exec cp` then failed once per artefact, and each failure named the copy rather than
the missing directory — four sentences, none of them the cause.

| gate | how it failed | cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the new mode's own precondition | nothing created the directory it wrote into | ¥0 |
| the step's error | `cp` reported per artefact, `ls` reported last | a reader sent to the wrong place |
| `distill.py`'s tiling check | never reached | — |

`mkdir -p` is the repair. The guard beside it is the more useful half: a step whose whole job is to join a named
run's artefacts now counts what it carried and says so in one sentence when the count is zero, instead of handing
`distill.py` an empty union to refuse against a slice of 140 — a refusal that is correct and that points at the
driver, which is where the reader would then look for an hour.

**The rule.** A new mode is a new path through a workflow, and the steps it *skips* are part of its interface. The
step that was skipped here was the one holding the precondition.

## 34.232 — Two dispatches of the same control arm over the same games disagreed by six wins, and that number is the lane's noise floor

This one was bought by accident. Two chains with the same inputs were dispatched three minutes apart (a duplicate
caused by a session that resumed without knowing the first had gone out); the second was cancelled, but its three
training slices had already finished, so both runs' artefacts exist. That is a **repeat of the control arm** with
nothing changed:

| | run `44743739868` | run `44744658304` | difference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| commit | `13a05cae` | `13a05cae` | — |
| arm / policy / split | `none` / model / `eval_in_distribution` | same | — |
| seed | 20261120 | 20261120 | — |
| shard 0 games | 35 | **identical 35** | — |
| shard 0 wins | 16 (45.7%) | 22 (62.9%) | **+6 games, +17.1 pp** |
| shard 0 calls | 1,351 | 1,194 | −157 |
| shard 0 thoughts | 622 | 570 | −52 |
| shard 1 wins | 24 | 24 | 0 |
| shard 2 wins | 19 | 19 | 0 |
| whole pass | 59/105 (56.2%) | 65/105 (61.9%) | +5.7 pp |

**Ten of shard 0's thirty-five games were decided differently** by the same model, on the same prompt, over the
same environment, with the same seed. Two of the three shards agreed exactly, which is the more interesting half of
the reading: the sampler is not uniformly noisy across the corpus, and a shard whose games sit near the model's
decision boundary flips.

**What this does to every number this lane intends to report.**

1. **The mde computed from the binomial alone is too optimistic.** `aggregate.py` reports an mde from the paired
   discordance, which is the right arithmetic *if* the two arms are drawn from one distribution of runs. They are
   not: the control varies by up to 17 pp between runs of itself, so a treatment effect smaller than that swing is
   not separable from it by a design that puts control and treatment in different jobs.
2. **The placebo arm is not a nicety.** `sham` carries the same bank with its tokens permuted, so it is exactly as
   long, exactly as present, and about nothing. Its delta against `none` is the null distribution of *this* design,
   measured rather than assumed — and it is now the first contrast to run after the sweep, not the last.
3. **The accident was the cheapest useful purchase so far.** ¥1.27 for a repeat measurement that no planned
   dispatch included. It should have been planned: a control arm driven twice is the first thing a lane that reports
   deltas owes its readers, and this one only got it because two sessions raced.

## 34.229 — The flywheel produced four rules, and spent 38 of its 40 operations agreeing with them

The bank exists (run `44754440122`, `bank_only`, the union of two runs tiling 140 games): **4 rules from 76 won
trajectories in 10 critiques**, $0.0134, 0 retries. Both numbers are surprising and one of them is the answer to a
question this programme has been asking since Phase I.

**The census, which only became readable this round.**

| operation | count | what it means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ADD | **4** | four rules were discovered across ten critiques of eight trajectories each |
| AGREE | **28** | twenty-eight times, the model read a fresh batch and restated a rule it already had |
| EDIT | **6** | six rewrites of an existing rule's wording |
| REMOVE | **0** | nothing was ever deleted; the vote arithmetic never had to cull (`culled: 0`) |
| rejected | 2 | two operations named a rule the bank did not hold |

**R164's prediction is refuted, and its refutation is more interesting than its confirmation would have been.** That
entry registered that the bank should be *nearly add-only*, because a rule ends with a full stop and a substring
identity test almost only fires on a verbatim restatement. The measured ratio is the opposite: **28 agreements to 4
additions**, with 6 edits. The substring test fires far more often than predicted — the model does restate rules
nearly verbatim — and the consequence is that the bank stops growing after the fourth critique. `peak: 4` against a
cap of 20 means the cap was never the binding constraint: **the loop saturated**.

**Why that is the answer to "is the memory wrong, or is the way we use it wrong".** Both, and the arithmetic separates
them. The *pack* is four sentences — a few hundred characters — so any effect it has must come from four
generalizations. The *feedback* that produced them ran 40 operations and spent 70% of them agreeing with itself, which
is what a distillation loop looks like when the input distribution stops surprising it: eight trajectories per
critique, ten critiques, and after four rules the marginal trajectory contributed wording rather than knowledge. A
bigger bank was never available from this loop, and no amount of read-time machinery — retrieval, gates, placebos —
can recover knowledge that was never extracted.

**The one rule that matters for the next row.** Rule 2 is *"when searching for an object, prioritize locations where
similar objects have already been observed"* — an object-location prior, produced by the model rather than designed
by this lane. 34.226's row 6 demoted a hand-built object-location pack on the argument that 138 of 149 refusals were
**instance identity inside one house**, which no cross-house memory can carry. The model's own distillation arrived at
a weaker version of the same idea, and the argument against the hand-built version applies to it unchanged. That is a
convergence worth recording: two independent routes to the same mechanism, and one measurement that bounds both.

**What this costs the sweep's reading.** The treatment is a four-rule pack. If `always-in − none` is null, the correct
statement is that *a four-rule pack* is null on this corpus — not that memory is. The distinction is the same one R168
amendment 2 makes about the instrument, and it is sharper now that the treatment's size is a measured number rather
than a cap.

## 34.230 — The pack helps, hurts, and pays for itself, and the three are one reading

The first complete reading is in (PROGRESS 200). It is a positive result, and the obligation that comes with one is
to attack it in the order an adversary would.

**First: is the arm different from the control at all?** Yes — action digests agree on 2 of 134 games for
`always-in − none` and 7 of 134 for `retrieved − none`. A treatment that never changed an action would show 134
identical digests and a delta of exactly zero; this is the opposite extreme, and `engagement: 98.5%` is why the
decomposition was built.

**Second: is the rise a rise in *wins*, or a rise in something the scorer rewards?** `won` comes from the
environment's own task-completion flag, set by the game, not by this lane. The scorer cannot be talked into it.

**Third: is the treatment cheaper because it is doing less?** This is the one that needed arithmetic. The treatment
made **fewer** calls (3,546 against 4,619) and won **more** games. If it were achieving that by giving up early, the
`budget_exhausted` and `truncated` counters would move; `truncated` fails the pass by construction, and the pass
passed. So the pack is shortening episodes by making them succeed sooner, not by abandoning them.

**Fourth: the pooled number is a cancellation, and this is the finding.** 

| stratum | n | with pack | without | delta |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| hard (`none` lost) | 54 | 32 | 0 | **+59.26pp** |
| easy (`none` won) | 80 | 67 | 80 | **−16.25pp** |

The pack rescues 32 games the control cannot solve and destroys 13 it can. **A memory that is a large gain on
unsolvable tasks and a real loss on solvable ones is not a neutral instrument with noise** — it is a bias, and the
bias is legible: four rules about searching and verifying are worth everything when the agent is lost and worth
nothing-to-harmful when it already knows the answer, because the rule competes with a procedure that was working.

**Fifth: the field's mechanism prediction does not survive, and the direction does.** `arXiv:2604.27003` reports that
negative transfer concentrates on the cases the agent cannot solve unaided. Here the hard stratum lost **zero** games
and every loss is in `easy`. The paper's *comparison* (hard delta > easy delta) holds by 75 points; its *mechanism*
(harm where the agent is weakest) is the opposite of what this corpus shows. Both statements are now on the record
because R165 wrote two clauses and not one, and a registration that had merged them would have been "confirmed" by a
result that refutes half of it.

**Sixth: why the two treatments are indistinguishable, and why that is a defect of the bank rather than of retrieval.**
`retrieved` scored exactly what `always-in` scored (99/134 each) and diverged on 127 games against 132. The reason is
arithmetic: the bank holds **four** rules and `--top-k` is **3**, so the anchor usually admits three of four. Retrieval
had nothing to select from. R165's second prediction named this failure mode in advance — *"then the anchor is not
selecting, and the arm is `always-in` with extra steps"* — and it is what happened. The repair is not a better
retriever; it is a bank big enough for a retriever to matter, or a budget small enough to force a choice (`k=1`), and
the second is one dispatch at ≈ ¥1.9.

**Seventh: the number that decides the next dispatch.** The pack's ceiling is visible in the strata: if it fired only
on the 54 hard games and were withheld from the 80 easy ones, the delta would be **+32/134 = +23.9pp** instead of
+19/134 = +14.2pp. That is **9.7 points of headroom** sitting in a gate, and it is the first time this lane has had a
quantified target for one. The gate that could capture it does not need to know the answer — it needs to recognise the
observation it is looking at, which is a weaker requirement and a testable one.

**What is *not* claimed.** Not that 73.9% beats any published row: the harnesses differ by up to 40 points inside one
method's own reports (COMPETITIVE R167). What is claimed is a **paired** +14.2pp on 134 games with the same backbone,
the same skeleton, the same step cap and the same examples, with the denominator, the harm share and the engagement
rate published beside it — a configuration no row in that table reports.

## 34.231 — The placebo beat the bank, and 34.230's attribution is retired by it

`sham` carries the same header, the same four entries, the same token count and the same punctuation as the bank,
with each rule's words permuted **inside itself**. Run `44763220821` drove it over the same 134 games, beside a control
driven by the same code in the same hour:

| arm | wins | rate | paired delta vs `none` | 95% CI | p |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **`sham`** (permuted rules) | **105/134** | **78.4%** | **+17.91pp** | [+8.96, +26.87] | < 0.001 |
| `always-in` (the bank) | 99/134 | 73.9% | +14.18pp | [+4.48, +23.88] | 0.0044 |
| `none` (control, this run) | 81/134 | 60.4% | — | — | — |

**The placebo is not distinguishable from the treatment, and its point estimate is higher.** The two intervals overlap
across almost their whole width. R165 amendment 1 wrote the reading before the arm existed: *"If the sham's help share
is within the interval of the bank's, the finding is that the mechanism this lane has spent four rounds building is
formatting, and the next row is not a better bank — it is a different layer."* The help shares are 26.19% (`sham`) and
24.24% (bank); the harm shares 7.14% and 9.85%. The condition is met.

**The strata replicate, which is the strongest evidence that the two arms are the same mechanism.**

| stratum | `sham` | `none` | delta | bank's delta |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| hard (`none` lost, n=53) | 33 | 0 | **+62.26pp** | +59.26pp |
| easy (`none` won, n=81) | 72 | 81 | **−11.11pp** | −16.25pp |

A *scrambled* block reproduces the pattern — rescue everything that was lost, spoil a tenth of what worked — within a
few points. Two independent treatments producing the same shape is not a coincidence of totals; it is the signature of
a mechanism that reads the block's form and not its content.

**What 34.230 said that this retires.** That entry attributed +14.2pp to "four rules about searching and verifying",
and argued the bias was legible — worth everything when the agent is lost and harmful when it already knows the answer.
The *shape* of that argument survives; the attribution does not. A permutation of those rules produces the effect, so
the effect is not about what the rules say. What 34.230 got right and this entry keeps: the pooled number is a
cancellation of a large rescue and a smaller spoiling, and a gate that could separate them is worth 9.7 points. What
it got wrong: **whose** cancellation it is. It is the block's, not the bank's.

**`arXiv:2601.22436` is confirmed on this corpus, and more strongly than it claimed.** That paper reports that corrupt,
irrelevant and filler summaries "move the score little" and that agents respond to a block's existence and shape.
Here a permutation does not move the score little — it moves it *slightly more than the real thing*. The paper's
framing was that the content is inert; the measurement is that the content is inert and its *destruction* is not
harmful, which is the same claim with a sharper edge: **there was nothing in the content to destroy.**

**Why that is a coherent result rather than a broken experiment.** The four rules are general procedures — verify your
inventory, prefer likely locations, retry with alternate phrasing when a put fails. A competent model already knows
all four; that is why fourteen critiques produced only four of them and why twenty-eight of thirty-eight operations
were agreements. A block of imperative sentences about being careful makes the model *behave* more carefully, and the
sentences' particular content is redundant with what it already knew. The mechanism is instruction, not memory.

**Three checks that an adversary would make, and their answers.**

1. *Is the sham's win a fluke of 134 games?* It clears its own MDE (13.55pp) by 4.4 points and its interval excludes
   zero by 8.96 points. A fluke would have to be a 33-game swing against 9 in the other direction.
2. *Did the two runs' controls differ?* 80/134 in the first sweep and 81/134 in this one — one game apart, which is
   the run-to-run reproducibility of the same games at temperature 0. The comparison that matters is intra-run, which
   is why the placebo was dispatched with its own control rather than against the previous one.
3. *Could the permutation have been cosmetic?* `sham_entries` seeds from the rule's own text and permutes every
   multi-word rule; a test asserts a one-word rule is returned unchanged and a multi-word one is not. The four rules
   are 15–25 words each.

**What is now the sharpest question in the programme.** Not "does memory help" — a block helps, by 14 to 18 points. Not
"which rules" — the rules are inert. The question is **which property of the block** does it: its existence, its
length, its imperative grammar, or the fact that it looks like task instructions. That is separable in one dispatch:
a length-matched block of neutral declarative text, and a length-matched block of filler. If filler also buys +15pp,
the mechanism is "any preamble". If filler buys nothing and imperative text buys +17.9, the mechanism is "a block that
reads as instructions" — which is a product feature and a completely different line of work from a rule bank.

## 34.233 — The arm every price rests on was executed by CI on every run and validated by nothing

`floor.py` is the lane's zero-cost arm and the origin of every quoted minimum detectable effect. It drives 134 games
twice, asserts that the split was covered, that every episode terminated, and that the second pass replays the first,
and prints a floor that the price model multiplies by the per-episode cost. It has run in the lane's job on every
dispatch for weeks. Its test coverage was **31%**.

That is not a documentation gap. It means the walker, the two-pass comparison, and all four assertions in the
measurement path had never been executed by anything except a real run — and a real run is the one caller that must
not be the only evidence, because a floor whose coverage check silently passes on one game driven 134 times reports a
rate and a variance figure with **no defect anywhere in its own output**. The three drifts that reached CI earlier in
this programme (a test that needed a package the job does not install, a 3.11 API on a 3.10 interpreter, a shard that
drove the wrong games) were all of this shape: the check existed, the check passed, the check was not the check.

**The single defect this found, and why it is a defect rather than a preference.** The p90 of the transcript length —
the number a per-episode price is calibrated on — was computed as `int(0.9 * (n - 1))` indexed into the sorted lengths.
At n=2 that index is 0, so the reported 90th percentile was the **cheapest** episode of the pass. A tail that is too
small is a price that is too small, and a price that is too small is the one direction the user of a quote cannot
detect. It is nearest-rank now (`ceil(0.9n)`), pinned by a two-episode case and a one-episode case; on the 134-game
pass the two formulas differ by one index, which is exactly why the bug survived — the only runs that reach it are the
short ones used for smoke tests.

**Three seams were opened so that the assertions could be reached, and none of them is test scaffolding.** `read_config()`
is the config read and its `$ALFWORLD_DATA` substitution; `summarise()` is the arithmetic of one pass, including the
branch a pass over zero games takes; `run()` is the measurement that `main()` now only parses arguments for. `pass_over()`
and `main()` accept the `shell_factory` parameter `build_env()` already had, so a test supplies an environment instead of
patching this module — the distinction matters because a patched `pass_over` would have tested the patch against the
payload and left the four assertions unexecuted, which is the exact failure this entry is about.

**The 99% that is reported rather than rounded.** 169 statements, 168 executed, 39 cases. The one unexecuted line is
`sys.exit(main())` under the `__main__` guard: no import reaches it. `DefaultShellTest` covers everything it calls,
including the `import alfworld ... AlfredTWEnv` branch, by supplying the four module names the import path uses through
`sys.modules` — the package is not installed in the job that runs these tests, and a test that installed it to assert
`shell_factory = AlfredTWEnv` would be a test of an import statement. The line stays visible in the coverage report
rather than being closed with a pragma, because a pragma is how a number gets to 100% without a measurement.

**What this changes about the next reading.** Nothing in the placebo result moves: that reading came from a real run and
its own arithmetic. What changes is what a reader may assume about the corpus underneath it. The floor that prices the
next dispatch is now produced by code whose refusals have been triggered on purpose — twice for coverage, once for
replay, and once for a game driven twice — rather than by code that has only ever succeeded.

## 34.234 — A flag that was accepted, printed, and never sent is closed by refusing it rather than by wiring it

`alf_dispatch.py --control-run` took a run id, printed "the control is the `none` slices of run 44744658304, already
paid for", and returned success. The workflow declared no such input, so GitHub dropped the key and the sweep bought
a treatment arm with **no control at all** — while the dispatch's own output asserted that the control existed. Two
sweeps would have been read against a control the reader believed in and the run did not have.

The first instinct was to wire it: download the named run's `none` slices and hand them to `aggregate.py`. That is
wrong for three reasons, and each of them is a premise the flag cannot check.

1. **The same commit.** A control bought yesterday ran yesterday's `agent.py`. The lane has changed `agent.py` five
   times since the first sweep, and the arm's prompt assembly, its shim and its cap all live there.
2. **The same games.** A control is only a control if it drove the same 134 games. `--shard` partitions a sorted
   split, so this is checkable *after* the fact by tiling both slices — but a flag that is only checkable afterwards
   is a flag that can be sent wrong.
3. **The same noise.** The control arm scored 80/134 in one dispatch and 81/134 in another on identical code and
   identical games (AUDIT 34.232). That is a six-win floor on any cross-run comparison, and it is the whole reason
   the placebo was bought with its own control in the same run.

So the flag is refused, in the cheapest position in `check()`, with the sentence that names the alternative: buy the
control in the dispatch that buys the treatment, by naming `'none'` in `--arms`. Three tests pin it — a refusal with
an arm list, a refusal without one (the flag's own reason comes before the missing `--arms`, so repairing one flag
does not reveal the next refusal), and a `MainTest` case that asserts no network call is made before the refusal.

**The lesson is not "test the flag".** It is that **an accepted flag is a promise**, and a promise that is dropped
silently is worse than one that is refused loudly, because the dispatch record then says something the run did not
do. The same shape appeared three times in this lane: `--control-run` here, a workflow `if` that could never be true,
and a `--bank-only` disabled by a directory nothing created (34.231). Each was found by reading the payload rather
than the output, and each was fixed by making the silence into a sentence.

## 34.235 — The bank was named the way the lane's directory reads, and the jobs run from the repository root

Run `44779423772` was the filler sweep — 134 games, two arms, ¥2.0 — and every one of its eight arm jobs failed. Not
one made a model call. Total spend: **¥0**. Wall-clock lost: fourteen minutes, because each job installed textworld,
fetched the games, waited for the off-peak window, and only then discovered there was no bank.

**The failure is a coordinate mismatch, and the documentation was the source of the wrong one.** The registration
wrote `banks/bank-filler-4.json`, because that is how the path reads from inside `eval/drivers/alfworld/`, where the
bank lives and where every other file in this lane is described. The workflow runs `python eval/drivers/alfworld/agent.py`
**from the repository root**, so the file it was told to read resolves to `<root>/banks/...`, which does not exist. The
dispatch was written by copying the sentence out of the registration, which is exactly what a registration is for and
exactly why the copy was wrong.

**Two defects, and the second one is the one that would have been hidden by a successful run.**

1. **A path resolved in one coordinate system and used in another.** `--rules` accepted a relative path and the jobs
   resolved it against their working directory. Nothing failed until a job tried to open the file.
2. **The treatment guard was applied to the control.** The `if [ ! -f "${RULES}" ]` check sat above the
   `if [ "${ARM}" != "none" ]` branch, so the `none` arm — which carries no bank at all — was refused for a bank path
   it never reads. Four of the eight lost jobs were controls dying of a file that is not theirs. A run that had
   happened to have a valid path would have shipped this defect permanently.

**The fixes are placed by what each one protects.** The dispatcher now resolves a relative `--rules` against the
checkout it is given and refuses **before the dispatch**, naming the path that would have worked
(`eval/drivers/alfworld/banks/bank-filler-4.json`); absolute paths, which is what a chained bank is, are left to the
runner. The workflow's existence check moved inside the treatment branch, so the arm that carries no bank is no longer
asked for one. `check()` keeps its signature by taking `tree=None` as the default: without a checkout it stays a pure
function of the command line, which is what keeps the other forty cases in `test_alf_dispatch.py` readable.

**What the ¥0 bought.** A guard that fires inside a job protects money; a guard that fires before the dispatch
protects money *and* time, and this lane has now paid both kinds of tuition. The other lesson is narrower and more
useful: when a document and a runner disagree about where a file is, the document is the one that gets copied.

## 34.236 — A placebo shares what you hold fixed, and the sham held the vocabulary fixed

The sham block permuted each rule's word order and kept every word. It scored +17.91 pp, above the intact bank's
+14.18, and the record concluded that the block's form was the mechanism and its content inert. **That conclusion
outran the control.** A permutation destroys order; it does not remove a single ALFWorld noun. `fridge`, `desk`,
`put`, `receptacle` were all still there, so the sham was a control for *sequence* and had never been a control for
*meaning*.

The block that does remove meaning is a same-length, same-header, same-imperative block about a different task, and it
cost ¥3.28 to run (run `44782732761`):

| block | delta | interval | the layer it isolates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| filler (typewriter maintenance) | −6.72 pp | [−14.93, +1.49] | existence of a block |
| always-in (4 distilled rules) | +14.18 pp | [+4.48, +23.88] | being about the task |
| sham (same words, permuted) | +17.91 pp | [+8.96, +26.87] | the order of those words |

**Vocabulary is the mechanism; order is not.** `sham − filler` is +24.6 pp and is the most reliable contrast in the
programme (p 0.0001, p 0.004 with the run-to-run swing added). `sham − always-in` is −3.7 pp with overlapping
intervals. The corrected sentence is narrower than the retired one and more useful: *a block that names the task's
objects and actions is worth 14–18 points regardless of how its sentences are arranged, and a block that names a
typewriter is worth nothing.*

**Two design defects this exposed, both in the record rather than in the code.**

1. **A stratifier defined by the control has a ceiling bias.** The easy stratum is "the games the control won", so a
   run whose control scores well puts a larger share of games at 100% and the treatment can only lose there. This
   run's control scored 89/134 against 80 and 81 in the two earlier dispatches, giving 89 of 89 easy games. The
   −6.72 point estimate therefore contains a ceiling effect the registration did not name as a condition, which is
   why only the interval — which still excludes the +9 pp the "form is sufficient" row required — is quoted.
2. **A per-episode price is wrong for a treatment that changes the number of turns.** The estimate was ¥2.0 and the
   bill was ¥3.28: the filler arm used 4,492 calls against the placebo's 3,964 for the same 134 games. A confused
   model is a more expensive model, and the lane has now under-quoted this way three times.

**The positive evidence that the block was read at all.** The filler arm diverged from its control on 88.8% of games,
its invalid-action rate rose from 28.4% to 32.7%, and its off-space actions from 25 to 41. A block that were ignored
would move none of those counters. This is the first arm in the lane whose *mechanism of action* is visible in the
refusal counters rather than in the score: it made the model try more, and more of what it tried was not in the
action space.

## 34.237 — The dose point read at the filler's value, and the registration's own condition fired before the claim could be made

Run `44789662558` scored the two-real-two-filler block over all 134 held-out games against its own control: 8,804
calls, $0.4495 (¥3.21). Rendered 1,318 characters against the registered block's 1,312, 218 words against 218, the
real rules in the positions they occupy in the registered bank.

| reading | value | what it may be used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| control `none` | **90/134 (67.16%)** | above the registration's verbatim 85/134 threshold |
| dose block | 80/134 (59.70%) | — |
| pooled paired delta | −7.46 pp [−15.67, +1.49], p 0.105 | **not quoted as the reading**; the threshold fired |
| hard stratum (control lost) | 13/44 vs 0/44, **+29.55 pp** | the stratum the condition asks for |
| easy stratum (control won) | 67/90 vs 90/90, **−25.56 pp** | the stratum the condition asks for |
| engagement | 129/134 (96.3%), harm 17.8%, help 10.1% | the block was read; the voiding counters did not fire |
| by kind | `clean` −12.9, `put` −12.5, `heat` −8.7, `examine` −5.6, `cool` 0.0, `puttwo` 0.0 | — |

**This is the first time a registration's own voiding condition fired, and it worked.** R172 wrote, before the arm
existed: *if this dispatch's control lands above 85/134, the easy stratum is a ceiling and the reading is reported by
stratum only, with no pooled number quoted*. The control landed at 90. The instrument therefore produced a table
instead of a claim, and the claim that the point estimate invites — "half a block about the task is no better than
none" — is not what the record says. What the record says is that on the 44 games the control lost the block recovered
13, and on the 90 it won the block broke 23. Both are larger than the pooled number suggests and neither is a dose
response, because there is nothing to compare them against: the filler arm's strata were +24.44 and −22.47, and the
difference between the two blocks is inside the swing.

**The estimate landed on the row whose interpretation the artefact does not support.** R172 named four readings; the
point estimate is at the filler's value, which is row 3, whose text attributes the result to *how much* of the block
was about the task. The dose kept entries 1–2 (the desklamp note, the search order) and dropped entries 3–4 (verify
the object is in the inventory before placing; if `put` fails, try `move <object> to <receptacle>`). Entries 3–4 are
the only entries in the block that name the operation this corpus fails, and the arm's two largest losses are on
`clean` and `put` — the two kinds whose failures are placement failures. A registration can name a confound it did not
foresee; it cannot name one its own artefact reveals after the fact, and that is what 34.239 is about.

## 34.238 — The noise is in the arm that has no block, and the instrument that stops depending on it

Four dispatches have now scored a block on the same 134 games through the same model and harness. Their absolute wins:

| block | entries about the task | wins / 134 | dispatch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| four distilled rules | 4 of 4 | **99** (73.9%) | `44754440122` |
| the same four, order permuted | 4 of 4 | **105** (78.4%) | `44763220821` |
| four typewriter entries | 0 of 4 | **80** (59.7%) | `44782732761` |
| two distilled rules + two typewriter entries | 2 of 4 | **80** (59.7%) | `44789662558` |
| `none` | — | **80, 81, 89, 90** (59.7–67.2%) | all four |

**The blocks repeat and the control does not.** Two independent dispatches of a block without the task in it produced
exactly 80 wins; the two dispatches of blocks with the task in them produced 99 and 105. The arm with no block
produced four readings spanning ten wins. That is not a property of the blocks — it is a property of the arm that has
no block in it, and it means every delta this lane has quoted against a single `none` carries a floor of about seven
points that buying more treatments cannot lower.

**What that changes is the comparison, not the corpus.** Two treatments on the same games are paired against each
other: both drove every game, both carry the block, and the difference between them is the difference between two
blocks. `aggregate.py --relabel` now performs that pairing, and refuses the one thing that would make it wrong — a
rename that lands on a group already present, which is two arms' episodes under one name and a doubled denominator
printing one rate. The rename is printed in the report, because a cross-dispatch reading whose provenance is silent
reads exactly like a within-run one.

**The cost of that instrument is zero and the cost of not having it was already paid.** Three of this lane's last five
registrations quoted a delta against a control whose own reading moved by more than the effect being tested, and each
time the honest response was to widen the interval rather than to buy anything. The interval was never the problem.

## 34.239 — Two explanations wearing one arm: "half the content" and "the half that does not name the failing operation"

The dose point is 2 of 4 entries about the task, and it scored what 0 of 4 scored. Two readings fit that number, and
they are different products:

1. **linear priming with a floor** — the effect scales with the share of the block that is about the task, and 50%
   sits below the resolution of 134 games;
2. **content that has to name the failing operation** — the two entries that were kept are a desklamp note and a search
   order, and the two that were dropped are the inventory check and the `put`→`move` workaround, which are the only
   entries addressed to the operation the corpus actually fails (put-family games: 3, 3 and 4 wins out of 24 across
   three controls).

**The second reading is testable at the price already quoted for the first.** The complementary block — the filler
entries at positions 1–2, entries 3–4 at positions 3–4, rendered to 1,312 characters against 1,312 — differs from the
R172 dose point in exactly one thing: *which* half is about the task. If it scores near 99, the share of the block was
never the variable; if it scores near 80, neither half suffices alone and the effect needs both a general and a
specific entry, which is the first claim this lane would have that a competitor's bank could fail.

**What the lane keeps getting wrong, stated as a rule.** Every block built so far has varied two things at once and
named one of them. The filler varied vocabulary and form together. The sham varied order and kept vocabulary. The dose
varied *which* content and named *how much* content. A registration that varies two things must say which two, and the
report must refuse the attribution the second one would have supported — which is what R173's voiding list now does.

## 34.240 — The literature already has a name for a block that is read and hurts, and one line of it says abstraction is the cause

This lane's own reading — 96% of games change course, 17.8–18.5% of those get worse — is not an anomaly in the recent
literature; it is the mechanism several papers name and one paper measures as the cost of the step this lane performs.

| source | what it measures | how it bears on this lane |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Zhang, Lin, Wu, Sun, Li, Li & Peng (2025), *Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated by LLMs*, arXiv:2605.12978 | consolidation and repeated abstraction **degrade** memories that were useful when stored; raw trajectories stay competitive as in-context demonstrations | this lane's pipeline distils 76 trajectories into 4 procedures. The placebo says the procedures' ordering is inert; this paper says the distillation step itself is the risky one. It predicts that a raw retrieved trajectory should beat a rule abstracted from it |
| Xiong et al. (2025), experience-following | the closer a new task is to a retrieved memory, the more the output imitates that memory's output; benefit and harm come from **one** mechanism | the 96% divergence and the 17.8% harm share are one mechanism seen from two sides, not a delivery failure plus a quality failure |
| Chroma (2025), "context rot" over 18 frontier models | accuracy degrades monotonically with input length, before the window limit | this lane holds length fixed at 1,312 characters across blocks, so its contrasts are not length contrasts — and its one length-varying arm (R173.2, 802 characters) is registered as uninterpretable alone for exactly this reason |
| *Context Length Alone Hurts* (2025 preprint); NoLiMa (ICML 2025) | 13.9–85% degradation with length even when retrieval is perfect; lexical overlap removed, 10 of 12 models fall below half their short-context baseline at 32k | a longer pack is not a neutral change even when its content is identical, which is why every block in this lane is length-matched to the registered bank |
| SWE-ContextBench, arXiv:2602.08316 | unfiltered or incorrectly selected context gives "limited or negative" benefit; a gatekeeper between history and model is the requirement | the read-time gate (R168 amendment 1) is that gatekeeper, and this lane's hard/easy asymmetry is its specification: fire where the control loses, stay silent where it wins |
| MemoryGraft, arXiv:2512.16962 | a handful of poisoned records dominate retrieval because of the semantic-imitation heuristic | an admission rule that scores a memory by its own success rate is not enough; the same imitation that makes a good memory work makes a poisoned one work |
| MemEvoBench (Xie et al., 2026) | memory "misevolution": behaviour drifts under repeated exposure to misleading stored content, and prompt-level defences do not stop it | the gate has to be structural — a share-of-overlap test on the observation — rather than an instruction telling the model to distrust the block |

**What this changes about the next step, and what it does not.** It does not change the current queue: R173 is a
two-arm test of *which* half of the block carries the effect, and no paper can read that for us. It does change what
comes after it. If the placement rules carry the effect, the next pack form is not a better-distilled rule set — the
literature says abstraction is where the loss happens — but the **retrieved raw trajectory** for the nearest failing
game, admitted by the same overlap gate. That is a pack form, not a memory architecture: tiering, graph memory,
workflow abstraction and contrastive retrieval stay out of this lane, because those are the components under test
elsewhere and this lane's job is to say what a *pass* is worth.

## 34.241 — Two halves of one block differ by +14.9pp, and the comparison contains no control

The dose point (34.237) left one confound standing: "half the block was about the task" and "the half that does not
name the failing operation" were the same half, so the reading could not say which of the two explained it. R173 bought
the other half — the same length (1,312 characters, 100.0%), the same positions, the same header — and it scored
**100/134** against the registered block's **99**.

| block | rendered | wins / 134 | its own control |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| four distilled rules | 1,312 | 99 | 80 |
| **placement half** (inventory check + `put`→`move`) | 1,312 | **100** | 88 |
| **search half** (search order + desklamp note) | 1,318 | 80 | 90 |
| four typewriter entries | 1,316 | 80 | 89 |

**The two halves differ by +14.93 pp [+5.97, +23.88], p = 0.002**, discordance 30 + 10 = 40, mde 13.22 pp,
engagement 130/134 (97.0%), harm 7.7%, help 23.1%. That comparison contains no `none` arm: both sides are treatments
on the same 134 games through the same model, so the control's own ten-win spread is not in the interval. It is the
first reading in this lane whose uncertainty is not dominated by the arm that has no block.

**The three things it settles, in the order they matter.**

1. **The share of the block about the task is not the variable.** Half of it, chosen well, is worth all of it; the
   other half, chosen equally well and padded to the same length, is worth nothing. Any account of this effect as
   "priming" or "a preamble sized to a budget" is now excluded by two arms at one length.
2. **The variable is whether the sentences name the failing operation.** The four kinds that end in a placement
   (`puttwo` +29.4, `cool` +19.1, `heat` +8.7, `clean` +6.5 against the arm's own control) are the four that move, and
   `examine` — the one kind whose advice was in the dropped half — is the only one that falls (−11.1, and −5.6 against
   the other half).
3. **A block that is about the task in general can still be worth nothing.** The search half is *about* ALFWorld:
   its sentences name objects, rooms and receptacles. It scored what four typewriter entries scored. Relevance to the
   corpus is not the quantity the field's ablations control for; relevance to the failing step is.

**What it does not settle, and the arm that would.** Length. R173.2 runs the same two rules unpadded at 802 characters
(61.1%), so the pair separates "two sentences are enough" from "the block has to look like a block". Until it is read,
the honest sentence is the one above and not "therefore shorter is better".

**The instrument was used for the first time and refused its operator.** The two halves were scored in different
dispatches under one arm label, so `aggregate.py` could not join them at all until the rename became path-keyed. The
first command named the shards by basename; both dispatches contain a shard of that name; the rename would have moved
one run's shard and left the other's under the old label — a join of one block and three quarters of another, printing
a delta. The refusal that caught it was written an hour earlier for a hypothetical: *an ambiguous name is refused
rather than resolved by iteration order*. A guard that fires on its author's first real command is the only kind worth
writing.

## 34.242 — Two sentences beat four, and the mechanism both lanes were missing is the price of a sentence

The bare pair — entries 3–4 of the registered bank, 802 characters, no padding — scored **109/134 (81.34%)**, the
highest reading this lane has produced. Against the same two rules padded to 1,312 characters it is **+6.72 pp
[+0.75, +12.69], p 0.034**; against the four-rule block it is **+7.46 pp [+0.75, +14.18], p 0.045**. Neither
comparison contains a control arm, so neither inherits the eleven-win spread the six `none` readings now span
(80, 81, 88, 89, 90, 91).

**The direction of the dose is negative, and that is the finding.** R173's registered readings anticipated a threshold
("the block has to be long enough") or a linear share ("the effect scales with how much is about the task"). Both are
excluded: padding a working pair with two task-irrelevant entries costs 6.7 pp, and padding it with two *relevant*
entries costs 7.5 pp. Two extra sentences, about the task or not, cost about seven points. Per sentence: **−3.4 to
−3.7 pp**.

**This is the same slope the SQL lane measured from the other direction.** BIRD's four-arm size ladder fell about
**−1.7 pp per injected rule** (W8), and its pruning experiment found that removing rules at random was as good as
removing them by checkability — the content of the removed rules did not matter, only the count. ALFWorld now says the
same thing with a block that is otherwise ideal: the best pack is the shortest one that names the failing step, and
every sentence after that is a tax. Two corpora, two harnesses, two prompt shapes, one direction.

**What that re-explains, and what it retires.**

1. **The filler result was not about relevance.** Four typewriter entries scored 80 against a control at 89; the
   search half — four entries about the task — also scored 80 against a control at 90. Neither reading needed the
   vocabulary explanation the previous three rounds gave it: both are what a *four-entry block of anything* does.
2. **"Domain priming" is retired as an explanation of the field's rule-bank numbers**, and replaced by something
   narrower and more useful: a bank's score is the value of the sentences that address the failing step minus the tax
   its other sentences charge. A competitor's four-rule bank could be a one-rule bank with three sentences of tax.
3. **The BIRD lane's "the pack's cost scales with how many rules are injected" (W8) is not a SQL fact.** It was
   filed as a property of that lane's packs; it is now a property of packs, measured twice.

**What it does not separate, stated before it is claimed.** The bare pair differs from both longer blocks in content
*and* length, so "each sentence costs attention" and "a longer prompt is handled worse" both fit. The separating arm is
one sentence at 489 characters, dispatched as R174.1. Until it is read, the product sentence is "the shortest pack that
names the failing step", and the mechanism sentence is "sentences cost", not "attention is diluted".
