**What it says about the project's own question, which is the part that generalises.** Memory does not make this agent
verbose; it makes it concise. 9.23 thoughts a game in the control become **4.2** with the scoped bank, and the heavy
count falls 19 → 5. So the surviving thought-heavy games are the ones the pack **failed to reach**, which is a statement
about coverage and not about harm — the opposite of the framing every previous round would have produced from the same
ten numbers.

**The discipline repeated for the third time.** `not counted` is printed when an arm file predates the field, exactly as
`dropped` (34.259) and `recovered` (34.262) do. Three counters, one rule, and the rule is worth stating once: a zero
from a file that never recorded the field is not a measurement of quiet.

## 34.271 — Four dispatches that bought nothing, because the bank was not on master yet

R188's first four dispatches (`44972734686`, `44972752117`, `44972768133`, `44972780849`) all failed inside twenty
seconds, on `no bank at eval/drivers/alfworld/banks/bank-turnbudget-1.json`, because the bank file had been written,
tested and registered **locally** and the workflow checks out `master`. The four runs cost **¥0**: the guard is the
first step of the job and no job reached a model.

Two things follow, one procedural and one structural:

1. **The order is push, green, dispatch, and it is enforced by the dispatcher.** `alf_dispatch.py` refuses unless
   `ci.yml` on the head of `master` has completed successfully, which is what makes the sequence impossible to invert —
   the commit that carries a bank must be green before the bank can be bought. What it cannot check is whether the
   *bank* is in that commit; that is what the workflow's own existence check does, at zero cost, in twenty seconds.
2. **A zero-cost failure is only zero-cost because the failure is early.** The same mistake one step later — a bank that
   parses but whose tags do not line up — would have failed after the environment install, and a mistake two steps later
   would have spent the round's budget on an arm carrying the wrong sentence. The lane's habit of putting a check before
   the first paid call is what makes four failed dispatches a footnote rather than a ¥6 loss, and it is worth naming as
   a property rather than relying on as a habit.

## 34.272 — A class defined by one draw, and four ways the round could have been wrong before it was bought

R188 was registered against a class R186 had defined: five of ten losses were "thought-heavy" — 24 to 46 thoughts over 4
to 26 environment steps — and the round's hypothesis was that an instruction about the turn budget would reach them. The
instruction was written, length-matched against its own permutation, and bought at 548 games. It is **inert**
(264 vs 266, paired −0.73 pp, p = 0.66), and the reason is better than the hypothesis:

**The five games won on a redraw.** Under the instruction, four of five won at 1 to 10 thoughts; under the permutation,
five of five. The same happened to the other family — R186's five search-heavy losses went 3/5 and 2/5 — so of the
twenty game-slots that were lost in R186, **three stayed lost**. The pool read 264, 264, 266 across three packs.

That makes the class **transient**, and it is the fourth member of one class of defect in this record, each time with a
different denominator:

| round | the number | the population nobody named |
| --- | --- | --- |
| R183 | a mean over **lost** games | nine losses became three, so the mean was over the survivors |
| R184 | a counterfactual over a **sampled** policy | a prediction read as a floor |
| R186 | a band over a **pool** that is 91% one kind | a stratum read as a population |
| **R188** | a class of losses over **one draw** | a draw read as a property of five games |

The generalisation is now sharp enough to be a rule: **an observation conditioned on an outcome is a statement about the
draw that produced the outcome.** Wins are not conditioned — they are the outcome — which is why the pool is the only
statistic in this record that has survived every round unchanged.

Three defects were caught in the design rather than in the readback, and they are worth recording because they were
caught *because* of this file:

1. **The rumination cell had no band.** Registered as "thoughts a game fall by at least 0.5 against the placebo". On the
   148 games with byte-identical packs between R186 and R187, the same prompt read **3.68** and **4.80** — a band of
   **1.12**, more than twice the registered threshold. The cell could not have been read in either direction, and the
   band was computable from artefacts that already existed (rule 1 of 34.267, applied one level down: a cell needs a
   band, not just a value).
2. **The first four dispatches bought nothing** (34.271): the bank was not on `master`. ¥0, twenty seconds, one guard.
3. **The placebo was mandatory and would have been skipped by a lane in a hurry.** Without it the round reports an
   instruction that "reduced rumination by 0.66 a game" — a number inside the band, in the direction the hypothesis
   predicted, from an arm indistinguishable from its own permutation. The placebo is the difference between a finding
   and a story.

**What it costs the project's plan.** The registered refutation named the location prior as R189, on the premise that
eight of ten losses are search. That premise is a one-draw statement like the one this audit retires, so it is retired
with its parent: a plan aimed at "those eight" would aim at a draw. What is left is a **state** — 1.34% of games enter a
rumination loop and each one costs the game — and a state is reachable with a conditional intervention (R189's guard)
rather than with knowledge about particular tasks.

## 34.273 — A guard's ledger needs a denominator, and a reply that carried a command under a thought is not a relapse

R189 changes one string: a reply that carried no command is answered `OK. Reply with one command only.` instead of `OK.`
That is a conditional intervention, and the condition is the point — it cannot fire in a game that never enters the loop,
so the round's first reading is not a score but an **engagement** count. The driver therefore records three numbers per
episode, and the first draft had two.

**The near-miss.** The natural ledger is `fires` and `relapsed`: how often the line was sent, and how often the model
answered it with another commandless reply. Written that way, the relapse test is one line — `kind_of_reply != "action"` —
and on the reference channel it is correct. On the **any-line** channel it is not: a reply whose first line is a thought
and whose second line is a command is parsed as a `thought` and *executed* by the channel (AUDIT 34.262), so a recovery
would be counted as a relapse. The guarded arm would then report a 100% relapse rate on exactly the replies the harness
had just repaired, and the round's mechanism cell would read as a mechanism that does not work on the channel R184 to R188
were all measured on.

The repair is one line and it is in the record rather than in the diff: **the command is looked for before the branch**,
so "did this reply carry a command" is `kind_of_reply == "action" or refused_command(reply) is not None`. Two tests pin
it — one on the reference channel that a refused command is answered `Nothing happens.` and does not count a fire, one on
the any-line channel that a recovered turn does not count as a relapse.

**Why three counters and not two.** A fire on the last turn of a pass has no later reply to read. Counting it as checked
invents an outcome; counting it as relapsed invents a worse one. So the ledger separates the denominator (`checked`) from
the numerator (`relapsed`), and the difference between `fires` and `checked` is the number of fires the budget ended on —
which is a fact about the pass, printed, and zero in every game that did not hit the cap. The registered reading is then
a rate with its own denominator: `relapsed / checked`, not `relapsed / fires`.

**And the control carries the field too.** `guard: false` with three zeros, rather than an absent key. An absent key is
what `refused_actions` looked like for two rounds, and reading it required knowing which artefacts predated the field;
a control that says `off` cannot be mistaken for an old file, and an old file that says nothing is reported `not counted`
rather than `0 fires`.

## 34.274 — The fourth harness knob, and the two ways a conditional intervention can be pooled into nothing

Four rounds have now moved something that is not the prompt and is invisible in the arm's name:

| round | the knob | what the label carries | what a join refuses |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R183 | the reader (`reference`, `any-line`) | `@anyline` | a span over two channels |
| R184 | the step cap | `@c30` | a span over two caps |
| R185 | the bank, at an unchanged length | `@b<digest>` in the header | one label over two banks |
| **R189** | **the answer to a commandless turn** | **`@guard`** | **a span over two guard states** |

R189's two arms are one family, one bank, one channel and one cap — **the guard is the entire difference** — so every
mechanism in this file is the only thing standing between the round and a report that averages an armed arm with an
unarmed one. Three were added with the flag:

1. **The label.** `always-in@kind+anyline+guard` against `always-in@kind+anyline`. Without it both dispatches land in one
   group and `tile` refuses the doubled games only after both are paid for — the failure R183, R184 and R185 each paid
   to learn.
2. **The join's declaration.** `--expect-guard on,off`, with `absent` normalised to `off` for the span check and printed
   as `absent` in the counter. An R186 artefact and an R189 unguarded arm *are* the same driver for this knob, so they do
   not need a declaration; an R186 artefact and a guarded arm are two drivers and do.
3. **The header held to the episodes.** `summary.guard_commandless` is a claim; `episode.guard` is the fact. A file where
   they disagree is a file that was merged, resumed across a change, or edited, and it is refused rather than joined —
   the same shape as R185's bank swapped under an unchanged label, one field further out. Found while writing this round's
   own tests, not in a readback: the two are written by one flag in one process, which is exactly why a disagreement is
   evidence of a third process.

## 34.275 — A band of 20 to 120 fires, for an arm that can only fire once every time the model thinks

R189's third reading was written as "`guard_fires` is between 20 and 120 over 274 games, and every firing is followed by
a reply that carries a command within one turn". The second clause is the mechanism and it held at **825 of 825 checked,
0 relapsed**. The first clause was arithmetically impossible, and the arm proved it by firing **826** times.

**Where the band came from.** The round before had measured **11 thought-heavy games over 822 game-draws, 1.34%** — a
rate over *games*. The registration multiplied it by turns a game (≈15) and got ≈55 fires, then wrote a band of 20 to
120 around it. But a fire is not a rare event: it happens on **every** reply that carries no command, and a model writes
4.96 of those a game. The band therefore described an arm that thinks 0.07 to 0.44 times a game — a model that never
narrates, which is the arm this lane would love and has never seen.

**What the band was actually guarding against** was written in the same paragraph: "a guard that fires on 90% of turns is
a different treatment (it would be a permanent instruction, which R188 measured as inert)". That is a **ratio**, not a
count, and the ratio is what should have been registered: 826 fires over ≈4,100 turns is **20%**. A count over this arm
cannot distinguish "fires on every thought" (which is the design) from "fires on every turn" (which would be a permanent
instruction) — the two differ by what the denominator is, and the denominator was the thing left out.

**The family, one row each.** This is the fifth member and the first where the wrong denominator was a *rate* rather
than a population:

| round | the number | what it was over |
| --- | --- | --- |
| R183 (34.268) | a mean over lost games | the survivors of a filter |
| R186 (34.270) | ten losses, two families | one draw, read as a class |
| R187 (34.272) | a cell with no band | no variance estimate at all |
| R188 (34.274 family) | a class of losses | one draw, five games |
| **R189** | **fires 20 to 120** | **a game rate applied to turns** |

**What it costs when it is caught.** Nothing, this time: the band failed and the mechanism clause carried the round, so
the reading is reported as a band failure rather than as a null. That is the difference between a registration that
fails *informatively* and one that fails *silently* — and it is only informative because the driver recorded `checked`
beside `fires`, so the miss could be attributed to the band rather than to the treatment.

**The rule, restated.** A registered cell needs three things and R189 is the first round where all three were written
down: a **value**, a **band**, and a **denominator**. The value was right (engagement), the denominator was implicit and
wrong (turns), and the band inherited the error.

## 34.276 — A four-row table that was one artefact and three quantities

R190's first reading was written as "a rank correlation between the utility score of a bank's entries and the sign of its
measured effect: rho >= 0.6 over four banks". The round could not compute it, and the reason was in the table rather than
in the score.

**One row had no effect.** `bank-crosskind-44774801298` is not a treatment. It is the artefact a **run that drove no
games** writes: `calls: 4`, `elapsed_s: 7.0`, a bill of $0.0049 for the call that built it, and no episodes. It was
committed at R177 as a fixture and the registration picked it up as a bank with a measured delta. It also renders
**1,166** characters, not the 659 the registration quotes — so the row was wrong twice, and the second wrongness is the
one that matters: a number copied from memory rather than from the file.

**Three rows were three quantities.** `bank-putscope-2`'s +24.45 pp is a bank against `none`; `bank-turnbudget-1`'s
-0.73 pp is a bank against **its own word-permuted placebo**. Those are not points on one axis — the first asks "is
carrying this better than carrying nothing", the second asks "is this sentence better than its own words shuffled". A
rank correlation over both is a correlation between two experiments that were designed to answer different questions,
and it would have produced a number that looked like a validity coefficient.

**The repair is in the file rather than in the prose.** `measured-effects.json` now carries, per row, the `quantity` it
is an instance of and the sentence that names the comparison, and `score_bank.py` refuses a row without either. The
correlation is then computed **inside one quantity**, and the reader sees how many points that quantity has before
seeing a coefficient.

| quantity | rows | what the round could do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| bank vs no bank, one dispatch | 3 | rho = +0.500, one inversion |
| bank vs its word-permuted placebo | 1 | reported, not correlated: one point is not a population |

**What this is a third example of.** The record has a family of defects where a number was computed over a population
that does not exist: a mean over the survivors of a filter (34.268), ten losses read as a class (34.270), a cell with no
variance estimate (34.272), a game rate applied to turns (34.275). This one is the same defect one level up — not a
statistic over the wrong population but a **table** that was never a population — and it was caught by a script refusing
to load it, before any money was spent.

## 34.277 — An instrument whose range is narrower than the resolution it would be read at

R190's reading 1 failed at **rho = +0.500** against a registered 0.6, with one inversion. The tempting next move is to buy
more points. The arithmetic says not to, and the arithmetic is the finding.

**The score's range on this corpus is 1.62x.** Among single-entry 551-character banks, `bank-putmove-line-1` reads
0.00544 and `bank-putprecond-1` reads 0.00881. Nothing plausible sits outside that, because every plausible bank in this
record names a command and states a condition — which is what the score rewards — so the corpus cannot produce a pair
that differs by more than about 1.6.

**The lane's resolution is 9.7 pp on one dispatch.** The inverted pair differs by 2.55 pp. So the hypothesis "the score
orders these two correctly" is answered by a measurement whose noise floor is four times the difference it would have to
detect. Buying four more banks (≈ ¥4.4) would move the sample from 3 to 6 points and would not move the resolution: each
new point would be an independently drawn ±10 pp.

**So the honest verdict is not "the score is wrong".** It is that the score is **unfalsifiable at the price this lane
pays for a reading**, and the three things that follow are all operational:

1. **A gate that cannot be validated is not shippable.** The admission family in the literature is not adopted, not
   because it failed a test, but because no test this project can afford would distinguish it from a coin.
2. **The regression that would have been invisible.** Had the round reported rho = +0.500 as "positive, approaching the
   threshold", the next round would have shipped a score that separates two content-identical banks by **+28% on the
   strength of their tags alone**, with the record's own readings of them pointing 3.65 pp the other way — inside the
   five-game band, so not a contradiction, but not corroboration either. A number that moves for a reason its author
   cannot name is a number that will one day move for that reason at the wrong moment.
3. **What a valid instrument would need.** Either a corpus with a wider score range (banks that *do not* name commands,
   which is the filler family, and whose effect is known to be zero), or a resolution below 2 pp (which costs 25x the
   games per arm). Neither is worth buying while the mechanism family is still producing 8-of-10 cells for ¥2.95.

**The rule, restated for the fourth time in this record and for the first time about an instrument rather than a
statistic.** A registered cell needs a value, a band and a denominator (34.275). An *instrument* needs a fourth thing: a
range wider than the resolution it will be read at. R190 is the first round in this record to measure an instrument's
range before spending anything on it, and the answer was that it has none to spare.

## 34.278 — A registered band that contradicts the sentence justifying it

R191's reading 1 registered `ledger_fires` at **20 to 200 per arm** over 274 games. The paragraph three lines below it
justified the treatment's price with "the trajectory says that is **one to three turns a game**". One to three turns a
game, over 274 games, is **274 to 822**. The band and its own justification differ by a factor of four, and nothing in the
registration noticed, because the band was written as a plausible-looking interval and the justification was written as
prose.

The measurement is **413 per arm**. That is inside the justification and outside the registered band, which makes this the
sixth member of the record's wrong-denominator family — and the second consecutive round to produce one:

| entry | the number | what it was a number about |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 34.268 | a mean over the survivors of a filter | the games that survived, not the games |
| 34.270 | ten losses read as a class | ten games, not a rate |
| 34.272 | a cell with no variance estimate | one dispatch's two arms |
| 34.275 | 20 to 120 guard fires | a *game* rate applied to *turns* |
| 34.276 | a four-row table | one artefact with no games and three quantities |
| **34.278** | **20 to 200 ledger fires** | **a band that contradicted its own arithmetic** |

**The rule this entry adds, and it is a rule about writing rather than about reading.** A band has to be **derived** from
the sentence that justifies it, in the same paragraph, with the multiplication written down: "one to three failed actions
a game times 274 games is 274 to 822 fires, so the band is 250 to 850." The 20–200 band was not a miscalculation, it was
an **uncalculated** number — a shape copied from R189's registration, whose own band was wrong for the same reason.

**What it cost.** Nothing. The reading it was attached to was the engagement cell, and the cell's real content — "the line
reached all four named games" — is a count, not a band. The verdict on reading 1 is therefore *failed on the band, held on
the cell*, and the failure is reported rather than repaired after the fact.

## 34.279 — The state line licenses the loop it was written to break

R191's treatment lost three games the control won, and two of them are the same kind with the same shape:

| game | lines received | ledger | control |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `look_at_obj_in_light-AlarmClock-None-DeskLamp-323` | **40** | lost, 50 steps, 6 thoughts | won, 5 steps |
| `look_at_obj_in_light-Laptop-None-DeskLamp-328` | **16** | lost, 50 steps, 22 thoughts | won, 5 steps |

Forty lines on one 50-step game means the model issued a refused command on forty consecutive turns while being told,
every time, which commands it had already tried. **By the third repetition the line is a constant**, and a constant in
front of every turn is precisely what R188 measured as inert for ¥3.03.

This is the same phenomenon the negative-transfer literature names from the other side: a state that is re-rendered
without change is not a state, it is a prior with a timestamp. The literature's term for the fixed-up version is
*contrast* — flagging the confusable, direction-opposite experience rather than repeating the same list (`arXiv:2610.19386`);
its term for the discipline the ledger already follows is *anti-persistence* — guidance synthesized at the point of use
and discarded with the episode (`arXiv:2610.27406`).

**The mechanism that would fix it is cheap and is not registered yet.** A line that carries a **repeat count** rather
than a repeat — `Already tried this episode: take apple 1 (4 times)` — is shorter than four copies and says something the
fourth copy does not. The condition "only when the command changed since the last fire" turns the tail into a no-op
instead of a constant. Both are one-line changes to `ledger_line`, and neither is bought until the distribution round
(R192) has put the pool claim on an interval.

**What it means for the verdict.** The mechanism cell (4 of 4 named games) stands, and the pool (+0.73 pp, p = 0.597) is
"not worse". What this entry adds is the reason the pool is not better: the repair pays on the games where one failed
action is a fact, and it costs on the games where the failure is the loop — and the loop is exactly the state R191 was
chosen for. A state renderer that is cheaper on the tail is the next generation of this treatment, not a bug in this one.

## 34.280 — The arm that received no treatment changed its own trajectory in half its games

R191 renders its line **only** on turns whose command moved nothing. Twenty-seven of 274 games never had such a turn, so
their message list is the control's, byte for byte — the prompts are identical by construction.

**Fourteen of those twenty-seven took a different path.** One of them, `look_at_obj_in_light-Pillow-None-DeskLamp-323`,
lost at the 50-step cap under the control and won in 9 steps under the ledger without a single line. Across the whole
pool only **15 of 274** games have identical prompt totals between the arms.

**So the model re-samples the prompt it has already answered.** The lane has known this as *cross-dispatch control
drift* since AUDIT 34.232 — the control moved six wins between two dispatches of identical code — and until now it has
been treated as an accounting fact about dispatches. R191 measures it **inside one round, per game**, on the cleanest
possible sample: games where the treatment literally did not exist.

**Three consequences, all of which change how a round is read.**

1. **The pool claim is bounded by this, not by the split.** 2.89 pp mde over 274 games already said the pool could not
   resolve a two-game effect. This says *why*: the two arms are two samples, not one sample measured twice.
2. **A mechanism claim has to be made on the games where the treatment fired.** Four named games, four fires, four wins
   is a claim about a state; "267 against 265" is a claim about two draws of one pool.
3. **The instrument that would isolate it does not exist in this lane yet.** The seed policy is deterministic and proves
   the *driver*; the model cannot be pinned. The only affordable estimator is more draws — which is exactly what R192
   buys, and it is why the release number has to be an interval rather than a level.

## 34.281 — A registered reading whose condition the arm cannot reach

R193's registration named five readings. One of them was: **"`ledger_suppressed` is non-zero (a gate that never fired cannot
have closed the tail), and the arm's `ledger_fires` is below R191's 413."** The gate silences a fire whose three-command
window is the one the previous line named. The arm produced **2 silences in 479 fires** — 0.4% — and 479 is 16.0% *above*
the 413 the same reading required it to be under.

Both clauses are wrong in kind, not in degree, and the diagnosis is mechanical:

- **The first clause is one-sided.** "Non-zero" is satisfied by a single event out of 479. It was written as a
  presence check ("a gate that never fired cannot have closed the tail") but a gate that fired twice cannot have closed a
  tail either. The threshold that would have carried the claim is **a share** — silences as a fraction of the fires that
  met the trigger — and a share was never named. A presence check on a rare condition is a reading that passes for free.
- **The condition is not reachable by the treatment's own definition.** A counted line changes its text on every fire
  (`(2 times)`, `(3 times)`), while the window the gate compares is a function of the **commands**, not of the rendering.
  Counting therefore cannot reduce the number of windows; it can only change which commands are issued. A fixed-point
  loop — one command until the cap — would meet the condition on every fire after the first. **2 in 479 says the loops
  this driver meets are cycles over several commands**, and a gate whose predicate is "the state did not change" is blind
  to a cycle by construction.

**The general rule, and it is the fourth member of a family this record keeps producing.** A registered reading must
name (a) the **unit** of its threshold, (b) the **denominator** the unit is a share of, and (c) whether the treatment can
reach the condition at all. R191's fires band failed (a) and (b) — 20 to 200 "per arm" against a paragraph that
multiplied to 274 to 822 (AUDIT 34.278). R193's reading 5 failed (c). A reading that can be satisfied without the
treatment working is worse than a reading that fails: it spends a purchase and returns a green cell.

## 34.282 — The estimate that was not a written-down multiplication, three rounds running

R193 was priced at **¥2.70** in its registration and cost **¥1.36**. The estimate was not a guess: it took R191's
measured **$0.3735 ≈ ¥2.69** and applied it to the next round — but R191's figure was for **two arms, 548 games**, and R193
ran **one arm, 274 games** against a control that was already paid for. The price per game was right; the multiplication
was never performed, so the round was registered at twice its cost.

The same failure has now appeared three times in five rounds, and each time in a different place:

| round | quantity | registered | actual | the missing operation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R191 | `ledger_fires` | 20–200 per arm | 413 | 274 × 1–3 a game |
| R192 | dispatches per draw | "four dispatches" | eight | 4 draws × 2 splits |
| R193 | spend | ¥2.70 | ¥1.36 | 1 arm, not 2 |

R192 was the one that was caught **before** the money, by writing the arithmetic into the paragraph (`4 × 2 × $0.187`), and
it came in at ¥5.35 against ¥5.4. **Writing the multiplication down is the whole fix**, and it costs one line per reading.

## 34.283 — The number this record published was a draw, and the record knew it

Before R192, every pool number in this record was one pass of one arm on one 274-game pool. The record had already seen
the same bank produce 265, 264, 264 and 258 — a seven-game spread — and quoted each of them as a level at the time it
was produced, with a footnote at most.

R192 drew the published arm five times on purpose: **267, 268, 265, 268, 270**, range **5 games = 1.82 pp**, s.d. 1.82
games, pooled **1,338/1,370 = 97.66% [96.72, 98.34]**. The range is larger than R191's paired effect (+0.73 pp) and
larger than three of the four mechanism deltas the record has reported since R180. Two independent draws of 274 games can
only resolve **3.74 pp** at 80% power.

**Three habits follow, and they are now policy rather than advice.**

1. **A level is quoted with its draw count.** "267/274, one draw of five" is a different sentence from "267/274".
2. **A cross-draw difference is not an effect.** The registered comparison for any arm is a **paired join inside one
   dispatch**; anything else is two samples and the mde says so.
3. **The pooled interval is the publication unit.** Five draws buy 0.81 pp of half-width around 97.66%, and that is the
   number a competitor table may cite.

The uncomfortable part: the same 274 games, the same bank, the same code, and a 1.82 pp swing. Every mechanism claim this
record made stands on **named games that carried the treatment**, which is why each round named them before it began — and
every pool claim is properly read as "not worse", which is what the intervals have said all along.

## 34.284 — The treatment documented for two events has only ever seen one of them, and it is the one the design did not name

The state ledger's trigger is written in three places as **two** ways a turn can move nothing: "the world answered
`Nothing happens.`, or the action was not in that turn's admissible set". R191 and R193 together are 822 games with the
treatment armed, and the two counters say the second way is the only one that has ever happened:

| arm | fires | `invalid_actions` | fires − invalid | games where the two are equal |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `guard+ledger` (R191) | 413 | **413** | **0** | **247 of 247** firing games |
| `guard+ledger-counts` (R193) | 479 | 481 | −2 (two silences, one last-turn gate) | 247 of 249 |

**Every line either arm ever rendered answered a command the world had already refused.** In this corpus the admissible
set is the set of commands that *do* something, so `refused_by_world` implies `moved_nothing(last)` and the two triggers
are nested rather than disjoint. A command that the world admits and then answers with `Nothing happens.` did not occur in
822 games.

**What that reframes, in three places on the record.**

1. **The state family is an admissibility repair, not a search repair.** R191 was registered as an answer to four
   cap-losses and read as "search failures with the narration removed" (R189's diagnosis). The mechanism it actually
   exercised is smaller and more specific: *the model was proposing commands that do not exist in this world* — 42 in a
   row on `Laptop-328`, 35 on `Statue-216`, 27 on `Bowl-308`, each of the three losing at the cap with
   `invalid_actions == ledger_fires`. The list helped because `take apple 3; take apple 4` is evidence that apple 3 and 4
   are not there.
2. **AUDIT 34.279's "a repeated line is a constant" was about the wrong repetition.** What repeats in the worst games is
   the **world's** answer — a 16-character no-op, up to 42 turns in a row — while the rendered line changes every fire,
   because the commands change. The constant is in the observation the environment has always sent, and the ledger's own
   audit attributed it to the ledger.
3. **The hint that matches the failure is the admissible set, and it has never been rendered.** "You have tried these"
   is one remove from "here is one thing you can do", and the second is strictly closer to the failure for a model that is
   inventing objects. That is the next registration (R194), and its first step is an instrument rather than a dispatch:
   the admissible set's **size** was never recorded, so the price of naming one command — or all of them — cannot be
   computed from the artefacts already paid for.

**The reusable rule.** When a treatment has two triggers and a counter for each, the counter has to be **per trigger**,
not per treatment. `ledger_fires` was one number for two conditions, and it took three rounds and 822 games to discover
that one of the two conditions had never occurred. A pair of counters costs one field and would have said so on the first
read.

## 34.285 — The one field the cycle question needed was the one the artefacts never kept

**The question.** R193's fifth reading was `ledger_suppressed` non-zero — the change gate firing, which is the only
evidence that a line's *content* can be a constant the model has already seen. It fired **2 times in 479 chances**. The
reading was written as a one-sided test that passes on a single event, and it passed on two, so the round could not
distinguish "the gate is inert because the loops are not fixed points" from "the gate is inert because its condition is
narrower than the loop". AUDIT 34.281 names the same defect from the other side.

**The defect.** The condition is a repeated three-command window, and **no artefact has ever contained a command**. The
episode record keeps `ledger_fires` and `ledger_chars` per pass, `observe_chars` per turn, and `actions` as a **count**.
`attempted` — the history every renderer reads — lives only inside `run_episode` and is dropped when the record is built.
The consequence is not that the gate was wrong; it is that **the gate's mechanism could not be audited at all** from 822
paid games, and the next step had to be an instrument rather than a dispatch (the rule AUDIT 34.282 already paid for once).

**What the instrument is.** Two fields on every episode, on every arm: `commands` — the ordered history the renderers read,
including the commands the world refused and the ones the parser dropped — and `fire_turns` — the index of the command
each line answered, so `len(fire_turns) == ledger_fires` is a checkable invariant. Both cost no call, no prompt character
and no change to any rendering; the tests assert exactly that, including that the message the model reads at a fire is
byte-identical with and without the record.

**Why an index and not the window.** A renderer already recomputes its window from `attempted` at the moment it fires. If
the record kept only the commands, a reader asking "would a cycle-aware line have fired *here*" would have to guess which
turns carried a line — from `observe_chars`, an observation about a different thing. The index is the one integer that
turns the question into arithmetic: the window at a fire is `commands[:index + 1]`, and the turns without a line are the
complement.

**The reusable rule.** An instrument that records a *consequence* of a history (a count of fires, a character total) cannot
be used to ask a question about the history. The cheap field is the one that keeps the history.

## 34.286 — The deterministic fallback was `help`, and the registered arm never rendered the treatment

**What was registered.** R194: on a turn whose command the world refuses, one line naming the set the world *admits* —
`Admissible here: 7 commands, e.g. \`take apple 1 from countertop 1\`.` The example rule was written for reproducibility
rather than for content: **the shortest command sharing the refused verb, else the first command in the world's order.**

**What was sent.** Over 248 firing games of a 274-game pass:

| the example shown | games | share |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `help` | **220** | **88.7%** |
| another meta command (`look`) | 1 | 0.4% |
| a movement command (`go to bed 1`, …) | 26 | 10.5% |
| **a command carrying a task verb** (`take`, `put`, `clean`, `heat`, `cool`, `examine`) | **1** | **0.4%** |

The model was told `Admissible here: 29 commands, e.g. \`help\`` on the turns it was inventing objects that do not exist.

**Why both branches point at `help`.** `help` is admitted in every room, it is the shortest command textworld publishes
(four characters), and it is first in the world's own ordering. So:

* when the refused verb appears nowhere in the admissible set — which is the failure this treatment was built for, a
  `take apple 3` for an apple that is not in the room — the fallback selects the shortest command, and that is `help`;
* when the verb does appear, the verb branch selects correctly, and it did: **one** fire in 248.

A rule chosen for determinism was never checked for informativeness, and no registered reading could catch it. The five
readings measured the number of lines, the pooled rate, the characters and the named games; **none of them read the
line.** A renderer's content needs a reading of its own — the instrument that recorded `admissible_sample` was the only
reason this defect is visible at all, and it was added for a different purpose (pricing the line).

**The consequence for the experiment.** The hypothesis — *naming the admissible set repairs the tail* — was not tested.
What was tested is *naming its size and a meta command*. The two games that got worse are the two that received it most
often (`Laptop-328` 16 → 44 invalid commands, `Bowl-308` 2 → 14 and lost), which is consistent with a hint that consumes
a turn and points at `help`. Reporting the round as "the admissibility hypothesis is refuted" would be reporting the
wrong experiment as the wrong idea.

**A second defect, in the registration itself.** Reading 2 required **at least 2 of 3** named games to win; the
refutation clause read "the three named games still lose" — i.e. **3 of 3**. One of three won. The outcome therefore sits
in a region that **neither the acceptance nor the rejection condition covers**, and the round's verdict had to be argued
rather than read. Every registration in this lane that names a per-game condition and a per-game refutation has to make
the two **tile** the space: `k ≥ 2` accept, `k ≤ 1` reject, nothing between.

**The reusable rule.** A deterministic rule is not an informative one. Any renderer whose content is *selected* — an
example, a sentence, a snippet — needs a registered reading of the selection itself (a distribution over what was sent),
not only of its length and its effect. One field, `admissible_sample`, cost nothing and found it.

## 34.287 — The reader that decides whether the next dispatch is bought must refuse the slices that would answer wrongly

**What was built.** `cycles.py`, at ¥0.00, reads the command record (`commands`, `fire_turns`) that R194's driver started
writing and answers the question R196 was to be bought for: on how many turns did the model re-issue a command the world
had **accepted** — the one event a refusal-triggered line cannot see? It reports accepted repeats, the share of losses
that carried one, the characters a line naming them would cost, and chains (a command repeating two or three turns
back).

**Why it is a module with a suite rather than a script with a print.** It decides a purchase, in both directions: a count
too high buys a treatment with no purchase on the corpus, a count too low closes a mechanism that was never tried. So it
carries four structural refusals, each of which would otherwise produce a **number** instead of an error:

| refusal | the failure it prevents |
| --- | --- |
| an episode without `commands` | an artefact that predates the field read as a game with no repeats |
| `len(fire_turns) != ledger_fires` | a record that disagrees with the counter written beside it |
| `len(fire_turns) != invalid_actions` | a fire that is not a refusal, which makes "accepted" unknown for every turn |
| a game in two slices | one game's repeats counted once per shard |

**The identity it stands on, and why a refusal is the right response to its failure.** A turn counts as *accepted* when
no fire answered it, so the reader needs the fires to be exactly the refusals. That is a measured fact rather than an
assumption — 413/413 in R191's arm and 479/479 in R193's across 822 games (AUDIT 34.284), and **465/465 and 383/383 on
the two rounds since** — and where it fails the honest answer is to stop: a slice in which one refusal went unanswered is
a slice where one turn's verdict is unknown, and any repeat count over it would be a guess with a decimal point.

**What its first read bought.** 195 accepted repeats in 274 games, of which **177 are loops** — a repeat of a command the
world had already accepted — and 18 are retries, where a command refused at a distance was accepted after walking over.
Loops appear in 136 games but in only **3 of the 8 losses**, and five losses contain no loop at all. The mechanism's ceiling is therefore **+1.09 pp** on a split that resolves **2.29 pp**, which
cancelled a ¥1.4 dispatch before it was sent (AUDIT 34.288). The reusable rule: **a mechanism whose ceiling is below the
split's mde is not an experiment, and the arithmetic that shows it costs nothing.**

## 34.288 — A criterion satisfied without the treatment, and a family whose ceiling is below the split's resolution

**Two defects, one round, and both were in the plan rather than in the code.**

**The per-game criterion could be satisfied by a draw in which the treatment did not fire.** R195's reading 2 required at
least two of three named games to win, and it read 3 of 3. But `Laptop-328` — R194's cap-loss at 44 refused commands —
was won in **3 steps with 0 fires and 0 refusals** by the R195 arm: the line never reached the game, and the game was won
anyway. R194's 44 refusals were a trajectory, not a property of the game, and the criterion could not tell the two apart.
Every per-game reading in this lane now has to carry `ledger_fires > 0` on that game to count as engagement; a win
without a fire is a datum about the model's draw and is reported as one.

**A mechanism whose ceiling is below the mde cannot be falsified.** R196 was to be the cycle-aware line: fire when the
model re-issues a command the world accepted. The ¥0 read (`cycles.py`) found **177 loops** in 136 games, but in only
**3 of the 8 losses**, and five of the eight contain **no loop at all** — 49 to 50 commands that never repeated. So the
treatment's best possible outcome on this split is +3 games = **1.09 pp**, against a paired mde of **2.29 pp** at 5
discordant games. Whatever it did, the reading would straddle zero. **Not bought**, and the reason is arithmetic rather
than taste.

**What replaces it.** The family closes with four readings of two mechanisms (refusal and state) and one trigger: the
guard +2.55 pp, the list +0.73, the count −1.46, the admissible set −0.73, the admissible set with a command −0.36. The
residual is capability-bound, so the next measurement has to be a corpus with headroom — which is a statement about where
the next ¥2–3 goes, not about what the mechanism is worth.

**The reusable rule.** Before registering a treatment, compute its **ceiling** — the fraction of the population the
mechanism can even reach — and compare it with the split's mde. A ceiling below the mde is a null by construction, and the
¥0 instrument that finds it is cheaper than the dispatch that would have reported it as "no effect".

## 34.289 — The product shipped five knobs and the record could not name the reading behind any of them

**What was there.** `packages/core/src/capture/microglia.ts` reads `budget`, `note`, `budgetBasis`, `speakMargin`
and `credit` from `MicrogliaOptions`, defaulting four of them to absence. `packages/eval` varies the same five in
registered arms. `createServer` passed none of them. There was no artefact, comment or test that said which of the
two programs a deployment was running, and the failure it enables is silent in both halves: an arm can win a knob
and a deployment never learn it.

**What the record has to be able to say, and could not.** Not "what is the value" — a constant already said that —
but *which reading chose it*. A record of values without provenance is a second copy of the defaults, and it drifts
the same way. So the artefact is per field: a `reading` (id, artefact, delta, both bounds, alpha) or an
`unmeasured` reason, and the audit refuses a `reading` that does not resolve **and** a resolving reading on a field
the product ships at its default. The second refusal is the one that generalises: evidence about a knob nobody
shipped is the exact shape a benchmark result takes when it is collected for a report rather than for a release,
and a record that counted it would report coverage it does not have.

**The state, on the first run.** Five fields, **zero measured**. Each reason is a measurement rather than a shrug:

| field | shipped | why it is not measured |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `speakMargin` | absent (always speak) | R123 dispatched the 0.05 rung: episode −2.50 pp [−22.50, +17.50], p = 1.0000, n = 160, while the rung withheld a third of the packs |
| `note` | absent (renderer default) | R53's three levels over one store were built, pre-registered, never dispatched |
| `credit` | `true` | the ablation shows the module binds; no lane has run it off against on at the same n |
| `budget` | absent (`policy.defaultBudget`) | no arm has varied the character budget alone; the arms that changed a pack changed content |
| `budgetBasis` | absent (`note-included`) | an accounting declaration, not a treatment — only the note arms need it |

**The binding, and what makes it more than a comment.** `serveOptions()` is spread by `createServer` and by the
ablation control, so both read one constant; the node test compares the product's pack **hash** against a host built
from the same profile over the same store, which is an assertion about the bytes a deployment serves rather than about
an options object. `null` stays expressible because `speakMargin: 0` attaches `pack.decision` where an absent margin
does not: a helper that filled absences with defaults would change what a host receives and reprice every number
produced without one.

**The boundary, stated.** The gate binds the shipped defaults and the one host that is a control by construction. A
lane's treatment arm is `profile + Δ` by design and still sets its own knobs in the driver; making those literal is
the next step. A gate that claimed to bind them today would be the same defect it was built to catch.

## 34.290 — Two writers of one quantity, and the cheaper one wrote the committed arms

**The claim R197 was registered to test.** Where microglia sits on τ²'s **accuracy–cost** plane. The accuracy half has
four readouts; the cost half has never had one.

**Why not.** The committed τ² arm artefact reads `"calls": 0` (`eval/results/poc-l4.json`, and the two history arms
beside it), while the Python driver records usage on every call — `run_split.py` appends a litellm success callback,
adds `usage_stats()` into the results document, and `selfcheck_usage.py` grades the callback against fixtures. The
loss happens on the TypeScript side: `bin/l4.ts` contains **no reference to `usage`** and writes the constant `calls:
0` at the arm record, while `bin/l4-pair.ts` reads `firstUsage.calls` and `secondUsage.calls` and publishes them.

So the repository has two readers of one quantity: the pair artefact says what the arms spent, the single-arm
artefact says zero, and a projection that consumed the single-arm form would treat a paid arm as free. This is the
same shape as AUDIT 34.286 (a renderer whose content was never inspected) one layer down — a field that exists, is
written, and is not the measurement its name promises.

**Consequences, both of them bookkeeping and both of them blocking.**

1. Every τ² row on the board carries "—" in the price column while every ALFWorld row carries a counted bill. The
   asymmetry is not a policy about disclosure; it is a missing reader.
2. R197's reading (4) cannot be produced from the artefact, and adding a second dispatch would reproduce the defect
   at a higher price. **The dispatch is cancelled** and the reader is R198's first step: carry `usage` through
   `measureFromResults` and `measureFromDriver`, write `calls` from it, and make absence explicit (`usage_absent: 1`)
   rather than zero — the convention the cache census already follows.

**The reusable rule.** A quantity that two writers produce must be compared by a test, not by an author. `calls` was
"obviously" the same field in both artefacts until one of them was read.

## 34.291 — The bill had three states and the field had one, so `0` meant both

**What was claimed.** That an arm artefact says what the arm cost. `PocResult.calls` is in every artefact, the τ²
driver counts provider calls on every call, and `bin/l4-pair.ts` reads the census. Three files, one quantity.

**What was true.** `bin/l4.ts` wrote `calls: 0` as a **literal**. The census reached the artefact only inside
`tau2.usage` (via `instrumentation`), and the field a reader opens first said zero. So the committed τ² arms say
`"calls": 0` beside a driver that reported 2,667 calls for the same run, and the pair step — which reads
`tau2.usage.calls` — would have disagreed with the arm step if anyone had put the two side by side. Nobody had,
because both are plausible: an arm with no memory makes no *distillation* calls, and zero is what a run with no
distillation looks like.

**The class.** Not "a wrong number". A field whose domain has **three** states — measured, counted-without-tokens,
and nothing-measured — written as one integer that cannot express two of them. The mirror of AUDIT 34.290 (two
writers of one quantity): here one writer wrote a constant that a reader could not distinguish from a measurement.

**The repair.** `arm-bill.ts` reads the bill into `census | count | absent` and the artefact writes the state as
the flag pair `usage_absent` / `usage_counted` — `0/0`, `0/1`, `1/0`. Two flags because one cannot carry three
states, and a single `usage_absent` would have made a count and a census identical. A recorded `calls: 0` is read as
`absent`, deliberately: it is the literal this audit is about, and no artefact in the lane has measured a zero it
could prove.

**The reusable rule.** A quantity with three ways of being known needs three ways of being written, and the encoding
must be total — the pair of flags, not one of them. The test that keeps it: one document, written into two arm
artefacts, paired, and the three call counts compared.

## 34.292 — Two arms of one dispatch were not the same program, and nothing compared them

**What was claimed.** That a treatment arm is the shipped configuration plus the treatment. R197a bound the product
(`createServer`) and an ablation control to `serveOptions()`, and left the drivers building their own
`openMicroglia({...})` argument lists.

**What was true.** `tau2-driver.ts` wrote `budget`, `note`, `budgetBasis` and `speakMargin` by hand. Two of the four
are set on every dispatch, so the arm and the product agreed only by convention; a treatment that moved a third was
indistinguishable, in the artefact, from one that did not. That is the same split AUDIT 34.289 recorded between the
product and the record — one layer down, between the product and the arm that is supposed to measure it.

**The repair.** `armServeOf()` derives the arm from `serveOptions()` plus the fields the dispatch named, each with
the variable or registration that named it; the driver spreads it, so no profile-owned knob can be set outside the
mechanism; the run prints the delta before its first model call. Two refusals (a field named twice, a moved field
with no reason) and one preserved distinction (a field named at the shipped value is kept as *named and unmoved*,
because "asked for the default" and "never mentioned it" are different dispatches).

**The acceptance is a type, not a paragraph.** The driver is imported twice — once with no variables (zero fields
moved: the baseline arm *is* the product) and once with three (exactly those three, in profile order). A hand-written
argument list cannot pass that test, which is the point.

**The reusable rule.** When a configuration is "the same as X plus a delta", the delta must be a value the code
computes, not a convention the author remembers — and the baseline must be *derivable* with an empty delta, or the
two sides drift the first time somebody adds a knob.

## 34.293 — The pool was two populations, and the only replicating number had never been computed

**What was claimed.** That the τ² memory arm costs **−4.64 pp [−11.45, +1.60]** over **194 pairs / 114 clusters**,
and that this is the pooled census of the transfer experiment.

**What was true.** The 194 pairs are four folds: `official` (40), `r152` (40), `r152c` (40), `swapped` (74). Three of
them carry the treatment key `unit=correction/form=lesson/scope=all/model=…/traceClaims=6`; `r152c` carries the same
key **plus `rotation=fair-share`**, which is a *serving* policy — the bounded arm caps how many packs travel. So the
published number averaged two mechanisms, one of which had been registered as a separate experiment (R152) precisely
because it was expected to move the outcome.

**The class.** Not "a wrong number". A **claim about a population that was itself a mixture**: the arithmetic was
right (−4.64 pp is exactly `(18 − 27) / 194`), the artefacts were right, and the sentence was still not a sentence
about one thing. Compare AUDIT 34.290 (two writers of one quantity): here one reader summed two quantities that
were spelled the same way.

**The repair.** `pack-ledgers.ts` pools by treatment key and reports every key separately, and it does not discard
the published figure — it *recomputes* it, so the difference between "arithmetic error" and "mixed population" is
visible:

| reading | episodes | broke | repaired | delta |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| the four post-R152 folds (as published) | 194 | 27 | 18 | −4.64 pp |
| key with no rotation declared | 154 | 20 | 14 | −3.90 pp |
| bounded arm only (`rotation=fair-share`) | 40 | 7 | 4 | −7.50 pp |
| pre-treatment artefact (`unstated`) | 57 | 6 | 4 | −3.51 pp |
| all five | 251 | 33 | 22 | −4.38 pp |

Every key is negative, so the *conclusion* — this pack costs accuracy in this lane — survives the correction; the
number does not, and neither did the claim to have pooled one experiment.

**The other half: a number that was available and never computed.** The same two blocks define inertness exactly —
`inert = served − repaired − broke` — and no round had quoted the share. It is **78.1% [72.6, 82.8]** over 251
served packs, and it is the only quantity on this lane that replicates across folds (70.3–87.5%) while the delta
flips sign. A census that had been in every artefact since R144 was never read as the primary reading, because the
lane was organised around the delta.

**A second layer, found while writing this up.** The key is not total either. `rotation` is projected only when an
arm declares one, so `poc-l4-pair-r152` carries none while its registration pins `serveRotation: fair-share` — which
means the "no rotation declared" pool above still contains a bounded fold. So the published pool was a mixture, and
the *replacement* pool is a smaller mixture: pooling by the artefact's declaration is necessary and not sufficient.
The repair is R202 (write `none` explicitly, so absence stops meaning two things), and until it lands the keys are
quoted as what the artefact declares.

**The reusable rules.** (1) A pool states its keys, and a key is whatever the treatment block carries — including
serving policy — but a field that is omitted when absent cannot be a key, because "none" and "not recorded" print
the same way. (2) When a claim flips sign across folds and another quantity does not, the stable quantity is the
finding, and the flip is the instrument's resolution talking. (3) A definition in the data (`inert` is "the verdict
did not change") is a measurement, not an assumption, and it should be quoted as one.

## 34.294 — The guard that refused a run and told the operator to dispatch at the hour it was warning about

**What was claimed.** `windowFit` refuses a dispatch whose run would cross into a peak band, and its refusal names
the hour to put in `not_before` so the next attempt lands in a window that fits. The message read:

```text
off-peak window: 52 minute(s) left against an estimate of 109 — the run would cross into the window that opens at
01:00 … Dispatch with not_before: 01:00
```

**What was true.** 01:00 is the hour **peak billing begins**, not an off-peak window. `windowFit` computed
`windowOpensAt` as `now + minutesRemaining`, and `minutesUntilPeak` returns exactly that moment — the *closing* edge
of the current stretch. So the field named "the hour the guard is waiting for" carried the hour the guard exists to
avoid, and an operator who followed the advice would have bought the same run at **double price** (the card bills
peak at 2× on input and output) or been refused again per phase, losing the half it had already paid for.

**How it was found.** R198's step 2 was dispatched at 00:07 UTC on a Monday, five minutes after the ledger round
was pushed. The job installed the τ² environment, counted the corpus's labels, and was refused by this guard before
its first model call — **¥0.00 spent**, which is the guard working. Reading the refusal is what exposed the advice:
the run needed 109 minutes against the 52 left before 01:00, and the message told the operator to dispatch at 01:00.

**The class.** Not "a wrong number". An **instruction that contradicts the rule it is enforcing**, emitted by the
same function that enforces it. The guard was correct and its advice was the inverse of its purpose; an operator
who trusted the line would have produced the failure the line was written to prevent.

**The repair.** `WindowFit` now carries two hours: `peakOpensAt` (what the run would cross, 01:00) and
`windowOpensAt` (the next off-peak stretch long enough to hold the estimate, 04:00 here). A `nextFittingWindow`
walk finds the second: from a peak edge it moves to the next off-peak start, measures the stretch, and if it is too
short jumps past the peak to the following one — so a 227-minute run is told 10:00 rather than 04:00, and a card
whose every stretch is an hour long raises rather than naming a moment that is peak.

**The deeper defect: the test asserted the advice.** `window-fit.test.ts` expected
`Dispatch with not_before: 06:00` for a 05:30 start, and its own comment two lines above said the run needed the
*04:00* stretch. The expectation was written from the implementation's output rather than from the rule, which is
how a guard keeps a wrong instruction for as long as nobody reads the message as an instruction. Both cases now
assert the *fitting* hour: `04:00` for a 00:47 start, because that morning's stretch is 120 minutes against a
109-minute estimate, and `10:00` for a 05:30 start, because the 04:00 that would have fitted has already passed and
the next off-peak start after the 06:00 peak is 10:00. `window-fit.ts` is 100% covered on all four dimensions.

**The reusable rules.** (1) A refusal's advice is part of the guard and needs the same test as the refusal.
(2) When a message names an hour, the test should assert the *property* of that hour (it fits), not the string;
a string that came from the implementation cannot detect that the implementation is wrong.

## 34.295 — The reader was asked to supply a fact only the writer had

**What was claimed.** The ledger gate pools folds by a treatment key that includes `rotation`, and R200's docstring
said the key describes "what the file declares, not what ran", with R202 named as the round that would "make the
field total by writing `none` explicitly". The round was registered as one line of projection and ¥0.

**What was true.** The registration understated the work by naming the wrong layer. `treatmentOf` omitted `rotation`
when no arm stated one, so `poc-l4-pair-r152` — whose registration pins `serveRotation: fair-share` and whose
artefact says nothing — produced the *same key* as the three unbounded folds. Four folds, one label, one bounded arm
inside it: the mixture R200's pooling was supposed to have removed was removed for exactly one fold (R152c) and
preserved for the other.

**Why the tests did not catch it.** They could not: every fixture constructed its treatment object by hand, so the
key function was tested against inputs a producer never emits. The defect lived in the *seam* between `treatmentOf`
and `treatmentKeyOf` — one site that omitted, one site that honoured the omission — and no unit test owned both ends.
The end-to-end pair test asserted a treatment block without a rotation field, which is the defect written down as an
expectation: the test had been written from the artefact's shape rather than from the rule.

**The class.** A **fact assigned to the wrong layer**. A reader cannot know whether a missing field means "declared
nothing" or "written before the field existed", and asking it to decide produces a label nobody earned. The repair
is at the producer, because the producer ran; the reader's omission rule stays, because a committed key may not move
because a file was re-read — which is the same shape as 34.287's rule that an artefact may not be re-labelled by
re-reading it.

**The repair.** `treatmentOf` writes `rotation` unconditionally (the agreed value or `none`) and `Treatment.rotation`
is a required field, so a future call site cannot omit it; `l4-pair` states the memory arm's policy unconditionally
and leaves the control arm silent, which is its actual state. Five properties are asserted: a fixture pair that
declares nothing writes `none`; one that declares `fair-share` writes it; the two keys differ; every one of the five
committed keys is unchanged; and `pnpm eval:pack-ledgers --check` reports no drift against the committed record.

**The reusable rules.** (1) Totality of a compared field is a property of the producer; a reader that fills blanks
is inventing treatments. (2) A test whose expectation was copied from an artefact's shape tests the artefact, not
the rule — assert the property the field is supposed to have. (3) When a registration names a layer ("one line of
projection"), check that the defect is reachable from that layer before pricing the round.

## 34.296 — A purchase was priced before anyone checked whether the data already existed

**What was claimed.** R201 was registered as "three margins that withhold ≈0%, ≈35% and ≈70% of packs, 40 held-out
retail tasks × 4 trials", priced at **≈¥4–5**, and left queued. The round was written as a dispatch because a
dose–response is a curve and a curve sounds like an experiment.

**What was true.** Every committed pair artefact already carries `serveSweep`: a ladder that prices **every** rung
(0, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.08, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25, 0.3) against the same episodes, with `served`, `withheld`, `kept`
and `broke` per rung. The three registered margins are three rows of a table that had been bought five times and
never read as a curve. The round's answer was ¥0, and the ¥4–5 would have bought a sixth draw of a population whose
curve was already known to within a fold's width.

**How it was found.** Reading R201's acceptance predicate against the artefacts rather than against the pattern of
previous rounds: "keeps ≥4 of 22 repairs while preventing ≥4 of 33 breaks" — 22 and 33 are the *corpus* totals, so
the predicate is a statement about a table, and the table existed. The `serveSweep` block had been in every pair
artefact since R123's rung lost, and no reader had consumed it as a dose.

**The class.** **A purchase priced before the inventory was checked.** Three of this project's rounds have now
repaired the same shape at different layers — a claim that needed a number, a number that needed a dispatch, and a
dispatch that needed nothing because the artefact already held the reading. The reusable test is the acceptance
predicate: if it names counts the corpus already reports, the round is a reader until proven otherwise.

**A second defect, found while reading it.** The obvious dose table reports *one* inert column, and that column rises
to 1 with the rung **by construction** — a withheld pack is inert because withholding cannot change a verdict the
pack did not change. A round that published only it would have certified any threshold as a success. The module
therefore reports two: `inertAll` (the gate's own reading) and `inertServed` (the ledger's, over survivors), plus
`selectivity = prevention − repairLoss`. The corpus then says the thing one column could not: at rung 0.01 the gate
loses 18.2% of the repairs to prevent 18.2% of the breaks — exactly proportional, selectivity +0.0pp — and through
0.05–0.10 it is **negative** (−10.6pp, −1.5pp), i.e. the margin silences *helping* packs faster than harming ones.

**What was not done, and why it matters.** No dispatch was sent to confirm the counterfactual, because the sweep's
model — a withheld trial reverts to the control's verdict — is exactly what a `speakMargin` dispatch assumes too. A
confirming run would test the model, not the corpus, and the model is already the one the lane has been scoring
against since R123. The round is therefore recorded as a *reading*, and the dispatch that would test the model is
priced separately (≈¥1–2 at one rung) and deferred until the bill makes the trade decidable.

**The reusable rules.** (1) Price a round against the artefacts before pricing a dispatch. (2) When a metric is
guaranteed to move in the desired direction by construction, publish the construction's complement beside it.
(3) A threshold that meets a count while being exactly proportional to the corpus is a dose knob with a threshold's
name; the diagnostic is `prevention − repairLoss`, and it has a sign.

## 34.297 — The served count and the injected count were the same number until an arm separated them

**What was found.** The inert identity `inert = served − repaired − broke` has one denominator, and for six folds
that was safe for a reason nobody had written down: the block the facade served *was* what the agent read, so
`serveYield.renders` and "packs the model saw" were the same population. R204's transient arm breaks that identity of
reference without touching the identity of arithmetic — the facade still serves the block, but the agent injects a
sentence written from it, and an episode whose guidance call failed carries **nothing**. In that episode the facade
counted a render and the model read no memory at all, so the episode is inert by construction and would be booked as
an inert pack.

The size of the error is not incidental. The number this entire line of work is about is 78.7% inert, every gate in
the lane is judged against it, and a wiring defect that trades failures for inertness would move it in the direction
that looks like success. A fold of 40 episodes with a 10% guidance failure rate would report 78.7% as ≈81%, with
every gate green and no field of the artefact able to say why.

**Why nothing caught it.** Both quantities were correct in their own layer. The facade's count is what the facade did;
the agent's `injectedMessages` is what the agent did; and the pair published neither side by side. A defect that lives
in the *difference between two layers' accounts* is invisible to a test of either layer, which is the same shape as
AUDIT 34.295 (a reader asked to supply a fact only the writer had) and the same shape R48 found one level up.

**The repair.** The refusal is in the ledger rather than in the count, because a count cannot be repaired without
inventing a population: `pack-ledgers` refuses a `serveBody: guidance` fold whose guidance census reports any failure,
with the text `N of M guidance calls failed, so the rendered count is not the injected one`, and refuses the absence of
the census as a third state. The alternative — subtracting failures from renders — would publish a share over a
population no field of the artefact carries, which is the arithmetic AUDIT 34.296 (a purchase priced before anyone
checked the data) was written about.

**The near-miss behind it, recorded because it would have cost a dispatch.** The registration's first draft carried
`serveSupport: 2` from R198. Raw records are one verbatim event each, so every one of them has `supportTasks: 1`, and
the floor would have retired the whole store: the arm would have served an empty pack on every request and reported a
mechanism that did nothing. The floor is a filter on *claims with corroboration*, and the raw unit has none by
construction — a switch inherited from a neighbouring registration is a switch nobody re-derived.

**The reusable rules.** (1) When two layers each keep an account of "how many", publish both in one artefact and
compare them; the defect lives in the difference. (2) A treatment that changes the *object* of a count changes which
events are in it — check every counter whose denominator was the old object. (3) A switch copied from the registration
next door is a hypothesis about this one's unit, and the unit is what makes it true or false.

### 34.205 The state machine had three answers and the artefact had a fourth, and a failed prediction was reading as a pass

**What happened.** R204's readback was written before the dispatch, which is the discipline; its state machine was not.
Two of its exits were wrong in opposite directions. A pair whose `treatment.unit` was *absent* came back `DISCARDED` —
the state that means "this is another arm" — because the field was graded by inequality, and `None != 'raw'`. And a
planted arm that called the summariser once per *turn* rather than once per *episode* came back `GRADED` with three
lines reading `FAIL`, because that reading had been written as a prediction instead of a refutation.

**Why absence is not disagreement.** `cross-fit.ts`'s `agreement()` returns `value: undefined` when no arm states a
field, and deliberately so: a control arm serves no pack, distils nothing, and has no unit, form, scope or knobs to
report, so requiring every field twice would refuse the only pair shape the lane produces — the reason
`poc-l4-pair-official.json` still reads `treatmentAbsent: "the arms do not both state unit: reference record none"`.
A verifier that grades the pooled treatment therefore meets absence as a *normal* state, and reporting it as another
arm invents a mis-dispatched run and hides the real one behind it. The same file, run against that committed artefact,
now prints `serveBody absent: written before R204` and `NO_MEASUREMENT`.

**Why a prediction is not a refutation.** The two lists in these reports render differently on purpose —
`PASS`/`FAIL`/`n/a` against `FIRED`/`clear` — and only the second decides the state. Writing the call-count reading in
the first list made the strongest available evidence of a wrong mechanism (a plant that is not the registered one)
indistinguishable from a number that came out slightly off, and left the state saying the fold was gradeable. Every
reading the registration names as a refutation has to be one: the alternative is a verdict that the reader has to
re-derive from the lines above it, which is exactly the reading this record refuses to accept from other people.

**The reusable rules.** (1) A grading state machine needs a state for "the field is not there", reachable *before* the
inequality that would otherwise read absence as disagreement; absence, disagreement and failure are three facts about
three different runs. (2) If the registration says a reading would refute the arm, it goes in the refutation list —
a FAIL line under a `GRADED` verdict is a pass with a caveat, and no reader has ever acted on a caveat. (3) Prove the
absent-field path against a real pre-change artefact rather than a fixture: the fixture is written by the same hand
that wrote the state machine, and it will not disagree with it.

### 34.206 A structural copy of an unpublished package is a promise with one witness, and that witness was a cron job

**What happened.** Cortex's `createMemory` began emitting a `reads` field. Microglia's adapter re-declares cortex's
`MemoryValue` instead of importing it — `@agentix-e/cortex-core` is not on npm — so the copy went on describing twelve
fields while the substrate moved to thirteen. `ci` stayed green for as long as the change had been upstream, because
there is no compiler on the other side of a promise to a package that cannot be installed. The `cortex` lane, which
clones and builds the real package, was red on the next cron.

**Why the copy exists at all, and why that does not make it safe.** A structural copy is the honest response to an
unpublished dependency: it is checkable at the call site and it cannot drift behind a version range that does not
exist. But "cannot drift behind a version range" is not "cannot drift" — it drifts *silently*, in the one direction
nothing local observes, and it does so while every local gate reports success. The lane was written for exactly this
and had never fired; the first time it fired it was found by a *dispatch guard* that refuses to buy on a red tree,
not by anyone reading the lane.

**The near-miss fix.** `reads` defaults to `0` in the factory, so `reads: 0` in the projection would have made the
lane green in one line. It would also have been wrong: the field is cortex's retention tie-break — how many windows
have quoted an entry — and microglia already counts that event as `applied` ("runs in which this item was retrieved
and injected"). A projection that reset the count would hand the substrate a store where every entry looked equally
used, and the FSRS review schedule built on that rank would answer a question nobody asked. The conformance script now
passes the same `reads` into `createMemory` so the comparison is between two factories over one input, rather than
between one factory and one default — the earlier shape would have passed a projection that dropped the value.

**The rule this leaves.** (1) A promise to an uninstallable package needs a witness that lives outside the repository,
and the repository must not treat that witness as optional: it ran on a schedule, and a schedule is a lane that fails
when nobody is looking. (2) Whatever that witness can check, the local tree must check a *pin* of — the field set
written down as a list, so a change on this side is refused here rather than discovered there. (3) When a copy drifts,
ask what the new field *means on this side* before asking what it means to the compiler: the cheapest fix (`0`) was
available and would have replaced a loud failure with a quiet, plausible one.

### 34.207 The gate covered the actor nobody used, and the census was measuring the input

**What happened.** R204's transient arm ran once (run `45192820103`) and came back with `failures: 0` and
`refusals: 34` of 40. The ledger gate written the round before refused a transient fold whose `failures > 0`, on the
reasoning that a failed call injects nothing while the facade's block still counts as rendered — and it read this fold
as quotable, because the condition it named had not occurred. A refusal injects nothing for exactly the same reason:
the summariser was shown the records, judged that they do not bear on the request, and wrote `NONE`. The difference
between the two is *who declined*, which is a fact about the run and not about the population.

**Why the miss is structural rather than careless.** The gate was written from the failure branch of the code that had
been read most recently — `guidance()` catches an exception, counts it, and returns `""` — and the refusal branch
returns the same `""` three lines further down through a different path. Two paths, one effect, and the gate named the
one with a stack trace. A gate is a statement about *populations*, so it has to be written from the *effect* (this
episode carried no body) rather than from the *cause* (the provider was down), and the effect here had two causes from
the day the census was designed with three counters.

**The quantity that was wrong, and how wrong.** On this fold `serveYield` reported 50 renders, 6 repairs, 4 breaks and
40 inert, closing to 80.0%. Only six episodes carried a body. So 44 of the 50 renders were packs the agent never read,
and the 80.0% — the number the round was registered to move — is a statement about the input. `V1-pack-not-empty` has
the same defect one layer up: it certified "40 of 40 requests carried an item" for a fold in which six did.

**What was changed instead of the threshold.** The gate refuses refusals as well as failures, with the counts in the
message. The readback compares calls to the **episodes** rather than to `renders` — 40 calls against 50 renders is a
healthy fold, and the first draft of the refutation would have called it a per-turn plant — and it returns
`NO_MEASUREMENT` for a share it cannot attribute. And a negative token premium, which this fold produced (the memory
arm spent 146,081 fewer prompt tokens than its control), is reported as a failed prediction: no pack-serving arm
undercuts its control, so the sign is the refusal rate in another column rather than an efficiency.

**The rules.** (1) A gate is written from the population it protects, not from the branch that produced the condition;
if one effect has two causes, the gate names the effect. (2) When an arm's census counts a population and its ledger
counts another, the fold can support the readings that use the census and none that use the ledger — say which, rather
than publishing the one that looks like a result. (3) A premium with the wrong sign is a defect in the instrument
before it is a result about the mechanism, and the second reading is always the tempting one.

**Left open, deliberately.** The fix is the agent reporting per request whether a body was injected, joined by the
driver to the ledger. That is an instrument change and it needs a re-run, because the flag is absent from this
artefact; it is registered as R205 rather than patched into a threshold that would have made this fold look quotable.

### 34.208 The gate was written from the branch that had a stack trace

**What happened.** R204's transient arm came back with `failures: 0`, `refusals: 34` of 40, and a store that did not
move. The gate written the round before refused a fold whose guidance call *failed*, on the ground that a failed call
injects nothing while the facade's pack still counts as rendered. The condition it named never occurred and the fold
passed, carrying a share computed over fifty renders of which six carried a body.

**Why the branch was the wrong place to write it from.** `guidance()` catches an exception, counts a failure and
returns `""`; three lines below, a `NONE` reply returns `""` through a different path. Two paths, one effect — and the
gate was written from the one that produced a log line. A gate is a statement about a **population**, so it has to be
written from the effect (this episode carried no body) rather than from the cause (the provider was down). The census
had counted three outcomes from the day it was designed; the gate named one of them.

**What was changed.** The effect is a field: `injectedEpisodes`, one per boundary, raised where the injected message is
