built. The join drops the episodes that carried nothing and publishes the count, the pair carries
`serveYield.withheld`, and the gate asks the artefact whether it named its population instead of inferring it from a
counter. Refusals are no longer a refusal; a fold with no `withheld` still is.

**The two rules this leaves.** (1) **A parallel list is a positional join.** `episodeStarts` and `injectedEpisodes`
are only aligned if both are appended at the same site, so both are appended by `_open_episode()`; the fixture that
cleared one and not the other produced three cases reading a shifted population, which is the failure the pairing
exists to prevent and the reason the fixture now clears both. (2) **A refutation needs an interval, not a point.** With
six bodies the interval is 30–40 pp wide and contains the pool and everything above it; requiring the lower bound to
clear the band costs one branch and removes the class of verdict that a small sample produces by accident — the same
disease as reading a red gate as a green one, one layer down.

**Left open, deliberately.** Whether the refusal rate (85%) is a property of the *material* rather than of the body is
not this round's question. The literature's 59.9% summarises the failing trajectory of the task at hand and discards
it; these records come from other retail tasks and mostly do not bear on the next request. That arm is a registration,
not a patch.

### 34.209 Two refutations fired on a healthy fold, because both were written from a count

**What happened.** R205's fold is the first transient run with a named population, and my own readback marked it
`ABANDONED` twice over. The call rule fired on **42 calls against 40 episodes**, and the price rule fired on
**+3,454.9 tokens an episode**. Both were false, and both were false for the reason this project keeps re-learning:
the rule was written from a number that correlates with the defect rather than from the defect.

**The call rule.** The registration named one failure mode — a summariser called once per *turn* rather than once per
episode — and the rule that guarded it was `calls == episodes`. Two of the 42 calls are retries: the host re-asked the
same turn inside two episodes, the pack was decided again, and the agent counts that as `recallRepeats`. A per-turn
plant on this corpus makes ~400 calls; a retry makes one more. The rule is now two rules with the mechanism on each
side: `calls < episodes` means an episode was never asked (the arm is not the registered one), and `calls ≥ 2 ×
episodes` means the plant. The middle is the arm doing what it said.

**The price rule.** A per-episode premium is the body's price only when the two arms spend the same number of calls,
and that is a property of the user simulator rather than of the arm. This fold's memory arm made **750 calls against
683** — the treatment took a different path through the same task — so +3,454.9 tokens an episode was **67 turns**.
The comparable quantity is the arm's prompt total minus what its own summariser was shown, over its *agent* calls:
**4,693.4 against the control's 4,697.0**, a ratio of 0.9992. The body cost ≈ 583 tokens an episode and nothing else.
The rule now grades per call whenever the call counts differ by more than 5%, and quotes the premium beside the counts
that confound it.

**The third one, in the ledger.** `measured == rendered` is not an identity on a fold that withholds episodes:
`degradation` counts 40 paired trials, `serveYield` counts 9 renders. A ledger that refused this fold would have been
a ledger that refused every transient fold with a working instrument; a ledger that ignored the mismatch would have
stopped checking a real identity for every other arm. It is scoped instead: each census closes inside itself, the
cross-population triple is owed only where the populations are one, and a test states both halves with this fold's own
numbers.

**The rules.** (1) A refutation has to name the defect's *shape*, not a count that happens to separate the healthy case
from it — or the first honest fold refutes itself. (2) When one arm's denominator moves, the quantity that carries the
claim is the one divided by the unit that stayed put; the premium moved because the *simulator* moved, and the
per-agent-call cost did not. (3) A gate that fires on a good artefact is worse than no gate: the fold was `GRADED`
only after three rules were repaired, and each repair is a test built from the numbers that broke it.

## 34.298 — The corpus share was an average of two materials, and the fold that would have exposed it was never committed

**The defect.** `headlineOf` pooled every fold in `eval/results/` and published one number: 78.7% inert of 291
served packs. `serveBody` had been added to the treatment key in R204, so `pooledOf` separated a `guidance` fold from
a `rendered` one — but the *headline* still averaged them, and R205's fold was held out of the corpus entirely
rather than committed, which is how the defect stayed invisible: the corpus only ever contained folds it could pool.

**Why it is a defect and not a preference.** On a transient arm, `serveYield.renders` counts the summariser's inputs
(R204: 50 renders over 40 episodes of which six carried a sentence; R205: 9 renders with 35 of 40 episodes withheld).
A share pooled over `renders` therefore has two different denominators in one population, and the number that comes
out is a percentage of a quantity that means "served packs" on five folds and "things a summariser was shown" on the
sixth. Nobody reading `78.7%` could have known which.

**The repair.** `PackLedger.body`, read from the artefact's `serveBody` and defaulting to `rendered` — a fact rather
than a guess, since every artefact before R204 injected the block the facade rendered. `headlineOf` refuses a mixed
corpus and names both bodies; `headlineOf(folds, body)` pools one material. `packLedgersRecord` scopes the headline
to the body the corpus is mostly made of and publishes `headline.body`, so the committed record says what it is
about. `headlineLine` prints it: *"over the rendered body, pooled over 3 treatment(s)"*.

**The near-miss worth recording.** Refusing a mixed corpus outright was the first shape of the repair, and it was
wrong for a reason this repository keeps rediscovering: it makes the *gate* red when a legitimate fold is committed,
which teaches an operator to hold the fold out — the same behaviour that hid this defect for a round. The refusal
belongs to a caller that has not said which material it is asking about; the record's job is to say which one it
published.

**What the gate now catches.** A fold whose `serveBody` is new, a corpus of two materials, and a caller that omitted
the body — three states that were one state (`pool it`) before. Covered by four new tests in
`pack-ledgers.test.ts`, including the negative one: `headlineOf([fold('a'), fold('b', {body:'guidance'})])` throws
with both bodies in the message.

## 34.299 — A treatment that could not be written, and the three ways of writing nothing

**The defect the design avoided before it existed.** The note is written by the runner and read by the agent, and
the naive shape — a module-level dict, or a document cached at import — is a treatment that is a constant: rounds
share one process, so the cache would serve round one's notes to round four. The arm would look inert for a reason
that has nothing to do with the material, and every reading of it would be about the cache.

**The repair, and the case that proves it.** `_notes_document()` is keyed on `(mtime, size)`; the runner writes
between rounds and never during one, so a change means a new round rather than a race. The case
`a_note_written_between_rounds_is_read_by_the_next_episode` asserts the first episode serves nothing, the file is
rewritten, and the second episode serves the new sentence — which fails on any implementation that caches without a
stamp.

**The three ways of writing nothing, counted apart.** `refused` (the summariser answered `NONE` — the arm's gate),
`providerFailures` (the call failed — the run is about an unreachable summariser), `unreadable` (the reader could
not see the messages). Collapsing them into "no note" is how a broken run is published as a null result, which is
the collapse this file has recorded eleven times now. A fourth state — the sidecar exists and cannot be parsed — is
`notes.problem`: the agent serves nothing *and* the artefact says why.

## 34.300 — The binding was a sentence, and the sentence is re-written on every attempt

**The defect.** R206 binds its material to a task by hashing the message that opened the episode: the runner writes
the note under `note_key(first user message)`, the agent computes `note_key` from the message τ² handed it, and the
matching entry is served. The registration asserted the identity was "stable within a task and different across
tasks". Both halves are false on τ² retail:

| reading | measured |
|---|---|
| exact key reuse over 168 same-task pairs | 0.006 |
| within-task similarity min / mean | 0.132 / 0.444 |
| cross-task similarity max / mean | 0.562 / 0.099 |
| best fuzzy threshold | θ=0.30, 31 misses and 29 wrong servings |

The user simulator generates the opening per attempt, so one task opens four ways; and tasks 5 and 9 are the same
scenario for different users, so the *closest* text to a paraphrase of 5 is sometimes 9's opening. There is no
threshold with a margin, and the shipped mechanism would have served nothing even at 100% coverage.

**Why the pilot could not see it.** Its `hits: 0` was true and its cause was different: the summariser had written
no note, because both failures were refused. Two sufficient causes, one number. A report naming either would have
been wrong, and the wrong one ("no material was written") is the one a reader would have believed, because it is
what the census says out loud.

**The repair, in two parts.** An instrument (`eval/verifiers/opening_stability.py`) that answers the question for any
`results.json` before an arm is dispatched; and a registration (`R207-transient-identity`) that stops matching text
at all — one task per process invocation with its own sidecar, so the file the runner hands the agent *is* the
identity. The failing pilot is what makes the second part affordable to specify: it reuses the same six tasks, so
the two runs are comparable line for line.

**What the instrument deliberately does not do.** It does not recommend a threshold. It prints the best one it can
find and the two error counts that come with it, because a fitted constant presented as a property of English is
the failure mode this repository has a rule about — and here the fitting is done on 168 pairs, which is exactly the
sample size at which a threshold looks principled.

## 34.301 — A material derived from failures cannot be measured on a corpus that hardly fails

**The defect, and it is a design one rather than a code one.** R206's arm took six held-out retail tasks, four
rounds, and produced **two** failures in twenty-four treatment episodes; the summariser declined both, and one of
the two is an authentication dead end where escalating to a human is the policy's own answer. Coverage is therefore
0.000 over one failure, and the arm's own gate called it `ABANDONED` — correctly, because the number it needs is a
rate and one observation is not one.

**Why this is worth recording as a defect rather than as a result.** The registration's sample was chosen for the
*fold* (forty held-out tasks, the leaderboard's own half) and inherited by the pilot, where the base rate is
83–92%. A pilot whose subject is "does the mechanism act" needs failures to act on, and the population of failures
is a function of the corpus's difficulty rather than of the material. The next grid is therefore chosen **before**
its numbers are seen: the ten held-out tasks whose control attempt failed in the fold's own control arm.

**And the counter-check that must not be skipped.** A summariser that is handed a task's own failed trajectory and
still answers `NONE` may be right — the failing attempt on task 5 shows an agent doing what the policy asks. That
means the third possibility has to be stated: on this benchmark, most failures may not be the agent's, in which
case a failure-derived material is starved *by construction* and the finding belongs to the benchmark rather than
to the mechanism. The arm that distinguishes them shows the summariser the evaluator's verdict — a different
material, registered separately, because changing it now would make R207's result attributable to neither.

## 34.302 — Four files produced every number this lane published, and nothing measured how much of them ran

Found while building R207, and it is the same class as 34.224 and 34.251: a gate that existed as a *figure* rather
than as a requirement.

**What was true.** `notes.py`, `note_pilot.py`, `r206_readback.py` and `opening_stability.py` each carried a
self-check — 82, 76, 27 and 21 cases — and `ci.yml` ran none of them. `note-pilot.yml`'s contract job ran all four
and checked that they exited 0. Nothing anywhere asked how much of each file those cases reached, so a refactor
could take the instrument's coverage down and every job would stay green. Measured with `coverage --branch` over the
four, before any new case:

| file | lines+branches covered |
|---|---|
| `note_pilot.py` | 471 / 529 — **89.0%** |
| `notes.py` | 533 / 563 — **94.7%** |
| `opening_stability.py` | 172 / 215 — **80.0%** |
| `r206_readback.py` | 213 / 246 — **86.6%** |
| together | 1389 / 1553 — **89.4%** |

**Why it is a defect and not a number.** These four files are the entire instrument of the arm: the sidecar's format,
the producer that assembles the artefact, the grader that decides `GRADED`/`ABANDONED`, and the measurement that
told R206 its binding does not exist. A regression in any of them produces a *number about nothing* rather than a
crash, which is the failure mode this record has repaired twenty times and the one a green job cannot see. The
concrete instance: `opening_stability.py`'s `main` — the only path the workflow uses — was 0% covered, and its
`--json` branch had never been executed by any test.

**The repair, in three parts.** Cases first: every reader guard, every `main` branch (including the off-peak window
guard and the fixture writer), the new `scope`/`lookup`/`merge_documents` surface, and each of `rows_of`'s four
refusals. Then the *reporter*: `r206_readback.self_test` was restructured around `run_cases(cases) -> (passed,
failed)` so the suite can feed it one case with a deliberately wrong expectation and require it to be reported —
the failure path is now measured rather than unreachable, because a suite that cannot fail is a suite whose green
means nothing. Then the gate: the contract job runs the four under `coverage --branch --include=…` and fails below
**95% per file** with `--expect-files 4`, which is the same checker and the same floor `ci.yml` already applies to
the ALFWorld lane — one rule, two lanes, rather than a second convention.

**After:**

| file | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `note_pilot.py` | 89.0% | **96.9%** |
| `notes.py` | 94.7% | **95.7%** |
| `opening_stability.py` | 80.0% | **98.1%** |
| `r206_readback.py` | 86.6% | **96.6%** |
| together | 89.4% | **96.5%** |

**What the numbers say about the cases, not just about the coverage.** 138 + 132 + 44 + 35 cases replaced 82 + 76 +
27 + 21, and the growth is not padding: twelve of the new `notes.py` cases are the five ways `lookup` can produce no
note, which is the distinction between "the file had nothing for this task" and "the agent served nothing"; six of
the new `note_pilot.py` cases are the merge's three refusals and the two identity counters; four of
`r206_readback.py`'s are `rows_of`'s guards, each of which would otherwise let a malformed row be read as a score.

**The rule this records.** A file whose output is a judgment rather than a value needs a coverage floor as much as a
service does — more, because a service that breaks throws and a judge that breaks returns `GRADED`.

## 34.303 — Three refutations fired on an artefact that had nothing to refute

**Defect.** R207's pilot was graded `ABANDONED` with three refutations fired: *the treatment never read its
sidecar*, *the summariser wrote notes for too few failures*, *the notes restate the request*. Every one of them was
false about the mechanism. The grid produced one failure in 48 episodes and it arrived in the last round, which is
never distilled, so `failed` over the rounds a note is written from was **0** — and each gate translated that
absence into a claim about a different party:

| gate | what it asserted | the fact |
|---|---|---|
| `N1 and found one` (`hits > 0`) | the agent did not read the file it was given | the file held no note; `lookups` was 24 |
| `N2 coverage ≥ 0.6` | the summariser wrote for too few failures | there were no failures to write for |
| `N3 specificity ≥ 0.5` | the notes restate the request | there were no notes |

**Class.** This is the file's own documented failure mode — "a gate written from a cause rather than from the
effect" — committed by the file, one level up from the two it had already repaired. The general form: when a metric
is a ratio whose denominator is a count of events the arm is supposed to cause, a zero denominator makes the ratio
`None`, and `None` degrades to 0 in every comparison written as `(value or 0.0) >= bar`. The pattern appeared in
three gates at once because each was written the same way.

**Repair.** `N0b` grades the population before anything is computed from it: at least one failure must arrive in a
round a note is written from. Without one, the three predictions report `n/a` (the `Report` type already carried
`None` for exactly this), the refutations are conditioned on the same fact — `serviceable = written > 0` for the
sidecar gate — and the state is `NO_MEASUREMENT` with `reason: no-distilled-failure` in the context block. The
paired reading is still printed, because the one number a saturated grid has to offer is how saturated it was.

**Why `NO_MEASUREMENT` and not `ABANDONED`.** The two states ask an operator for different actions. `ABANDONED`
says *do not buy this material*; `NO_MEASUREMENT` says *this run did not try*. A saturated grid is the second, and
the distinction is what stops the next round from being a rewrite of the mechanism that was never tested.

**Why the workflow stays green.** The grading step reads the reason line, prints `::warning::`, and exits zero. A
red job for a too-easy grid teaches an operator to re-dispatch rather than to read — the same argument that made
`ABANDONED` green in R206.

**Evidence the repair is a repair rather than a relabelling.** Four new self-check cases read the *rendered report*
rather than the state: a saturated grid must contain no `FIRED` line at all, must still show that the file was
asked for, must name the population as the reason, and must mark coverage `n/a`; and a summariser that declined
every attempt must still abandon — on the coverage gate, with the sidecar gate clear. `r206_readback.py` stands at
96.3% with `--expect-files 4`.

## 34.304 — Three rounds of the note lane measured a truncation and called it a refusal

**Defect.** The summariser's call was made twice in the driver — once in `run_split.py`'s `write` closure and once,
later, in R208's ablation — and neither copy passed the provider's thinking switch. `deepseek-flash` answers in
thinking mode by default and **bills the reasoning against `max_tokens`**; the note budget is `96` tokens for one
sentence. So every call spent the budget before writing anything, returned an empty message, and
`notes.sentence_of` — which answers `""` to both "the model declined" and "the model was cut off" — read it as
`NONE`.

R208's ablation is the measurement that exposed it, and it did so with its own bill rather than with a hypothesis:

| reading | value | what a refusal would look like |
|---|---|---|
| paired calls | 170 | — |
| completion tokens, attempt arm | 8,156 over 85 | 85 × 2 = 170 |
| completion tokens per call | **95.95** | 2 |
| completion tokens, verdict arm | 8,160 over 85 | 170 |
| calls with content | 4 of 170 | 0 or 170 |

A call that returns `NONE` costs two tokens. Every call cost 96. The two arms' totals are 96 × 85 to the token.

**What it invalidated.** `R206a`, `R207` and `R208` each reported a refusal rate — 2 of 2, 1 of 1, and 82 of 85 —
and each reasoned from it: "the attempt alone does not let a summariser name the mistake", "the verdict is what the
summariser was missing". All three numbers were the token ceiling. R207's conclusion that its grid was saturated
survives (that is arithmetic on rewards), and so does R208's bank; the *material* question was never asked, because
neither arm ever produced an answer.

**Class.** This is the third instrument defect in the lane and the first one that is a lost keyword rather than a
wrong predicate. Its shape: **two copies of a call, one of which is edited.** The driver's own comment at
`run_split.py:784` documents that `deepseek-flash` thinks by default and that the agent and simulator calls disable
it; the note call was the copy written later and it did not. The repair removes the duplication rather than adding
the keyword twice: `notes.call_note_model` is now the only summariser call, and the self-check asserts its
`extra_body`, `max_tokens` and `temperature` — beside the request, where the next reader will see it next to the
agent's own.

**Second defect, in the same measurement.** `sentence_of` folds "declined" and "cut off" into one answer, and
`note_round` counted both as `refused`. The census now separates them: `truncated` is its own state and its own
counter, the census closes as `written + refused + truncated == failed`, and the ablation grades **P0 — no call was
cut off** — refusing to read a material at all when one was (`exit 2`, `tau2-ablation-truncated`). A budget fact
reported as a judgement is how three rounds went by without anyone asking why a model refused 96% of real failures
that the evaluator had *explained in writing*.

**Why the numbers looked plausible.** A refusal rate that high is not absurd on its face: most single attempts at a
retail task fail in ways that do not generalise, and "no actionable lesson" is a defensible answer. The tell was in
the bill, not in the rate — and the bill is only in the artefact because `note_bank.bill_of` was added one round
earlier for a different reason (a cost estimate that was wrong by 6.5×). An instrument that reports what it spent is
an instrument that can be caught.

## 34.305 — `P3`'s bar was unreachable, and the verdict it graded was one line repeated 85 times

**Defect.** R208's `P3` asked that a note contain a token its own failure's verdict held and **no other failure's**
verdict held. Measured on the bank that bar had a ceiling of **9.4%**: 77 of the 85 failures had an empty exclusive
vocabulary, because a retail verdict is mostly the schema (`REWARD`, `DB CHECK`, `ACTION met`) and the action names
recur across tasks. The 4.7% the ablation reported was therefore half of a ceiling that said nothing, and the
measure **inverts the incentive**: the action a note most needs to name — `exchange_delivered_order_items` — is
exactly the action other failures name too.

**The same round found why the vocabulary was empty.** `action_checks[].action` is `{"name": …, "arguments": {…}}`
and `_check_line` wanted a string, so every failure rendered `ACTION not met` and nothing else; the evaluator's
`justification` ("the agent told the user there are 12 options, not 10") was dropped by a reader that never looked
for it. The material the ablation priced was therefore a cost without content, and the verdict arm "won" on `P2`
by writing anyway.

**Repair, in two parts.**

1. *The content.* `_action_text` renders `name(arguments)`, `_check_line` appends the justification when it says
   something the detail does not, and `verdict_text` emits the head (reward, database verdict), then the failing
   checks, then the passing ones — a block cut off at 600 characters that shows twelve `ACTION met` lines and loses
   the one `not met` tells the summariser the attempt was fine. Measured on the bank with no model call: mean 169 →
   **439** characters, empty exclusive vocabulary 77 → **30** of 85.
2. *The measure.* A note is specific if it shares a token with its own failure's **failing lines**, and the same
   note against the other 84 failures' failing lines is its **chance** rate. Reported as a share, a chance rate and
   a lift, with McNemar's exact test over the two materials on the same failures.

**Why the amended measure is not a moved goalpost.** It is reported beside the registered one (`exclusive`), the
bar is unchanged at 50%, and on the amended measure the bar is **still missed** (44.7%). What changed is that the
measurement can now see the effect: 15 notes specific under the verdict and nowhere near it under the attempt
alone, against 1 the other way, **McNemar p = 0.0005**. A bar that a material cannot reach measures the bar.

**Class.** This is the third measure in the lane whose ceiling was never checked before it was used — after `N0b`
(three refutations on a population of zero) and `P0` (82 refusals that were truncations). The general form: a
measure computed over a *shared vocabulary* has a ceiling that shrinks as the population grows, and nobody computes
it because the first small sample looked fine. The repair that generalises is `--from-reading`: a measure can now
be recomputed from a kept artefact, so its ceiling can be checked before a dispatch is bought.

### 34.210 A fold was costed at ¥12.5 for an endpoint that could not move

**What was about to be bought.** Fifty failing tasks × two arms × four rounds = 400 episodes, ¥12.5, to measure
`pass^k` lift from carrying a note between attempts.

**Why it could not have worked.** `pass^k` is "all k attempts passed". A note is written only after a failed attempt
and only between rounds (`run_split.py:1290`). A task that receives a note has therefore already failed attempt 0 —
its `pass^k` is zero regardless of the note's quality — and a task that passes attempt 0 never has a note, so it
evolves exactly as its control. The treatment's `pass^k` equals the control's in expectation.

**The class.** This is the fourth measure in this lane whose ceiling was not checked before it was used: `N0b` fired
three refutations on a population of zero, `P0` graded 82 truncations as refusals, `P3`'s exclusive vocabulary
capped at 9.4%. The general form is sharper than "check the ceiling": an endpoint must be shown **reachable by the
intervention** before it is costed. A measure can be well-defined, correctly computed, and still unable to register
the treatment — and that failure looks exactly like a null result, which is why it survives review.

**The check that generalises.** For every registered endpoint, name the smallest change the intervention could
produce in it. Here the answer was "none": the note cannot appear before the attempt that must pass. The replacement
estimand conditions on the failure the note needs — `P(pass at j+1 | fail at j)` — which is reachable by
construction, has a paid counterfactual (65.2%, 15 of 23), and costs a quarter as much.

**Class.** Measurement design. The defect was not in the code but in the pairing of an instrument with a claim, and
the audit that catches it is one question per endpoint: *what would this number do if the intervention worked?*

### 34.211 The drift tolerance assumed independence that the seed design denies

**What was measured.** R211's arm passed attempt 0 on 38 of the same fifty tasks the bank passed on 27. The drift
gate fired — correctly — and the comparison was refused rather than published.

**The defect.** The tolerance had been justified as "one standard error at fifty, about 7 points, so four tasks is
one standard error rounded". That arithmetic treats the fifty tasks as fifty independent draws. They are not:
`run_split.py` derives round *i*'s seed as `base + i`, and **every task in that round is run under the same seed**.
The seed is a random effect shared by the whole attempt, so the unit of replication is the seed and an arm has one
of them. The between-world standard deviation is therefore not `sqrt(p(1-p)/50)` = 5.4 points but something nearer
the observed 22.

**Why the gate was still right.** A tolerance calibrated on the wrong variance would, if widened, have licensed
exactly the comparison it exists to block: two draws of two worlds, attributed to the material. The repair was to
the *design*, not the number — buy the control in the same dispatch at the same seeds, which is common random
numbers, and let `--baseline-dir` compare two arms inside one world. R212 then agreed to one task on attempt 0.

**The class.** This is the third defect in this lane of the shape "an assumption in the arithmetic rather than in
the code": `N0b`'s population of zero, `P0`'s truncations counted as refusals, and now an independence assumption
the seeding quietly contradicts. The check that generalises is one question per statistic: *what is the unit of
replication here, and does my variance know it?* For anything scheduled by seed, the answer is the seed.

**Cost of finding it.** ¥3.4 — the price of the arm that was refused. That is the cheapest defect this lane has
found, and it was found by a gate written before the defect existed.

### 34.212 Three rounds of nulls were read through an endpoint that nets two movements

**What was measured.** R210, R211 and R212 each asked "did the note help" and each answered with one number per
episode (`pass^k`) or one number per attempt (the rescue rate). R212's answer was 12/30 against 13/34: a wash.

**What the same documents say at requirement resolution.** Every episode is scored on a fixed set of requirements
— the database match, the named actions, the assertions, the communicated facts — and those move independently.
Counting them: the control repaired 38 of 85 unmet requirements (44.7%) and broke 37 of 332 met ones (11.1%),
net +1; the paraphrase repaired 40 of 83 (48.2%) and broke 43 of 334 (12.9%), **net −3**. The material repairs
3.5 points more and breaks 1.7 points more, and the sum of the two is negative.

**The defect.** Not in the code and not in the run: in the *resolution*. A rate that nets two opposite movements
cannot say whether a material did nothing or cancelled itself, and the difference decides the product. Three nulls
were read as "the sentence is not good enough" when the record was saying "the sentence is pointed at the wrong
requirement half the time" — the notes named 41 of the 82 requirements their source attempt missed (50.0%), and a
named requirement is repaired 53.7% of the time against 41.5% when it is not.

The naming test keeps two-letter tokens. A threshold of three made the database requirement unnameable, and a
requirement that cannot be named is one the association can never count; the correction moved one requirement in
82 and is recorded here rather than applied quietly.

**The class.** This is the fifth defect in this lane of the shape "the instrument cannot see the thing":
`N0b`'s population of zero, `P0`'s truncations graded as refusals, `P3`'s exclusive vocabulary with a 9.4%
ceiling, `pass^k`'s blindness to a note, and now a rate that hides a harm channel. The general check is one
question per endpoint: *if the intervention worked, which number moves — and if it also broke something, which
number would move the other way?* An endpoint with only the first has no way to distinguish help from harm.

**What it cost.** Nothing: the requirement rows were in every artefact the lane wrote. The reading was one
reader away, and three dispatches (¥17.6) were interpreted without it.

### 34.213 Every behavioural reading in this lane was taken through a noise floor larger than the effect

**What was assumed.** That a 24-task grid at four rounds, with both arms in one dispatch and shared seeds, could
resolve a 5-to-25-point effect. R212 was read that way, and its `NO_LIFT` was quoted as a property of the material.

**What R213 measured.** Three arms, one world, 288 episodes. At **attempt 0** — before any note exists, with the
same prompt and the same seed in every arm — the verdict arm passed 9 of the 20 tasks the control failed, against
the control's 13. Four tasks. Nothing differs between the arms at that point except the provider's own sampling.

That is the noise floor of the grid, measured rather than estimated: **20 points on 24 tasks**. And the
requirement-level reading reverses between worlds for the same reason: the control's net is +1 in R212 and −10 in
R213; the paraphrase's is −3 and +11.

**The class.** This is the sixth instrument defect in this lane and the first one that is not about a number being
computed wrongly — the numbers are right and the *replication unit* is too small. `N0b` fired on a population of
zero, `P0` graded truncations as refusals, `P3`'s vocabulary capped at 9.4%, `pass^k` could not see a note, the
debit's rate hid a harm channel, and now the grid itself is smaller than the effect. The check that generalises is
one question per design: *how much does this number move when nothing changes?* — and the answer has to be measured
(attempt 0, identical arms) rather than assumed from a binomial standard error, which is what the drift tolerance
did.

**Why the drift gate did not catch it.** Its tolerance is four tasks, which is the noise floor itself. A gate
calibrated at the size of the noise cannot distinguish noise from signal; it can only refuse the worst draws. R212
was read at a one-task gap and R213 at four, and both passed.

**The repair is the population, not the gate.** 114 tasks put the floor near 9 points for 114 episodes — less money
than the 96-episode grids it replaces. Any future behavioural claim in this lane is made on the bank's full
population or not made.

### 34.214 A directory is not an arm

**What happened.** R213's dispatch ran all 288 episodes, wrote every document, uploaded them — and then the job
went red in the reading step. A `mkdir -p "${RESCUE_DIR}/treatment"` survived from the two-arm version of the
workflow, so an empty `treatment/` existed beside `control/`, `paraphrase/` and `verdict/`. The reading loop tested
for the directory, called `rescue_rate` on it, and `rescue_rate` correctly refused ("no document under …", exit 4).
The failure then skipped the debit step, which was the round's primary reading.

**Why it matters beyond the bug.** Three separate decisions had to line up for this to be recoverable rather than
fatal: the artefact upload runs with `if: always()`, the reader is a document reader rather than a log scraper, and
the per-arm loop is a loop. R211 lost its per-task rows to a log-only reading and had to buy a second arm; this run
lost nothing but the summary.

**The repair.** The loop asks whether an arm produced a **document** (`compgen -G …/results-*.json`), not whether a
directory exists, and the stale `mkdir` is gone. It is the same lesson as `note_bank`'s census: an artefact that
exists is not an artefact that has content, and the code that decides has to look at the content.

### 34.215 The agent every paid dispatch loads had 352 assertions and no gate

`eval/drivers/tau2/selfcheck_agent.py` (53 cases, 223 assertions) and `selfcheck_usage.py` (38 cases, 129
assertions) both run without a provider, a harness or a network. Neither was named by any workflow. `ci.yml`'s
coverage source is `eval/drivers/alfworld` and its unit-test discovery is that directory's; `note-rescue.yml`,
`note-bank.yml`, `note-pilot.yml` and `sota.yml` all *use* the agent and none of them runs its suite. So the module
that decides how a treatment is served could have lost its note lookup, its pack-copy removal or its boundary
bookkeeping in any refactor, and every job would have stayed green.

This is the same class as the missing coverage floor (34.198) and the missing path filter (34.213): a gate that
exists for the code that is *new* and not for the code that is *load-bearing*. It surfaced because R214 changes the
agent — a new channel, a second tag, a per-turn render — and a change to a module whose tests nobody runs cannot be
reviewed with confidence.

**The repair.** `working-memory.yml`'s contract job runs both suites before any dispatch and on every push that
touches the agent, the driver, the parser or the workflow. It is free (no model call) and takes twenty seconds.

### 34.216 The census counted calls, so a board that was right was scored as noise

`goal_board.census` first counted *required write calls*: for each call, does the board hold an ask of that family.
Task 2 — "return the cleaner, headphone, and smart watch" — is a single `return_delivered_order_items` touching
three items, and the board's three asks were scored as one found and **two spurious**. The parser was being
penalised for reading the request correctly, and the resulting precision (34.0%) understated it by seven points.

**The repair.** Each required write is weighted by the number of order items it touches (`len(item_ids)`, 1 when the
call carries none), so the unit is the **object**. The reading moved to 79.6% recall at 41.4% precision, and the
gate is pinned to the object reading and to a separate **family** reading (152/180, 84.4%) because a set-phrased ask
— "modify all your pending tshirts" — is one ask covering two objects, and only the family reading measures that
fairly. Two numbers, because the two questions are different and one of them is not the other's shorthand.

### 34.217 Containment ran the wrong way for an address, and the test found it

The free-text branch of the attribution rule — the branch an address change needs, because it carries no item ids —
first required the *receipt's* words to be contained in the ask's. `modify_user_address(user_id="u1", address1="123
Main Street", city="Chicago")` therefore never settled "change the address to 123 Main Street Chicago": `u1` is in
the receipt and not in the request, and one extra word was enough. The rule was silently excluding every address
change from the board, which is 35 of the 226 required objects.

**The repair.** The direction is stated per branch and for a reason: a *named* product contains or is contained in
the ask, because the two sides abbreviate differently; a *free-text* value has to be spelled by the receipt, so the
ask's words must be a subset of the receipt's. The pinning test asserts both directions and the superset case.

### 34.218 A call whose result never arrived was credited as a receipt

`receipts_of` paired calls and results positionally and defaulted `ok = True` when a call had no result — the
episode ended, the tool raised, the message was dropped. A credit for a change the environment may never have made
is exactly the over-claim the board exists to refuse, so the default is now `False`: no result, no receipt.

**How it was found.** By writing the assertion before the fix — the case "a call with no result is a receipt that
did not happen" was written against the intended rule and failed. It is the twelfth defect in this lane found by a
test written against a rule rather than against the code.

### 34.219 The board's first render was eight lines of which three were noise, and the noise is a corpus property

The parser's first pass produced 4.4 asks a task with 41% precision. Two filters cut it without costing a single
required object — a clause that begins with a continuation word ("… but with clicky switches", "… same size",
"prefer polyester") is a modifier and not a new ask, unless it carries its own verb; and a negated cue ("do not
exchange anything") is not an ask, because a board that lists a forbidden action as pending sends the agent to do
what the user refused. Folding a *near*-repeat into the longer statement was tried and **reverted**: it costs ten
required objects across the corpus, because a comma list of products folds into the first one whenever two products
share a word (79.6% → 75.2%). Missing an object is the defect the lane exists to remove; a repeated line is not.

What is left is the corpus. Task 5 asks for two exchanges, then changes its mind mid-conversation and asks for a
return; a board that lists the exchanges is faithful to the text and wrong about the script. That is a stated limit
of reading what the user said (ARCHITECTURE 8.88), not a parser bug, and the run-time counters are what the reading
quotes.

### 34.220 A block that changes every turn invalidates the prefix, and the bill is 67% larger for 23 tokens

R214 served a 200-character goal board on every turn: 23 tokens against a 4,728-token prompt, **+0.2%**. The
arm's model bill came back at **$0.5094 against the control's $0.3044** — +67% — and the provider's own cache
counter says why:

| arm | prompt / call | cached tokens | hit rate | bill |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| control | 4,727.7 | 8,592,366 | 90.4% | $0.3044 |
| board | 4,716.9 | 7,080,426 | 75.1% | $0.5094 |

The system message is at the **front** of the prompt. A block that is rewritten every turn invalidates the prefix
the provider had cached, so every request re-buys the whole conversation at the miss rate ($0.15/M) instead of the
hit rate ($0.003/M). The lane has been quoting the *size* of its material since R92 — `injectedChars`,
`packChars`, tokens per call — and the size was never the bill. The bill is how often the material **moves**.

**Why this is the round's most transferable finding.** It applies to every design that re-renders context: a
rolling summary, an updated plan, a state board, a reflection written mid-episode. Each of them looks free at the
token count and costs a prefix. A lane that reports the cost of its memory as a length will systematically
under-price the designs it is most interested in, which is exactly what happened here: the round was registered at
≈ $1.0 on the assumption that a parser-built material is "free", and it cost $1.43.

**The repair is architectural, not lexical.** Emit on the event that changes the state — a successful
write-receipt — rather than on the turn. A board that changes three times an episode instead of twenty-five keeps
the prefix and re-reads itself only when it says something new.

### 34.221 The board closed 1.6 of 10.6 lines, and the second half of that sentence is the accuracy story

The arm's own documents, recomputed at the last turn of every episode:

| reading | value |
|---|---|
| asks listed at the end, mean | 10.6 |
| ticked, mean | 1.58 |
| open lines | 9.0 |
| episodes ending with nothing ticked | 30 of 114 |
| episodes at the eight-line render cap | 34 |
| state-changing calls | 187 |
| calls the board could not attribute | 62 |

The census that licensed the parser predicted **3.8 asks a task** and measured its recall against the evaluator's
own list. The run lists **10.6**, because asks were collected from every user message and a simulated user's
clarifications are sentences that name an object after a verb. The census was not wrong; it measured one message
and the run reads eleven. A material whose supply rule is "everything the user has said" grows monotonically, and
a list that grows and does not close is a to-do list rather than a memory.

The arm still attributed 79.2% of the episodes that made a change (84 of 106), which is why this is a diagnosis
with a next step rather than a dead end: the rule that ticks a line works; the rule that **adds** one does not.

### 34.222 The estimate was right about the episode and wrong about the material

The registration costed 228 episodes at the bank's $0.0044: **$1.0**. The control came in at $0.0045 an episode —
the bank's number was correct to a tenth of a cent — and the board at $0.0080, for the reason in 34.220. The
registration's other assumption was that a parser-built material is free because it makes no model call. It is
free to *build* and, if it is re-served, expensive to *serve*.

**The rule this buys.** A cost estimate for a memory arm has three terms, not two: the episode, the material's
own calls, and **the prefix the material invalidates**. The third is the only one that has ever surprised this
lane, and it is measurable before a dispatch from the rate card and the emission cadence.

### 34.223 The census the documentation quoted was not the census the code produced

`USER-GUIDE` §32.70 stated the parser's licence as **180 of 226** required objects, **152 of 180** required
families, **255** spurious asks and **86 of 114** tasks fully covered. Those were the census's numbers when R214 was
*registered*. Two parser filters and one reverted fold landed before the dispatch, and the code that ran produced
**176 / 150 / 238 / 84**.

Nothing failed. The gate in `working-memory.yml` asserted `found >= 170`, `familyRecall >= 0.82`, `spurious <= 280`
and `tasksCovered >= 82` — bounds wide enough to accept both readings, chosen when the point of the gate was to
catch a *regression* rather than to pin a *licence*. So for one round the documentation, the registration and the
artefact disagreed with one another, and every check was green.

**Repair, in three parts.** The gate now pins the measured values with two points of slack (174/226 objects, 0.82
families, 240 spurious, 82 tasks); the guide's paragraph carries the measured numbers and a note that the old ones
were wrong; and this entry is the reason the note exists rather than a silent correction. **A census is a
measurement, and a measurement quoted from a document is a number nobody re-ran.**

The general form is worth stating because this repository is built on it: a bound that accepts two different worlds
is not a gate, it is a memory of a gate. The slack in a bound should be the size of the noise the measurement has,
which for a deterministic parser over a fixed corpus is zero — and R215's gate is the first in this lane with no
slack at all.

### 34.224 The negation rule let "I don't want to return" through as a live ask

The parser refused "do not exchange" and "don't return" and passed **"I don't want to return the lamp"** as an
ask, because the rule allowed exactly one word between the negation and the cue. That is the form this corpus uses
more often than the bare one, and the consequence is the one the rule exists to prevent: a board line telling the
agent to do what the user ruled out.

The first repair allowed three words and cost a required ask: "if the agent doesn't allow **the** exchange" is a
*condition about* an exchange, and reading it as a refusal dropped task 107's second exchange from the board.
Recall fell 176 → 175 and noise 238 → 233 — a net loss dressed as a win, which is why the census is a gate rather
than a chart.

The rule as shipped reads the words between the negation and the cue: a **determiner** makes the cue a noun
("doesn't allow the exchange") and is not a refusal; `only` makes it a correlative ("not only return it, but
exchange it") and is not a refusal either; anything else inside three words is. Recall 176 of 226 — unchanged —
and noise 235, three below where the round started. Three self-check cases pin all three forms, and the two
rejected forms are the ones a plausible-looking extension gets wrong.

### 34.225 A set-phrased ask cannot be settled, and the transcript reader was hiding it

R215's contract listed 1.96 asks a turn against R214's 10.6, which is the supply rule working. The ticks fell from
79.2% of writing episodes to **32.7%**, and the artefact's own table says why:

| task 11 contract | task 11 receipt |
|---|---|
| `return everything two` | `return_delivered_order_items` on *Water Bottle, Mechanical Keyboard, Action Camera, Backpack* |
| `return everything related`, task 12 | `return_delivered_order_items` on *Water Bottle, Action Camera, Backpack* |
| `return cancel bunch recent basically anything related`, task 13 | `return_delivered_order_items` on four products |

`settles()` requires the ask's words to be contained in the product name, in one direction or the other. A set
phrase contains no product name, so **no receipt can ever satisfy it**; 73% of the round's 191 writes were reported
`unrequested` (77) or `unattributed` (62).

The rule already exists for the wordless case: "cancel the order" names nothing, and `board_of` settles it with the
first receipt of its family. A set phrase is the same shape — *"everything from my two most recent orders"* is one
ask over many objects — and it had no rule, because R214's ten-line list always happened to contain some product
name from a later clarification. **The transcript reader did not attribute better; it had more chances to.** That is
the general form worth keeping: a permissive supply rule makes an attribution rule look correct by giving it a
target for every arrow.

The repair is R216's: an ask whose words name no product **in the episode's own name table** is a *set* ask, and a
set ask is settled by a receipt of its family and absorbs the later receipts of that family rather than leaving them
unattributed. The name table is the only catalogue available and the containment rule already depends on it, so the
test costs nothing new: `not _names_a_product(item, table)`.

### 34.226 The 3-point cache bar was wrong, and the arithmetic says so before the next dispatch

R215's P2 required the arm's cache hit rate within **3 points** of the control's. Measured: 90.4% → 84.0%, −6.5.
The gate failed the run, which is what it was for. The bar itself was miscalibrated, and the reason is structural:

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| renders | 1,034 |
| turns whose block changed | 247 (23.9%) |
| — of which the episode's first turn | **114** |
| — receipt-driven | 133 (1.2 an episode) |
| prompt per call | 4,755.7 tokens |
| uncached input, control | 859,816 tokens |
| uncached input, contract | 1,484,893 tokens |

247 × 4,756 ≈ 1.17 M tokens of prefix, against a control that buys 860 k. **The cold start alone is 114 changes out
of 1,034 renders, and on a nine-turn episode a first-turn miss costs about six points of hit rate before any receipt
moves anything.** No block that shows state can be cache-neutral on this grid, so a 3-point bar is a bar no correct
implementation can clear — which means the round would have reported a mechanism failure for a design that was
working as specified.

**The rule this buys.** A cache bar has to be stated as a function of the grid: `changes × prompt` is the bill, and
`changes` has a floor of one per episode. The honest bars are "no more than one change per receipt" and "the block's
own length per change", not a fixed number of points. R216 registers both.

**What the gate proved anyway.** It failed the job, the artefact had already been uploaded by an `if: always()`
step, and the reading therefore exists with its failure attached. A mechanism gate that can only be satisfied by
not running is not a gate; this one was satisfied by the mechanism and failed by the *bar*, and the artefact carries
both numbers so the distinction survives the rerun.

### 34.227 A registered repair was worth two settlements in a hundred and seven, and only a replay could say so

R215's reading left one mechanism bar passed of four, and the round's diagnosis was written into 34.225: a
set-phrased ask names no product, `settles()` requires containment, therefore 73% of writes went unattributed. R216
was registered on that repair, a rule, a test suite and a gate.

The repair was then measured against the arm that produced the diagnosis, for free:

```
$ python3 eval/tools/goal_board.py --replay eval/results/working-memory/board.json
40 of 107 writing episode(s) ended with a tick (37.4%)
104 asks… 58 settled, 2 absorbed, 77 unrequested, 53 unattributed
```

**Two.** The set rule addresses two settlements out of the 130 writes R215 could not credit. The other four causes,
none of which the round had a name for:

| cause | episodes |
|---|---|
| a call of a family the contract never stated | 25 |
| an ask one word short of the product it names | 28 |
| a contract sealed on a greeting that carried no ask | 14 |
| a set ask | 2 |

The general form is the one worth keeping: **34.225 was not a wrong observation, it was a wrong denominator.** The
three episodes it quoted (`return everything two`, `return everything related`, `return cancel bunch recent
basically anything related`) were real, and they were 3 of 130. A diagnosis built from the first examples a reader
happens to look at is an anecdote with a percentage attached, and the percentage was never computed.

What made this findable is a counter that did not exist: nothing reported **which rule produced which tick**. The
artefact now carries `loose` (settlements at the weaker grade) and `absorbed` (calls a set ask took in), and
`replay()` reproduces the whole reading over a document that already exists.

The round's own accounting, since the discipline is the point: R216 was re-registered before its dispatch, so the
wrong repair cost a day of design and **nothing** in tokens. R214's version of the same mistake — two changes in one
arm, no way to separate them — cost $1.43 and a day.

### 34.228 An off-peak guard that refused a pilot it should have allowed

The round's dispatch was refused at 01:30 UTC:

```
tau2-pilot-peak-window: the run would be inside Wed 01:30 UTC, where the same tokens cost exactly twice the off-peak rate
```

The guard is right and it is doing what it was built for. It is also **duration-blind to the size of the run**: it
refuses any dispatch that would sit inside a peak band, and the rate card's bands are 01–04 and 06–10 UTC on
weekdays. A 342-episode grid inside one of those costs twice $1.75; a **single call** inside one of them costs
$0.0002, and that one call is exactly what de-risks the round's new placement.

Three ways out were available and two of them are wrong:

- *disable the guard for this dispatch* — the guard is the only thing standing between this lane and a doubled bill,
  and a switch that can be flipped under time pressure is a switch that will be;
- *run the whole grid at peak* — $3.50 for a number that arrives an hour later;
- **arm the dispatch for the first minute of the window and put the de-risking call inside the guarded job**, which
  is what the round does. The smoke step is a *step*, not a dispatch, so it runs in the 04:05 job for one call.

The general form: **a cost guard should be a function of the run it guards, and the pilot that de-risks a run is
usually smaller than the run's own noise.** Where it is not — where the pilot and the grid cost the same — the guard
is right to refuse both.

### 34.229 The tail placement writes into the conversation, and nothing in this lane had done that

Every block this lane has served went into `state.system_messages`, and the R137 invariant was built for that list:
"at most one block, and it is this episode's". `serve_tail` writes into `state.messages` instead, which is a
different list with a different owner — the orchestrator appends to it, the recorded transcript comes from the
orchestrator's copy rather than from the agent's state, and a message the agent inserts therefore affects the prompt
and **not** the artefact a reward is computed over.

That last property is what makes the placement safe for validity rather than merely cheap: a block that appeared in
the recorded `messages` could satisfy a natural-language assertion the agent never made, and a tick in the reward
would be the board's, not the model's. Verified rather than assumed — R215's artefact carries only `user`,
`assistant` and `tool` roles across 114 episodes, so the system-block injection never reached the transcript, and
the tail placement reaches it through a list the orchestrator owns.

What the placement risks instead is **interpretation**: a system turn arriving after the user's may be read as an
instruction rather than as context. Nothing in this round distinguishes "the board helped" from "the board's
placement helped", which is why the grid has three arms — `tail − front` is the placement with the parser held.

### 34.230 A block appended to `state.messages` splits a call from its results, and the provider refuses the request

R216's first dispatch lost an entire arm to one line:

```python
kept = kept + [injected]          # appended at the end of the conversation
```

The provider's rule is exact — `An assistant message with 'tool_calls' must be followed by tool messages responding
to each 'tool_call_id'` — and the agent's own conversation violates it for one turn out of every two: the turn a call
is made ends with the assistant message carrying the call, and the results arrive as the *next* input. Anything
appended there sits between the call and its answer, and the whole request is refused.

**94 of 114 episodes** recorded no messages at all, and the 20 that survived were the ones whose first turn carried
no call. Four attempts per task, then a recorded empty episode: the arm's `simulations` count was right, its
per-episode bill was a seventh of the control's, and its accuracy was 8.8%.

The repair is a computed position rather than an appended one. `tail_index(messages)` finds the last assistant
message that carries calls, counts the run of tool messages after it, and returns *before* that assistant message
when the run does not answer every call — a half-answered pair of parallel calls included, which is the case a
"put it before the last message" rule would have got wrong.

What makes this worth an audit entry rather than a commit message is that **the shape is not a property of this
lane's material, it is a property of the tool-calling protocol**, and it will bite the next person who appends
anything to a conversation: a reminder, a plan, a scratch pad. The front placement never met it because a system
block is not in `messages` at all. R137's invariant — "at most one block, and it is this episode's" — was satisfied
throughout.

### 34.231 A cost ceiling is satisfied by an arm that stopped early

The mechanism gate's job is to refuse a run whose material cannot be quoted. On dispatch `45546028726` it passed an
arm that had reached the model on 20 of 114 episodes, and the reason is the bar's *shape*:

| bar as registered | value the collapsed arm showed | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `tailAppends ≤ changes` | 798 ≤ 798 | pass |
| `tailHeld > 0` | 2,679 | pass |
| block ≤ 500 chars | 142.2 | pass |
| bill per episode ≤ 1.20 × control | **0.16 ×** control | **pass** |
| attribution ≥ 60% | 0.0% | fail — but this is the *next* step |

A one-sided cost bar cannot distinguish "cheap because the block is small" from "cheap because nothing happened". The
number that separates them is not a cost at all: it is how many episodes reached the model. So the gate now reads
that first —

```python
assert live >= 0.95 * max(alive.values()), f"{arm} reached the model on {live} of ... episode(s)"
```

— and the cost bar is a **band, −20% to +20%**, because a large negative is the same finding as a large positive and
the registered derivation (+15%, R215's front placement +37%) only bounds one of them.

The general form: **a guard that prices a cost must also bound the state a cheap cost implies.** Two of the three
bars in this lane's history were wrong in the same direction — R215's 3-point cache bar was unachievable, and this
one was achievable by failing — and both were found by reading the artefact rather than the verdict.

### 34.232 A cron armed for the off-peak window did not fire, and the window is 4 hours wide

R216's first dispatch was refused at 01:30 UTC by the rate guard, so the round armed itself:

```yaml
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '5 4 25 11 *'      # the first minute of the first off-peak hour, 25 November
jobs:
  board:
    if: ... || (github.event_name == 'schedule' && github.event.schedule == '5 4 25 11 *')
```

The workflow was on `master` at 01:44 UTC, two hours and twenty minutes before the trigger, and the run never
appeared: `event=schedule` has no `working-memory` entry and the workflow's own history shows the 01:44 push and
nothing between it and the 04:19 manual dispatch. GitHub's scheduler is documented as best-effort and can delay or
drop a trigger, and a trigger that has never fired once is the one this lane has no evidence about.

Consequences, in the order they matter:

1. **A window is a deadline, not a schedule.** The off-peak band is 04:00–06:00 UTC and the grid takes ~55 minutes,
   so a dispatch that waits for a trigger which never comes loses the whole window; the dispatch was made by hand at
   04:19 and finished at 05:42 with 18 minutes to spare.
2. **The arming is still the right shape, and it now needs a fallback.** The cron stays in the file — a trigger that
   fires is free and one that does not costs nothing — but the round is not *waiting* on it: the operator's dispatch
   is the primary, and the second dispatch is recorded with the exact call that reproduces it.
3. **The guard's granularity is minutes and the schedule's is hours.** Nothing in this lane can now be dispatched
   between 06:00 and 10:00 UTC without paying double, which is 4 of every 24 hours at the wrong multiple. That is a
   constraint on when work happens rather than on what work is, and it is worth stating because three of the lane's
   last four rounds were dispatched inside that band's neighbourhood by luck rather than by design.

### 34.233 The control's "drift" is turnover, and the arithmetic says so before the narrative does

Three dispatches read the same control over the same 114 tasks at seed 400: 98 (R214), 95 (R215), 90 (R216). Seven
tasks across two days looks like decay, and PROGRESS 246.8 named two hypotheses — sampling noise, or a provider change
the board's material buffers.

The artefacts settle it. R215's control and R216's control, task by task:

| | tasks |
|---|---|
| pass in both | 80 |
| fail in both | 9 |
| **passed in R215, failed in R216** | **15** |
| failed in R215, passed in R216 | **10** |

Twenty-five flips for a net −5, on an arm whose rate is 0.86. Under independent sampling the expected turnover is
2 × 0.86 × 0.14 × 114 ≈ **27**, and McNemar on 15 against 10 is p ≈ 0.42. The observed turnover is *exactly* what the
null predicts and the net is indistinguishable from zero.

**So there is no drift to explain, and the two hypotheses in 246.8 were both answers to a question the data does not
ask.** What is real is the *turnover*: a fifth of this grid changes answer between two dispatches of the same arm,
which is why a paired, within-dispatch contrast resolves nine points and a cross-dispatch comparison of two arms
resolves almost nothing.

Two consequences, and the second is the one that matters for the paper:

1. **The registered floor was optimistic in the right direction.** 114 tasks was chosen for a ~9-point floor on a
   *paired* comparison; the 22% turnover means the *unpaired* floor is roughly twice that. Both statements are
   consistent, and only the first is the one every bar in this lane is written against.
2. **A single-dispatched arm is a coin.** R216's +7.9 pp rests on 15 moved against 6 broke, which is a paired
   statistic and survives this; a claim like "the board reached 86.8%, up from 87.7%" would not, because both numbers
   carry ±22% task turnover and neither differs from the other.

The general rule this lane keeps re-learning: **compute the turnover before writing the explanation.** A 22% churn
under a stable rate is not a signal, and the arithmetic that says so costs one join over two artefacts.

### 34.234 A three-domain mean was quoted as a retail cell for eight rounds

Every competitive table from R213 to R216 carries a row `Qwen3.5-397B-A17B | 87.9% | pass^1, mean over domains |
τ²-retail`. The third column says "mean over domains" and the header of the table says retail; the two cannot both be
true, and nobody reconciled them because the number was right — 87.91 *is* the mean of that entry over retail,
airline and telecom.

The board's own file says retail is **84.43** (airline 81.5, telecom 97.81). So the row overstated the retail SOTA by
**3.5 points**, and every "1.9-point gap" written against it was 5.4 points against the wrong number and 1.4 points
against the right one — with the board's actual retail top, Claude Sonnet 4.5, at **86.20**.

Fixed by `eval/tools/submission.py`, which will only place a row in a domain it names, and by the pinned snapshot
that makes the number re-derivable. The prose correction is COMPETITIVE §R218a.

### 34.235 A competitor's row carried another model's number

The same tables carry `Claude Opus 4.5 (alone) | 85.3% | pass^1`. The board's `claude-opus-4-5_sierra_2026-02-26`
states retail **79.61** — and 85.3 is `gemini-3-pro_google_2025-11-18`'s retail cell. The row is a 5.7-point
overstatement attached to the wrong vendor's model, which is the failure mode a table invites: cells are copied by
position and the model name is retyped.

`--census` and `--position` read the model name out of the same object as the number, so the two cannot separate.

### 34.236 The metric was compared across k, and the tool refuses the comparison

The lane's own row was `pass^1` at one attempt; the rows it was compared against state `pass^4` over four. Sixteen
board rows state `pass^4`, and for every one of them `pass^4` is **20–30 points below** its `pass^1` — 84.43 → 59.65
for Qwen3.5, 81.58 → 58.77 for GPT-5. The two quantities are accuracy and reliability, and the lane had been reading
its accuracy as a near-miss on everyone else's reliability.

`--position --metric pass_4` on a one-attempt artefact prints `UNRANKED` and exits `1`. That exit code is the audit:
a pipeline that treated it as a rank would fail rather than publish.

### 34.237 The mean that included the retrieval domain

The first version of `mean_over_domains` averaged every domain the entry stated, and read Qwen3.5's three-domain mean
as **68.38** instead of 87.91 — because `banking_knowledge` was in the average (its banking `pass^1` is 9.79). The
suite caught it on the assertion that pins 87.91, which is the only reason this defect is a paragraph and not a
fourth wrong number in a table.

`TEXT_DOMAINS` is now a named constant with the reason attached: banking is a retrieval benchmark with its own tab,
its own configuration and a task shape that is not a customer-service conversation.

### 34.238 The entry was `custom` and nothing said so

The board's `standard` entry is a general-purpose model through the benchmark's own agent scaffold; a submission that
adds a planner, a router, a custom tool or modified control flow is `custom`. This project replaces the scaffold —
`agent_info.implementation` in every dispatch document reads `microglia_agent` — so the entry has always been
`custom`, and no document in this repository said it. That is the difference between a claim a maintainer will list
and one they will mark and question.

`--emit --harness replace` forces the type, requires notes and references, and declares `modified_prompts: true`. It
is not possible to emit a `standard` row from an artefact whose agent is not the stock one, because the tool reads
the agent out of the document rather than out of an argument.

### 34.239 The smoke test certified a dialogue the benchmark does not run

R216-1's tail arm died on **94 of 114 episodes** with a `BadRequestError`, and the step whose entire purpose was to
prevent that had passed four minutes earlier. It had passed because it built its conversation out of *user* turns:

```python
messages = [system, user, system, user]   # what the smoke test sent
```

A τ² retail episode is almost nothing but `assistant(tool_calls)` followed by `tool(result)` — the block lands in a
conversation that is 90% tool traffic, and the naive append put a `system` turn **between a call and its result**,
which the provider refuses. The smoke test therefore certified the one dialogue shape in which the naive append is
legal, and the shape it did not send is the shape the benchmark sends.

The cost of that gap was $1.2739 of dispatch plus a re-dispatch, and the lesson generalises past this lane: **a
precondition test is only as good as the shape of its input.** A test that asks "does the provider accept a system
turn after the user's" answers a question about a conversation; the driver needed an answer about *this* conversation.

Fixed by building the real shape — a tool definition, an assistant turn that calls `get_order`, and the tool result —
and sending the block in two positions: where `tail_index` puts it (asserted), and between the call and its result
(printed, not asserted, because a provider that tolerated it would be news rather than a step failure). Three calls
at eight tokens each.

### 34.240 Three arms were armed to answer a question one contrast asks

R216b was armed as R216's three-arm grid: control, front, tail. The tail arm is the only one whose number the round
does not already have, and `control → front` was measured inside R216-1 at +7.9 pp.

The redundancy is not merely expensive ($0.50 of 228 episodes it does not read); it is **not even a replication**.
R216's own per-task comparison found the same arm turning over 22% of its tasks between two dispatches (15 pass→fail,
10 fail→pass, p ≈ 0.42), which is why this lane's rule is that only within-dispatch pairs may be quoted. A second
control would have produced a third statistic that is neither the old number nor a confirmation of it.

Changed to `arms=placement`: `front` then `board`, 342 episodes → **228**, ~$1.82 → ~$1.32.

The change exposed two gates that named `control` as their left arm and would have **skipped rather than failed**:
`if control and treated:` is false when no control ran, and `--compare control.json …` would have killed the step
under `set -e` only *after* the money was spent. Both now fall back to `front`, and `compare_of` carries the names of
the files it compared — a reading that called its left arm "control" when the file was `front.json` would have been
the same class of defect as §34.234, a number attached to the wrong label.

### 34.241 A funded dispatch was armed on a clock that does not fire

R216b's first arming was a `schedule:` entry — `2 10 25 11 *` — with a comment explaining that 10:02 UTC was the
first off-peak minute after the previous dispatch returned. At 10:02 UTC nothing happened. No run, no error, no
notification: GitHub's own documentation says scheduled events are **best-effort and may be dropped under load**, so
there was nothing to fix. It was the second time in this lane (`AUDIT 34.232`), and the second time is what makes it
a design defect rather than an incident.

The defect is not that the timer is unreliable. It is that **spending money was delegated to something whose
execution is not guaranteed** and whose firing nobody confirms. A cron that fires at the wrong moment is as bad as
one that does not fire: it would dispatch into a window, a configuration and a budget that no one re-read.

Both halves are now fixed, and they are different kinds of fix:

- **The dispatch is a `workflow_dispatch`.** Nothing that spends money fires on a clock.
- **The debt is a file, and CI asserts on it.** `eval/manifests/rounds.json` lists every round this project owes
  with its date, its arms, its episode count and its estimate; `eval/tools/round_clock.py` reads it on every push and
  exit `1` if a `registered` round is past its date. The failure mode this catches is not a wrong number, it is a
  round that quietly stops being planned — the exact state R216b was in for four hours while the plan said it was
  armed.

### 34.242 A fabricated history is a history the provider will not accept

Rebuilt on the real dialogue shape (a `tool_calls` turn and its result), the provider step failed with:

> `The reasoning_content in the thinking mode must be passed back to the API`

`deepseek-flash` answers in thinking mode unless told otherwise, and the assistant turn the test hand-wrote had no
`reasoning_content` to give back — because there was no reasoning behind it. The fix is not a field: it is that
**the first call is real**. The model is asked to call a tool, and the turn it returns, with whatever fields the
provider demands be echoed, is the turn the placement tests are built on.

### 34.243 Thinking mode does not support a forced tool choice, so the smoke test cannot guarantee its own coverage

The third attempt forced the tool with `tool_choice={"type": "function", …}` and got:

> `Thinking mode does not support this tool_choice`

Three attempts, three constraints, each discovered by the previous one failing:

| attempt | shape | outcome |
|---|---|---|
| R216-1 | `system, user, system, user` | **passed**, and the arm died on 94 of 114 episodes |
| R216b-1 | hand-written `tool_calls` turn | `reasoning_content must be passed back` |
| R216b-2 | real turn, forced `tool_choice` | `Thinking mode does not support this tool_choice` |
| R216b-3 | real turn, choice left to the model | **reports what it covered** |

The fourth row is the design change. A precondition test that is all-or-nothing cannot say what it verified, so this
one prints which placement it covered: if the model declines to call the tool, the step still checks the placement a
τ² conversation spends most of its turns in — a `system` turn after an assistant turn — and says in its own output
that tool-call adjacency was **not** covered.

**What the three failures cost, and it is the argument for the step.** R216b-1 and R216b-2 spent **$0.00** between
them, because a precondition test runs before the grid. The one that passed spent **$1.2739** and bought a dead arm.
A gate that fails is the cheapest thing this lane produces; a gate that passes while testing the wrong thing is the
most expensive.

### 34.244 An arm was named in three places, and the third one only fails when the money is already spent

The paired-reading step had to learn the same lesson twice. `AUDIT 34.240` recorded two places where `control.json`
was the left arm by name — the bill band and the `--compare` line — and both were changed to fall back to `front`
when a dispatch runs no control. There was a **third**: the block that prints "the parser, under R215's placement",
guarded by `if [ -f front.json ] && [ -f board.json ]`, opening `${BOARD_DIR}/control.json` unconditionally.

R216b dispatched `placement`, so `front.json` and `board.json` both existed, the guard passed, and the block raised
`FileNotFoundError` — **after $1.3007 had been charged and before the reading was written**. The step is the last
thing that runs, which is exactly why a defect there is the most expensive kind: every gate before it passed, and the
number the money was spent to produce was never assembled.

The fix is a gate on the control's own file plus a line that says so:

```
--- no control arm in this dispatch: the parser's price is R216-1's reading, not this one's ---
```

The reading was recovered from the job log and the uploaded artefact at no cost, which is the only reason this is a
paragraph and not a lost round. The general form of the defect is worth naming: **an ablation grid is a grid of arms
that may or may not exist, and every reference to an arm must be a lookup rather than a name.** Three greps found
three; a fourth may be in a place this round did not read.

### 34.245 The estimate that said 24% and the measurement that said 4%

§248.9 registered that confirming the tail placement would make every subsequent dispatch **24% cheaper**, on the
reasoning that a block behind the conversation keeps the prefix, so its per-episode bill should fall to the
control's ($0.004420). R216b measured **$0.00558** — **4%** below the front arm, and 26% *above* the control.

The premise was wrong in a way the arithmetic could have caught: **the block only moves on 23% of turns** (262 changes
in 1,116 renders). The front arm therefore re-buys its prefix on a change, not on a turn, and the per-turn price the
estimate assumed was never being paid. A placement saves what its cadence spends; a low cadence is a small saving
from any placement.

What survives is the comparison that matters and it is still the right call: same accuracy (p = 0.68), 4% cheaper,
and one message fewer in the system block. What does not survive is the sentence about 24%, which is now the third
forecast this lane has had to retract and the only one where the error was in a mechanism rather than in a
denominator.
### 34.246 `--check` refused the field and accepted the block that was missing entirely

Found while covering the new verification branch, not while reading the function. The board's prose rule is that a
submission declares whether it modified a prompt. `check` enforced it here:

```python
if methodology is not None:
    if isinstance(methodology, dict):
        verification = methodology.get("verification")
        if verification is not None:            # <- the requirement lives inside three guards
            require(isinstance(verification, dict), ...)
            require(isinstance(verification.get("modified_prompts"), bool), ...)
```

An entry with `verification: {}` was refused. An entry with **no `verification` key**, or with **no `methodology` at
all**, fell through every guard and was read as having nothing to state. The omission that says the least was the one
the check did not see.

The class of defect is the same one this lane keeps meeting: a requirement inside a guard is a requirement with a
silent exemption, and the exemption is always the emptier document. The repair moves the requirement out of the guard
and reads the field once:

```python
verification = (methodology or {}).get("verification") if isinstance(methodology, dict) else None
require(isinstance(verification, dict), "verification is not an object: an entry must declare modified_prompts …")
```

Three assertions now hold it — present-but-not-an-object, methodology present without the block, methodology absent —
and the file's coverage went from 99% lines to 100% statements with one branch remaining, the module's own exit.

### 34.247 A registration shipped without a header, so the gate that reads it was red on the previous commit

`prereg/R218b-pass4.md` opened with `# R218b — four attempts, and the reliability column`. Every other registration in
the repository opens with a `---` header block. `readPrereg` returned `{prereg: undefined, problems: [header: the file
must open with a --- header block]}`, and `prereg-pack.test.ts` — which iterates every file in `prereg/` — reported
`R218b-pass4.md: 1 problem(s)`.

It shipped anyway. The suite that catches it was run in this iteration, not the one that added the file, and the
push went out on the strength of a green CI from the *previous* push. Two things follow, and both are cheap:

1. the header is now written, with the fields the gate requires (`id`, `step`, `opened`, `arms`, `sample`, `gates`)
   and `## Prediction` / `## Refutation` sections whose bullets are each falsifiable — the previous prose had the
   falsification test but not in the section the validator reads;
2. the validator refuses angle-bracket placeholders anywhere in the body, which is why `--date <dispatch date>`
   became `--date 2026-11-25`; the placeholder rule is what makes a copied registration fail rather than pass with a
   template's text.

The audit finding is not the missing header. It is that **a repository-wide gate is only a gate if the pre-push path
runs it**, and the fix belongs there rather than in a resolution to remember.

### 34.248 A board name and a board path were the same argument
